events.title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
events.summary: Swedish defense giant Saab on Friday reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales, while orders trippled. New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor, up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier. "The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said. Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine. New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor. Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor. The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability. Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030. "The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement. Orders booked in the quarter also include a 10.1 billion kronor order for its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order for systems for German frigates. Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. Even with an ever-growing order book , booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.

events.title: Japan core inflation in September surges to its highest this year at 2.1%
events.summary: Headline inflation came in at 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which excludes prices of fresh food and energy was at 2.4%. Higher inflation could push the Bank of Japan for another rate hike this year. The increase appeared to be driven by price increases in the prices of durable goods and public utilities charges. Japan's Lower House began debating a bill on Tuesday to cut the consumption tax on food to 1% from 8% for two years, in an effort to contain price rises. Japan's core inflation in September hit its highest this year at 2.1%, overshooting analysts' expectations, pressured by steeper import costs due to a weak yen and the indirect impact of higher energy costs. Core inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food, was in line with estimates by economists polled by Reuters, and accelerated from the 1.7% in the prior month. Headline inflation came in at 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which excludes prices of fresh food and energy and is the Bank of Japan's preferred gauge, was at 2.4%. "That acceleration was noteworthy, not least because it occurred despite a sharp slowdown in fresh food inflation and continued energy deflation," said Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics. Rice prices notably declined 20.6% year on year, however, Surya said that this sharp drop could not prevent overall goods inflation from picking up to 2.8%, up from August's 2.6%. "One reason may be that the indirect effects of the energy shock are continuing to feed through, with inflation in 'other industrial products' rising to a 13-month high of 3.9%," Surya added. Consumer energy prices, which fell 0.6% in September, have mostly declined so far this year, despite the Iran war, due to subsidies handed out by the Takaichi administration. Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 declined 1.62% on Friday, while the yen strengthened to 156.15 against the dollar. Higher inflation could push the Bank of Japan for another rate hike this year, after a 25 basis points increase in September, as the central bank normalizes its monetary approach after decades of reflationary policy. Japan raised rates to a three-decade high of 1.25% in September. With underlying inflation back above the Bank of Japan's 2% target, the case for further tightening remains on solid ground, Surya said, forecasting that another hike will happen in December. Inflation appears to be driven by price increases in the prices of durable goods and public utilities charges, government data showed. Services inflation also increased slightly from 1.2% to 1.5%. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told parliament on Wednesday that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also contributing to price growth. Oil import costs have risen as Japan buys energy from more expensive U.S. sources and switches away from Middle Eastern suppliers oil due to the Iranian conflict. Weakness in yen is also making oil cost more for Japan. When Katayama was asked by a lawmaker whether the government's tax cut plan could conflict with the central bank's efforts to combat inflation with interest rate hikes, he said, "I see no gap between the view of the government and that of the BOJ," Reuters reported. On Tuesday, Japan's Lower House began debating a bill to cut the consumption tax on food to 1% from 8% for two years, public broadcaster NHK reported. It also includes provisions for support payments to workers based on income levels. Despite accelerating inflation, Japan is still wary of declaring a victory over deflation. On Friday, Japan's Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi reportedly said that the government needs to "comprehensively" look at factors driving inflation and GDP deflator figures before formally declaring an end to deflation.

events.title: Oil hits five-month high as global stocks wobble on AI fears; retail sales in Great Britain fall as shoppers cut back - business live
events.summary: Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears grow Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy. A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns. The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day. And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June. Jim Reid , of Deutsche Bank , says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market: As storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020. Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl. So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024. And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says: …In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%. Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%. Ipek Ozkardeskaya , an analyst at Swissquote , says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting. Given the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst. These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found. Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft , Google , Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results. Elsewhere this morning , British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%. An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday. Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said : The drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end. At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October. But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role. 9.30am BST: Flash PMI for UK, construction statistics for Great Britain 2025 11.30am BST: Russia’s interest rate decision 3pm BST: Flash PMI for US, University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence index 29m ago Government says it will 'slash red tape' to save businesses £800m 55m ago Brent crude hits $114 a barrel 1h ago UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites 1h ago Gloomy picture for retailers in Christmas quarter, economists warn 1h ago Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears grow While less red tape will be welcome news for small businesses, the chancellor is still facing pressure from bigger companies in the UK for more support.

events.title: Harry Kane hopes Ballon d’Or produces ‘special night’ in hometown
events.summary: Kane, who scored 73 goals for club and country last season, is among the favourites for award with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is hoping for a “special night” at Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in his hometown of London, where the England captain is the bookies’ favourite. The 33-year-old scored 73 goals for club and country last season, the second-best mark in history after Lionel Messi’s 82 in 2010-2011. list 1 of 4 FIFA President Infantino’s re-election endorsed in U-turn by Asian football list 2 of 4 FIFA announces USA to host first Women’s Club World Cup in 2028 list 3 of 4 Real Madrid’s complaint over La Liga chief’s Nazi slant sent to tribunal list 4 of 4 Man United captain Fernandes slams Carrick’s tactics after Como hammering But in continuing his habit of tormenting old foes Arsenal on Wednesday, the former Tottenham striker again demonstrated how complete a player he has become since moving to Germany in 2023. At one point, dropping back to take goal kicks to ignite Bayern’s attack, Kane also set up Alphonso Davies’s first-half equaliser with a pinpoint long-range pass. In the second half, Kane won and then converted a penalty, giving Bayern the lead before England teammate Declan Rice scored late to grab a share of the spoils for Arsenal with a 2-2 finish. Kane is odds-on to claim what would be his first Ballon d’Or, but the outcome is anything but certain in one of the most open fields in recent memory. The Bayern striker faces stiff competition from Spain’s World Cup-winning duo Lamine Yamal and Rodri along with France captain Kylian Mbappe and teammate Michael Olise. While Yamal and Mbappe in particular have taken to the airways to extol their suitability for the award, Kane has been typically circumspect despite constant media questioning. Repeatedly asked about his chances after Wednesday’s star showing, Kane said: “I try not to think about it. Obviously, it’s hard. “There’s rumours flying around, so you try and stay away from it. I’m going to try and enjoy Monday night as much as possible. It’s a big occasion and a big event.” Officially, there are three broad criteria upon which the Ballon d’Or is awarded: individual performances and impressive character, team performances and class/fairplay. In recent years, recipients have either won the Champions League and/or World Cup or have made their case through sheer weight of numbers. Kane clearly satisfies the latter criteria. Long criticised for a failure to win team trophies at Tottenham, Kane brought his total to five with Bayern after last year’s league and cup double, but the Bavarian giants’ dominance of Germany may count against him. Bayern made the semifinals of the Champions League, going out narrowly to eventual champions Paris Saint-Germain. England finished third at the World Cup with captain Kane scoring six times and laying on an assist. After scoring against Arsenal, Kane has at least one goal in each of his past 10 Champions League matches, one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record of 11. “Whenever you’re in any conversation with Ronaldo it means you’re doing something special, especially in this competition,” Kane said. Bayern coach Vincent Kompany praised Kane’s team-focused efforts, saying: “What made Harry happy the most in recent years is that he finally won his first team trophies here. “Now if he can crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be deserved for the way he plays for the team.” After Wednesday’s match, Rice had special praise for his international captain. “Harry is the clear winner [of the Ballon d’Or]. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he had is remarkable. “For a striker to play that pass for their first goal, then take the penalty how he did, … he’s ridiculous. He’s such a good player.” Former Three Lions midfielder Steven Gerrard on Wednesday joined Jude Bellingham in calling Kane “arguably the best England player there’s been” after Kane’s masterclass against Arsenal. Michael Owen was England’s last Ballon d’Or recipient, winning it in 2001, while in 1981 another striker, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, was the last Bayern player to claim the honour. “Monday could be a special night. We’ll have to wait and see,” Kane said on Wednesday. “I’m trying not to think about it too much because we have important games and another one on Sunday. “I know it’s a massive event. I am looking forward to it for sure. Hopefully, it’ll be a special night.”

events.title: Why is Gen Z revolting?
events.summary: From France to India, young people are taking to the streets over growing inequality, failing public services and bleak prospects for the future. Senior Lecturer in International Public and Social Policy at the University of Bristol. We are currently experiencing a wave of protests across Europe and beyond. Many have been dubbed “Gen Z protests”, with young people aged roughly 13 to 29 leading demonstrations over issues that particularly affect their generation. In France, protests started several weeks ago over deteriorating conditions in severely underfunded schools. They have been growing in strength, with between half a million and 800,000 protesters reportedly taking part in them across the country last weekend. In India, the Cockroach movement has emerged as the strongest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s increasingly authoritarian leadership. Last week, its leader was arrested as anger grew over the removal of more than 130 million names from electoral rolls. In Spain, anger has arisen over a broken housing system and laws that fail to protect households against eviction. First there was the forcible eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. Then parliament voted down widely popular legislation that would protect households against evictions, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call snap elections. Maricarmen died two weeks after her eviction. While the context in each country is different, grievances over inequality are at the centre of the current protest wave. This inequality has two aspects. One is about class and one is about generation. Across Europe, inequality has increased significantly since the 2008 crisis. This can be seen in growing income inequality and spiralling wealth inequality. The effect on people’s lives is worsened by the erosion of the once-proud European welfare states. High-quality public services for all were once meant to offer a guaranteed minimum standard of living and a meritocracy in which everyone had the chance to succeed. But years of austerity have eroded the state’s capacity to deliver good education, healthcare, social care and other services. The gradual retreat of the state exacerbates growing income and wealth inequalities, as some can pay for better services while many cannot. These growing inequalities are often felt more acutely by young people and are compounded by other challenges they face. In one area after another, young people are experiencing failures in governance that give them a bleaker outlook and much worse prospects than their parents and grandparents had. Underfunded education systems have no doubt played a significant part in the sharp decline in reading and maths skills laid bare by the most recent PISA results. A common explanation for this decline is worsening mental health and associated school absences, with social media often cited as a contributing factor. Another driver of declining educational attainment is the rapidly increasing use of AI. These are governance failures of another kind. Efforts to regulate both social media and AI have been slow and hampered by strong lobbying from tech giants. The AI revolution also affects young people as they seek to establish themselves in the labour market. While AI’s impact on employment is still in its infancy, it is already clear that entry-level work in particular is increasingly being done by machines. Housing is another essential aspect of life in which young people are disadvantaged. Today’s young people spend a much higher proportion of their income on rent than any previous generation did. This is, again, a failure of governance. On top of all this comes the climate crisis, which perhaps represents the largest governance failure of them all. The latest IPCC report illustrates starkly how much more precarious life will be for those born in 2020 than for their parents and grandparents. More equal societies would be much better placed to withstand the instability that climate change brings as they would offer collective forms of adaptation. Instead, the increasingly unequal societies we now see will put the burden of adaptation on individuals and households. In other words, multiple governance failures and the erosion of state capacity have created an explosive situation for young people. This is the anger being expressed on the streets of Paris, New Delhi, Rome and Madrid. Predictably, the main government response has been repression. This follows a global trend of criminalising and repressing protest. Whether through anti-protest laws, arrests or police violence, repression is on the rise. Repression sometimes succeeds in killing off protest movements. At other times, it instead inflames them. That has certainly been the case in both France and India so far. What is really needed are genuine efforts to address the inequalities and governance failures that motivate young people to take to the streets. Without them, political crises are bound to ensue.

events.title: Sundar Pichai says Google is far from the ‘end state’ of self-improving AI
events.summary: Sundar Pichai says Google's researchers are using AI to help build the next AI models. Hardik Chhabra/ The India Today Group via Getty Images Sundar Pichai said Google was still in the early phases of recursively self-improving AI. Researchers are working with AI agents to build better models, he said. Sergey Brin recently said Google was "starting to get onto that RSI treadmill." Google's AI models may be helping to build their successors, but CEO Sundar Pichai says the moment of fully self-improving AI is still a while away. Speaking on an episode of the "Big Technology Podcast" this week, Pichai said that Google researchers were using AI agents to assist them when building models, but caveated that it was still early days. "We are pretty far from the end state of RSI," said Pichai, referring to recursive self-improvement. "The right way to describe it is, you have RSI loops along with AI researchers in various aspects of model development. I would say you almost have agents helping AI researchers, in some automated way, work together to build these models." Pichai added that he expected that continuum to keep making progress into next year. Earlier this month, Google cofounder Sergey Brin said the company's Flash series of models, as well as Gemini 4, were demonstrating how AI was helping to build itself, and that Google was "starting to get onto that RSI treadmill." "And now our researchers and the model work hand in hand to make the next version of the model," he said. Brin has been increasingly involved in Google's Gemini efforts and has leveraged his power as cofounder to shift resources to projects he deems most effective, Business Insider previously reported. This has included pushing for more focus on RSI. A report from the firm Gladstone AI, published earlier this month , said that most researchers interviewed from companies including Anthropic and DeepMind believed RSI will start within the next three to 12 months, and possibly sooner without government intervention. In another moment on the "Big Technology Podcast," Pichai was asked about how much AI was being used to code internally. The company said in April that 75% of new code inside Google was generated by AI. "That number in our world today is like meaningless in the sense that every part of code we now touch is influenced by AI deeply," Pichai said. With Gemini 4 Argon, he said, people were going to tackle harder problems. He also said Google was seeing a one-third decrease in code rollbacks, where software is reverted to a previous version because of a bug or system issue. "And so I think people are writing code more productively, and better code with it," he said of AI tools. Pichai also uses AI to track Google's model development and internal discussions, he told the "Sources" podcast this week. Have something to share? events.title: Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war?
events.summary: With emergency stocks at multidecade lows, analysts say the world may have only a month or two if Hormuz shuts again. Oil prices have climbed towards their highest levels in five months as attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz mount and efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran are deadlocked. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, close to a five-month peak. list 1 of 4 US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award list 2 of 4 Trump says Musk restored Ukraine’s Starlink access amid Russia war list 3 of 4 Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections? list 4 of 4 Ilhan Omar plans to move out of her Washington DC home after federal raid A day earlier, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two tankers were “set ablaze” after hitting mines at what it called an illegal crossing point in the strait. Then, on Thursday, the IRGC said it hit seven more tankers although Washington dismissed the claim. In a statement, the IRGC said four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. In September, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized territory in Yemen close to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical chokepoint into and out of the Red Sea and a gateway to Egypt’s Suez Canal. The escalation came as the world’s emergency oil stocks, already tapped heavily since the Iran war began on February 28, sit at their lowest levels in decades. Al Jazeera put a question to analysts: If fighting resumes in full, the Strait of Hormuz is shut off completely and Houthi attacks choke off Bab al-Mandeb, how long could the world’s reserves last? What emergency oil reserves are there? Strategic oil reserves are stockpiles of crude oil and fuel held by governments or by companies on their behalf for use in a supply emergency. The International Energy Agency (IEA), which was established in 1974 after the Arab oil embargo, coordinates most of them. Its importing members must hold at least 90 days of net imports. China and India are not members. How much of the reserves has already been released this year? On March 11, days after the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to make 400 million barrels available from emergency supplies, more than double the volume released after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The US pledged 172.2 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and Japan 79.8 million, according to IEA figures. The SPR has since fallen to 283 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982, according to the US Department of Energy. Much of that oil was lent rather than sold and must be returned with extra barrels, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Far less than before the war began in February, and not all of it can be used. Aaron Kildow, a senior crude oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Al Jazeera that global strategic stocks excluding China and Iran have fallen by nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December 2025 with the US, Europe and Japan accounting for about 95 percent of the draw. He estimated that leaves only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves worldwide, excluding China’s stockpile, which is unlikely to be exported, and Gulf stocks, which could be cut off by a total closure of Hormuz. Nearly half of these available stocks are in Japan. Europe has about 76 million barrels uncommitted, but members such as Germany are holding some back for a local emergency, Kildow said. “Europe is the real wildcard, both on timing and willingness,” Kildow said. Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude stocks stand at 1.13 billion barrels, down from 1.23 billion in late February but still enough for about 80 days of refinery intake, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera. India’s reserves cover just eight days of its imports, the Reuters news agency reported. What would a full closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb mean? Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, or roughly 20 million barrels of oil a day, passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has increased the amount of crude it transports from its oilfields in the east to its Red Sea port of Yanbu in the west via the East-West Pipeline, thereby bypassing Hormuz. But there have been strikes on that pipeline, and tankers heading south from Yanbu must pass through Bab a-Mandeb, where the Iran-backed Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July. Only a confirmed 373,000 barrels a day of Saudi crude have transited Bab al-Mandeb so far this month, the lowest level since February, Xu said, with most Yanbu cargoes now heading north via Egypt instead.

events.title: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bites
events.summary: Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain. With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living. Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum. The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown. The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “ Burnham bounce ”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey. Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.” It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases. Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills. With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household. Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades. Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month , while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn. In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure. According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large. The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills. Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October. Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated. Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages. “Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.” The Treasury has been approached for comment.

events.title: UAE's G42 signs pacts to explore AI infrastructure in Greece
events.summary: Abu Dhabi-based G42 has signed an initial pact with public and private partners in Greece to explore artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country. The deal was part of the 18 memorandums of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships valued at €12.75 billion ($14.3 billion) signed between the UAE and Greece during an official visit to the European country by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. The pacts were signed at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum in Athens. G42 and five of its portfolio companies also signed initial agreements with Greek entities for government services, life sciences and smart cities, the company said in a statement on Friday. The agreements “mark an important milestone in expanding G42’s intelligence grid across Europe, bringing together advanced compute infrastructure and proven AI platforms for government and industry”, said Mansoor Al Mansoori, chief executive of G42 International. The intelligence grid covers the full AI value chain, from data centres and advanced compute to cloud infrastructure and industry-specific applications. Under agreements with Greece's Copelouzos Group, Khazna Data Centres and Core42 will explore the development of an AI factory in Greece, G42 said. Khazna will lead the development of the physical infrastructure, while Core42 will provide cloud and AI compute capabilities to support organisations in sectors including banking, telecoms, shipping and government. Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Prime Minister of the Hellenic Republic, have attended the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum in Athens and witnessed the announcement of 18 MoUs, agreements and commercial partnerships valued at €12.75bn. pic.twitter.com/BlVL1bvpwV — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 22, 2026 The deal “strengthens the country’s position as a strategic digital and energy hub in South-east Europe”, said Christos Copelouzos, chief executive of Copelouzos Group. The factory will support the digital transformation of the Greek economy, attract new investment and create highly skilled jobs, he added. G42 has been working to help countries build domestic AI capabilities. In February, G42 signed a framework agreement with a Vietnamese consortium to develop sovereign AI capabilities and cloud infrastructure across the South-East Asian country. Urban planning and life sciences G42 said its subsidiary Presight will also collaborate with Greece’s Ministry of Digital Governance to explore the use of AI-powered analytics and real-time intelligence capabilities focusing on urban mobility and municipal operations. The collaboration will initially focus on using agentic AI to support municipal waste management and water network monitoring through analytics, G42 said. “Cities generate enormous volumes of data every day, but their real value comes from turning that information into intelligence that improves how cities function and how people live,” said Thomas Pramotedham, chief executive of Presight. Meanwhile, Inception42 will work with Greece’s Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence to use agentic AI across government and education. Areas of focus include using AI-powered tools to support cabinet meetings and monitor progress against government priorities, training government officials to work with AI agents, and developing AI tutors and learning platforms to enhance educational outcomes. Tech-enabled health care company M42 has also signed an initial pact with Athens LifeTech Park (ALTP) for a partnership spanning life sciences research, genomics sequencing infrastructure, population genomics, clinical development and connecting institutional biobanks. The deal is aimed at supporting biomarker research in priority areas including oncology, rare genetic diseases and neuroscience, the statement said. The pact also covers a bilateral programme offering UAE life sciences start-ups a base at the ALTP Incubator for European market entry, and Greek and European ventures access to the UAE through M42’s network.

events.title: Europe needs a war economy
events.summary: With US support increasingly uncertain, Europe must mobilise its financial and industrial power to defend itself and counter Russia. Fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. For the past four-and-a-half years, the war on Europe’s doorstep has haunted policymakers. Yet they have treated it as a looming threat rather than one already eroding the very foundations on which Europe stands. Russia’s war has devastated much of Ukraine’s south and east, even as the front lines have shifted only slowly. For Europe, however, the challenge has never been confined to the battlefield. Supporting Ukraine and constraining Russia have tested the continent’s economic resources and political unity. Now, as United States President Donald Trump seeks to force a disadvantageous settlement on Kyiv and repeatedly threatens to withdraw US support, Europe faces the prospect of shouldering even more of that burden alone. Even if the latest crisis is averted, Europe can no longer assume that Washington will guarantee its security. It must develop the financial capacity to sustain Ukraine’s defence, the industrial strength to defend itself and the economic leverage to constrain Moscow. To meet these challenges, Europe must build a war economy. The past four years offer lessons in how Europe can finance such an effort, but also warnings about the divisions that could undermine it. The European Union has already been at the forefront of Ukraine’s recent financing, moving from an 18.1-billion-euro ($21bn) share of the G7’s $50bn Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) loans in 2024 to finalising a new 90-billion-euro ($100bn) loan this April, one that came without US commitment. Yet internal divisions remain over numerous issues, particularly as they pertain to constraining Russia. This month, the EU adopted its largest-ever round of sanctions listings. But while the measures added a record number of designations, they did little to broaden the scope of restricted activity and did not accelerate the phase-out of Russian energy imports, with pipeline gas imports still permitted until autumn 2027. European leaders have also expressed concern over Trump’s decision to waive new Russia-related sanctions as he seeks to grapple with the costs his foreign policy has wrought. However, the US-Israel war on Iran has, if anything, shown that Europe’s measures against Russian hydrocarbons could have gone further. Before February, some 20 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude and oil products and roughly 110 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year of liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz. By comparison, Russia exported about 6.5 million bpd of oil and products in September, and some 43bcm of LNG last year – about a third of Hormuz’s oil and two-fifths of its LNG. As the crisis continues and Trump seeks additional Russian supplies, Europe must complement its efforts to constrain Moscow with greater investment in its own security. The first and most important step is to establish a standing framework for joint EU borrowing – not only to finance Ukraine’s continued defence, but also to fund the defence industry Europe will need to sustain its own defence and, if necessary, prevail against future threats from Russia. Crisis begets innovation, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic, when EU member states pushed past their long-held aversion to mutualised borrowing, creating the 750-billion-euro NextGenerationEU recovery fund in 2020. The EU’s contribution to the ERA loans and this year’s 90-billion-euro facility, both financed by common EU borrowing, extended that logic to wartime finance. But these remain crisis-by-crisis improvisations. Deepening fiscal and capital markets union and building a genuine fiscal-military state would provide the foundations of Europe’s power and its ability to deter and win wars. The same logic plays out in the US today, where deep capital markets have given companies such as SpaceX, which invested heavily for years before seeing returns, the space to develop technologies such as its Starlink network that have reshaped modern warfare. The importance of this technology is now keenly felt on Ukraine’s battlefields, where Kyiv’s communications have rested on a network subject to the whims of one man, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Europe therefore needs the fiscal capacity to fund its own technological development and procurement. There are understandable jitters about the existing indebtedness of European states such as France and the United Kingdom. However, Russia’s frozen sovereign assets offer a potential way to support further borrowing. Divisions remain over using these assets, with Belgium, which hosts the lion’s share at Euroclear, opposing such a move over fears of Russian legal action and damage to its position in the global financial system. The bloc must come together to share that risk, which is overblown in any case .

events.title: The $18 billion Ford Foundation is getting its biggest overhaul since 2015 to fight autocracy—with about $700 million in grants expected in 2027
events.summary: Less than a year after leaving Yale Law School to run one of the wealthiest private foundations in the U.S. , Heather Gerken is putting her stamp on the Ford Foundation and its $18 billion endowment . The Ford Foundation on Thursday laid out a new strategy that reorients the 90-year-old grantmaker around what it calls the “preconditions for thriving democracies,” from the rule of law to trustworthy information and inclusive economies. Some have considered it the Ford Foundation’s most significant strategic shift since 2015, when former president Darren Walker focused the foundation around fighting inequality.  The announcement also lands less than two weeks before the midterm elections. “The Ford Foundation’s new vision is an evolution, not a revolution, of our work, and a reflection of this era’s rapidly changing global landscape,” Gerken said in a statement.  Despite the name, the foundation operates independently of Ford Motor Company. Edsel Ford (Henry Ford’s son) started the foundation in 1936 with $25,000, and from the start it was meant to stand apart from the car company. When Edsel died in 1943 and Henry Ford in 1947, the money they left vaulted the Ford Foundation to the top of the world’s foundations, according to a 2024 Fortune commentary co-written by Walker. Henry Ford II, Edsel’s son, later steered the foundation toward independence. The foundation took on a global mission, added trustees from outside the family, relocated to New York City in 1953, and ultimately sold its stake in the automaker, the foundation has said . Ford Motor Company has its own charitable arm, Ford Philanthropy , which is funded by the company’s earnings.  Today, the Ford Foundation is headquartered in New York, runs 10 offices overseas, and funds more than 2,300 grantees. Its endowment has grown from $13 billion in 2019 , when it was giving away more than $600 million a year, to $18 billion now, according to the foundation. Historically, the Ford Foundation supported civil rights lawsuits beginning in the late 1960s and helped build public interest law into a field of its own. Fighting autocracy and inequality The Ford Foundation frames its new plan as its answer to rising autocracy, widening inequality, and fading public trust. “Conditions have changed since our last strategy review, and we are marshaling all of our resources to respond to these new challenges while staying true to our legacy as a social justice foundation,” Gerken said in a statement. The foundation expects to award about $700 million in grants in 2027, a figure that could rise, a Ford Foundation spokesperson told the Associated Press . The organization is also changing how it hands out that money. It says it will make bigger grants, commit more money over multiple years, and expand general operating support. The foundation cites decades of research and learning showing that grantees with flexible, long-term funding were better prepared for the unexpected. “Throughout the strategy review process, it became abundantly clear that this unpredictable and volatile period requires much from philanthropy,” Nicholas Turner, Ford Foundation’s executive vice president of programs, said in a statement.  Grantmaking will now run through seven funding areas: democratic governance and the rule of law, inclusive economies, information as a public good, safety and justice, gender equality, global cooperation, and racial justice. It will roll out strategies for each in stages throughout 2027. The foundation will also create a dedicated racial justice fund. Its gender equality work will also expand to include the entire range of reproductive health care, and its information work will try to influence how digital tools get built, rolled out, and overseen.  The shift will cost some current grantees their funding. The foundation will eventually wind down certain programs, but Turner told the AP it was “too early to say” which would be affected. He promised the foundation would leave those areas “with respect and grace and care and support.” The foundation’s pivot comes as the Trump administration ramps up pressure on nonprofits. President Donald Trump threatened last year to revoke Harvard University’s tax-exempt status, and earlier this month the administration proposed a rule that would strip colleges and private schools of that status if they run race-based programs, the Chronicle of Philanthropy reported. Vice President JD Vance, while running for Senate in 2021, argued that major foundations should lose their tax exemptions and called the Ford Foundation and others like it “ cancers on American society .” Gerken stressed to AP that her organization’s democracy work is nonpartisan, pointing to the millions of dollars the Ford Foundation has put toward groups defending election results this year. “Our commitment to social justice and to communities that have been pushed to the margins, denied equal justice or economic opportunity, will remain a throughline across all of our areas of work,” Gerken said in a statement.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: CHIPS Act funding The U.S. Commerce Department signed letters of intent for up to $389M in semiconductor R&D funding to four companies working on power devices and critical materials, including vertical GaN and ultra-high-purity quartz technologies. Under the proposed agreements, the government will receive minority, nonvoting equity stakes as a condition of the awards. Company Award R&D Focus Helion Up to $175M High-voltage power semiconductors for fusion systems. Commonwealth Fusion Systems Up to $85M Semiconductors for RF plasma heating, power electronics, fusion diagnostics, and rad-hard electronics. Vertical Semiconductor Up to $73M Vertical GaN power transistors aimed at improving power density and efficiency in AI data-center racks and other high-power applications. Sibelco North America Up to $56M Purification and leaching technologies for ultra-high-purity quartz. Manufacturing capacity Nvidia expanded capacity agreements across its manufacturing supply chain , including deals with: Amkor to expand advanced packaging capacity in S. Korea, bringing the companies’ combined Arizona and S. Korea agreements to $3B. The expansion targets more than a fourfold increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. SPIL to expand optical-engine assembly capacity for CPO in Taiwan; Samsung Electro-Mechanics to expand ABF package substrate production in S. Korea; KYEC to build new semiconductor testing facilities in the U.S., with a $1.1B advance; IBIDEN to expand package substrate capacity in Japan; Unimicron to increase package substrate production in Taiwan. Advanced packaging and inspection UMC and AP Memory announced a technology and manufacturing collaboration to develop silicon-capacitor power-delivery solutions for AI and HPC systems, using UMC’s deep-trench-capacitor technology to move capacitance from the board into the interposer, substrate, or landside of advanced packages. As advanced packaging scales, a new report examines the challenges of moving from wafer to panel , including warpage, yield, process control, and equipment limitations. Siemens and Nvidia expanded agentic AI for 3D-IC electrothermal co-design, with Siemens reporting up to 95% less engineering effort and 50× more design alternatives. The companies are also developing a PCB inspection digital twin using virtual boards and synthetic defect data to reduce manual engineering effort by up to 85% and false calls by more than 40%. Fig.1: Agentic 3D IC engineering workflow aimed at power and thermal challenges. Source: Siemens AI data center power delivery Infineon and Nvidia expanded their collaboration on 800 VDC power architectures for AI data centers, focusing on GaN-based intermediate bus converters (IBCs) designed to improve power efficiency and density for high-power AI systems. Explore the shift to 800 VDC power delivery in AI data centers and the safety and reliability challenges posed by higher-voltage architectures. Standards Advanced Photonics Coalition released its first portfolio of five specifications and recommended practices for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics . Accellera released Functional Safety Language Standard 1.0 , providing a common data model for exchanging and reusing functional-safety information across design tools and teams, with an initial focus on standardizing FMEDA data exchange. China Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reportedly are upgrading their China NAND fabs to produce more advanced memory, with Samsung targeting 286-layer V9 NAND production in Xi’an and SK hynix moving toward 240-layer or higher NAND in Dalian, despite U.S. restrictions on chipmaking equipment exports, according to Reuters. ByteDance , Alibaba , and Tencent have reportedly placed more than $35B in orders for Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX PRO 5500 GPUs, according to Reuters. China’s access to AI computing power could nearly double to 8.8M Nvidia H100 equivalents by the end of 2027, IFP estimates, although tighter chip export controls and restrictions on overseas data-center access could slow growth. Memory Micron outlined a memory technology roadmap featuring vertical HBM stacked directly on logic, targeting volume production in 2028. Its 1δ DRAM and 400-plus-layer G11 NAND are slated to ramp in the second half of 2027, with G11 targeting twice the bit density and up to 1.5× the I/O speed of G9. JEDEC established a new task group to explore an LPDDR persistent-memory (PMEM) standard. Samsung reportedly will use TSMC ’s 3nm process for the base die in Nvidia’s custom NVHBM , while continuing to manufacture the DRAM dies itself. Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to standardize NVHBM base dies on TSMC’s process to simplify performance validation. Indium is expanding its Rome, New York, operations to restart U.S. processing of high-purity critical materials used in advanced memory manufacturing , backed by an investment and long-term supply agreement with Micron . Funding Tenstorrent raised $1.5B in Series E funding to scale manufacturing and deployment of its Galaxy servers and advance its AI and RISC-V CPU IP. Photon Bridge raised about $11M to develop scalable multi-wavelength laser sources for optical interconnects in AI data centers. Earnings Notable: Lam Research reported record quarterly revenue of $8.2B, up 54% YoY , with systems revenue rising 62% to $5.7B amid strong AI-driven wafer-fab equipment demand. Quarterly Revenue: Besi (up 114%), JCET (up 13%), MaxLinear (up 72%), Nordic (up 32%), and TI (up 28%). By the numbers Global wafer shipments are forecast to grow almost 12% in 2026, per SEMI . Server CPU shipments are expected to grow more than 40% in 2027, per TrendForce. ESD Alliance reported Q2 electronic system design revenue rose ~ 12% YoY. Q3 global PC shipments fell 21% YoY, as rising memory and component costs pushed up PC prices and led consumers to delay upgrades, per Counterpoint. events.title: 'Safe air' bill passes NT parliament following Inpex, Santos scandals
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Air pollutants from the gas industry will be monitored following a bill which passed NT parliament this week. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) A scheme to monitor and publicly report toxic air pollutants emitted by the gas industry on Darwin Harbour can now be set up, after a bill passed Northern Territory parliament. The NT Environment Minister says the scheme will be running by "the middle of next year" and will monitor volatile organic compounds such as cancer-causing Benzene. An independent politician and the NT opposition say details about the scheme should have been enshrined in law. Toxic air pollutants emitted by the gas industry on Darwin Harbour are set to be monitored and publicly reported after new laws passed Northern Territory parliament on Thursday. The Country Liberal Party (CLP) government's "safe air" bill allows an environmental monitoring scheme to be established, following a toxic emissions scandal involving Inpex and a decades-long methane leak and cover up by ConocoPhillips and Santos at the Darwin LNG facility. NT Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne said although there were already air quality monitoring stations around Darwin Harbour, they did not measure volatile organic compound emissions such as cancer-causing Benzene. Joshua Burgoyne says the scheme will be operational by the middle of next year. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) The only current measurements of volatile organic compounds in Darwin are being undertaken by gas companies, as required under their licence conditions. Darwin gas leak kept secret from public in 'national scandal' Documents reveal the scale of carbon pollution leaking from a Darwin LNG tank was like adding 8,300 new cars to the road every year. It is about to be filled again. Inpex is being prosecuted by the NT Environment Protection Authority after under-reporting benzene emissions by 13,000 per cent and toluene emissions — which can irritate the eyes, skin and respiratory tract — by 11,000 per cent. Under the scheme, which Mr Burgoyne said would be "in place" by "the middle of next year", six new monitoring stations around Darwin Harbour would measure for volatile organic compounds. "The will give Territorians certainty that the air they breathe is safe," he said. "We want them to know that as we industrialise the harbour, and as we continue to have companies that come to the Northern Territory, that we can continue to develop, and that it's safe to do so. The bill passed NT parliament on Thursday. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Mr Burgoyne said the scheme would be paid for by industry and "Territorians will not be paying", although the bill only states "specified persons or classes of persons" may be required to "make contributions towards all or part of the costs". The scheme will be overseen "by the environment department and the NT EPA", Mr Burgoyne said. "We, as a government, are saying to those that want to come to the Territory and obviously put carbon dioxide and other volatile organic compounds into the air, that we want to ensure that it is monitored. "That we can monitor how much of that is going into the Darwin airshed, so that we can tell whether or not we can continue to industrialise." The environment department and EPA will oversee the scheme. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Both a crossbench MLA and the opposition have criticised the government for not creating laws about the scheme in the bill. Independent Justine Davis said "it beggars belief that a bill with 'safe air' in the title contains no definition of safe air". "[There is] no clarity about what toxins will be measured, no information about where monitoring will take place, and what happens to companies who do the wrong thing," she said. "Both [Mr Burgoyne] and the department have said they are committed to safe air for Territorians and being transparent about it, so it's hard to understand why none of that is actually spelled out in the bill. "Instead, the detail will be left to [departmental] regulations, which can be written behind closed doors and changed at the discretion of a minister." Justine Davis says the scheme should be governed by laws, not regulations. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Ms Davis said the NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment revealed consultation about the scheme had so far only been undertaken with industry. "'Trust us' is not good enough when we are talking about the same industry that under-reported its cancer-linked benzene emissions by 13,000 per cent in 2025." Manuel Brown has called for pollution limits.

events.title: Europe wants more than promises from American tech
events.summary: Margot Edelman – Global Tech Practice Lead, Edelman Camilo Lascano Tribin – Senior Director, Tech Advisory, Edelman European businesses are questioning how much control they have over the technology they depend on. For American tech companies, that creates a growing test of credibility, with consequences for how they compete and earn trust.  “We want to be sure nobody has a kill switch.” That was European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen’s warning when Brussels unveiled its latest technology sovereignty proposals in June. It captured a concern increasingly relevant to European businesses: what happens if access to the American technology supporting critical operations is disrupted by decisions made outside Europe?  Europe relies heavily on US cloud infrastructure, and the Commission is turning concerns about that dependence into measurable requirements. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework assesses providers against 48 criteria covering legal control, data, operations and supply chains. Although developed for public procurement, the Commission encourages private organisation to use the framework too. Its proposed Cloud and AI development Act would extend sovereignty assessments across public-sector cloud services, with higher requirements for more sensitive uses. Virkkunen has acknowledged that some of the highest levels would be difficult for American providers to reach because of US legal obligations.  For American technology companies, this presents a growing commercial and reputational challenge. They have spent years demonstrating what their technology can do. European customers increasingly want to understand what providers can guarantee when political circumstances change. The answers depend on how services are operated and the commitments companies are prepared to make. Those business decisions are shaping the credibility of corporate promises long before they are communicated.  Three areas show how these expectations are changing.  The first is the control European customers retain over their technology.  In April this year, a European consortium led by Belgian telecommunications company Proximus won one of four contracts together worth up to €180 million under the Commission’s sovereign cloud procurement programme. The consortium uses services from S3NS, a French company controlled by Thales that operates Google Cloud technology. American technology therefore qualified for the Commission’s own sovereign cloud requirements through a European operating structure.  The three providers built around European technology received a higher sovereignty rating. That distinction shows both the opportunity for American technology and the limits imposed by remaining dependencies. How a company structures its service affects the control it can offer customers and the strength of the claims it can make about that control.  The second is what happens when a provider’s commitments are tested.  Microsoft offers one useful example. In April 2025, Brad Smith announced that Microsoft would challenge any government order to suspend its European cloud operations through available legal avenues, including the courts. The company subsequently made that commitment legally binding in contracts with European national governments and the Commission.  Smith also explained what would happen if a legal challenge ultimately failed, including continuity arrangements with European partners and backup copies of Microsoft’s code held in Switzerland. For the technology leader responsible for keeping essential services running, these details provide a basis for assessing what protections exist and what happens in an extreme scenario. For executives, they make the risks attached to a critical supplier easier to understand. The commitment does not eliminate every possible disruption, but it gives customers a clearer account of what Microsoft has undertaken to do and where the limits remain.  The third is the substance of a company’s presence in Europe.  The Commission’s sovereignty framework considers the extent to which investment, jobs and value creation remain within the EU and European Economic Area. Public trust creates a separate pressure towards meaningful local commitment.  Edelman’s 2026 Trust Barometer found that people trusted companies headquartered in their own country more than foreign-headquartered companies in every market examined for that comparison. In Germany, 63 percent trusted German-headquartered companies, compared with 34 percent for companies headquartered abroad. When asked how a company from a country they distrust could earn their trust locally, respondents globally most frequently identified long-term community investment and local hiring.  These findings point to the importance of substantive local relationships for multinational companies. The Barometer describes a “polynational” approach centred on long-term commitments to the communities in which companies operate. For American technology providers, that raises questions about how their European presence is reflected in the business itself, including where they invest and how much authority sits within their local operations.  As sovereignty becomes measurable, claims about European control are becoming easier to challenge. Procurement teams can assess them against published criteria, while journalists and competitors can examine the dependencies behind them. Companies that describe their services as sovereign without being clear about those dependencies risk accusations of sovereignty-washing.  This is where reputation and communications become part of the business decisions. The credibility of a company’s European commitments depends on the operating arrangement and protections behind them. Communications leaders can help organisations anticipate the expectations those decisions will need to meet, bringing an understanding of customer concerns and public trust into the discussion before commitments are made.  American technology companies have established what their products can deliver. Europe’s changing expectations mean they now need to demonstrate what they can guarantee when circumstances change. Their reputation will increasingly depend on how clearly they explain those guarantees and how well the underlying business decisions support them.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Maradona death: Verdict in trial to be delivered on December 22
events.summary: The trial of seven healthcare professionals accused of negligence in Maradona’s death concludes, December verdict set. The verdict in the trial over the 2020 death of Argentinian football legend Diego Maradona will be delivered on December 22, the court announced Thursday, after six months of hearings. The trial of seven healthcare professionals accused of negligence in the star’s death concluded on Thursday with brief statements from Maradona’s daughter and several of the defendants. list 1 of 4 Maradona doctor was made ‘scapegoat’ for his death, Argentinian court told list 2 of 4 Prosecutors in Maradona death trial seek sentences up to 12 years list 3 of 4 Maradona’s ‘Hand of God’ ball from Mexico sells for $3.35m list 4 of 4 Diego Maradona’s doctors missed renal red flag, Argentinian court told “I hope my father receives the justice he deserves … like anyone else,” said Dalma Maradona, her voice breaking with emotion. The main defendant in the case, Leopoldo Luque, Maradona’s primary doctor, declared: “I am innocent.” Maradona died at age 60 from heart failure coupled with pulmonary oedema. The larger-than-life star, who had a history of substance abuse, was found dead in his bed on November 25, 2020. He was at his residence in Tigre, north of Buenos Aires, rented for his convalescence following minor neurosurgery. His death plunged the country into mourning in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. Lawyers for Maradona’s doctor say he was made ‘scapegoat’ The trial , which began in April, included testimony from more than 70 witnesses. Prosecutors requested prison sentences ranging from four to 12 years for six of the seven defendants, with the heaviest sentence – 12 years – sought for Luque. In closing arguments on Wednesday, Luque’s defence lawyers rejected the prosecution’s argument that Maradona’s death was foreseeable, calling their client a “ scapegoat ” in the case. Throughout the trial, Luque was by far the most combative defendant, speaking several times when he felt he was being implicated. His legal team played audio recordings, presented scientific articles and even a video of Maradona’s autopsy, provoking the anger of the footballer’s daughters. “It’s easy to attack me because I’m the one who had the most contact with Maradona,” Luque said in court, asserting that “the only one who would defend me would be Diego. “I cared deeply for him, I loved him, he was my idol and my friend,” he said. The case has revolved around whether the doctors’ decision to allow Maradona to convalesce in a private home, instead of in a hospital, was negligent. The prosecution pointed to the near-total absence of medical equipment, such as a hospital bed, defibrillator or a quickly available ambulance, as evidence of what they presented as the defendants’ dereliction of duty . Several medical experts testified that Maradona’s caretakers failed to react to key warning signs – he was suffering from oedema, tachycardia and had difficulty breathing – in the lead-up to his death.

events.title: What smart people are saying about the cybersecurity 'vulnerability tsunami' that's roiling the internet
events.summary: Cybersecurity flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language. Annette Riedl/picture alliance via Getty Images Executives and AI analysts alike are warning of major cybersecurity threats. Experts say critical systems, from energy and water to healthcare, may be especially exposed. Here's what smart people are saying about the biggest threats to the internet at the moment. CEOs and AI analysts alike are sounding the warning on cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could not only expose large swaths of personal data but also allow bad actors to wreak havoc on the internet. On Wednesday, OpenAI said its agents helped detect severe cybersecurity vulnerabilities . Two "critical" flaws were found in the infrastructure of PHP , an open-source programming language that 70% of websites use. Here's what smart people are saying about the biggest cybersecurity threat of the moment. Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer Anthropic's deputy security chief, Jason Clinton, warns that a "vulnerability tsunami" is coming — and says critical infrastructure hasn't caught up. Clinton posted on X on Wednesday about the need to "patch critical infrastructure" before core network vulnerabilities get exploited. On Thursday, he issued another warning to companies. "As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better," he wrote. "Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)," he added. Andrew Curran, AI analyst Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, weighed in on several cybersecurity threats from Wednesday to Thursday. "Regarding potential attacks on energy, food, and water infrastructure, the threat is quite real. Someone is currently probing infra and feeling it out, it is an active threat. Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case," Curran wrote on Wednesday in response to an NSA cybersecurity advisory about threat actors. On Thursday, Curran also highlighted a hack of Quest Diagnostics, which he said serves "roughly half" of the US's hospitals and physicians. Matt Shumer, AI investor In February, Matt Shumer, the former CEO of Hyperwrite, published a viral essay on his website titled "Something Big Is Happening," in which he warned of large-scale disruptions wrought by AI that could upend the world order. Shumer published another essay on Thursday on his website and LinkedIn, this time titled "The Internet Is Under Attack. Here's How to Protect Yourself and Your Family." "Right now, as you read this, swarms of AI agents are likely trying to break into the websites you use. Not one of them. Many of them," Shumer wrote. "We are in the middle of the biggest cybersecurity moment in years." This is what could happen, per Shumer's post: Your information leaks, so scammers know your name, birthday, address and bank, and their calls and texts sound real. Your accounts get taken over through some site you used once, years ago, with the same password you use everywhere. And the things you depend on, like an app, a pharmacy or a store's website, go down for days. To be clear: this is ongoing, but the worst-case scenarios people are most scared of haven't happened. I hope they never do. But it's better to be safe than sorry, especially since this is going to keep happening. Shumer also outlined four ways people can protect themselves, including updating all their software and staying off sites they're unfamiliar with while companies and websites alike make their security updates. He also advises that people protect their bank accounts by being extra cautious about any and all codes and links that they receive. People should also "close the doors you aren't using" by unplugging smart gadgets and deleting apps that aren't being utilized. "Every connected thing is another way in," Shumer wrote. Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff Business Insider Marc Benioff agreed with Anthropic's Jason Clinton in an X post on Thursday. "Jason is 100% right. Code red," Benioff wrote, along with a red alarm emoji. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg owns 13% of Meta but controls 61% of its votes. California’s wealth tax would bill him on the 13%
events.summary: California voters will decide on Nov. 3 whether the state’s billionaires should pay a one-time 5% tax on their net worth. Some of them have already left, like Peter Thiel and Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. They join seven billionaires so far who have publicly moved out of the state, taking about $540 billion, or 30% of the state’s billionaire wealth. Meanwhile, others like Jensen Huang are staying. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg looked, up until now, as if he would also join Huang in staying in the state where his company is headquartered. But Meta’s new SEC filing that posted this week shows that’s in part because of the key difference between owning a company and controlling it. What he owns and what he controls Ownership is a share of a company’s value. Control is a share of its votes. For most shareholders they are the same because each share carries one vote. At Meta, they are not. Zuckerberg holds mostly Class B shares, which carry 10 votes each. Ordinary Class A shares carry one. So of every $100 of Meta’s value, about $13 is his, but of every 100 votes, about 61 are his, according to a filing Meta released Wednesday. That majority lets him elect the entire board and decide nearly every shareholder vote. A wealth tax bills the first number—and to pay it, Zuckerberg would have to sell stock, thereby losing control. When Class B shares are sold, they turn into one-vote Class A shares, so every sale to pay the tax would cut into his control. According to the filing, Meta’s board feared that loss of control. According to the committee of independent directors that negotiated with Zuckerberg, they found he was “not on the verge of losing voting control.” But it named the wealth tax as one of the main reasons that could change, saying it “has the most significant impact because it would require him to sell shares, or at least borrow against them.” The filing says he “could become liable for a significant, multi-billion dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company.” Zuckerberg also argued that ownership and control don’t need to line up. At an Aug. 26 meeting, he “questioned why the preservation of the status quo with respect to the ratio of his voting control to his economic interest in the Company should be a consideration for the Special Committee, citing precedent in other companies where relatively small economic ownership nevertheless conveyed founder voting control,” the filing read. That’s why the committee proposed in August a dividend of new non-voting stock that would be payable “if, and only if, California Proposition 40 became law and a tax payment by Mr. Zuckerberg became due and payable,” sized to cover his bill. Zuckerberg wanted more, saying “he did not wish to go through additional protracted negotiation processes in the future if taxes similar to California Proposition 40 were proposed in other jurisdictions.” Under the final deal, which Fortune reported Wednesday , every shareholder gets one non-voting Class C share for each share they hold. The committee wrote that Zuckerberg could immediately sell 20% of his new shares, “representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because he takes a $1 salary, the committee said, the tax would otherwise leave him “effectively be paying to serve as the Company’s chief executive officer while residing in California.” The board didn’t want a remote CEO Unlike the billionaires who left, Zuckerberg runs a company whose board wanted him in the building. In July, the committee said it was “crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.” It said it “was mindful about the difficulties the Company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Mr. Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the Company’s management team.” On Sept. 6, Zuckerberg told the committee he “would need to begin taking steps by mid-September in order to establish residency outside California by mid-October.” The final agreement commits him to stay in California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years, “absent material unforeseen circumstances.” Meta told Fortune the new stock is mainly about financing its AI spending. In its earnings release , the company said the new class would “provide Meta the ability to finance its growth and help the company remain a leader among fierce competition both domestic and international.” It credits Zuckerberg for Meta’s stock rising more than 1,700% since its IPO, against about 495% for the S&P 500, and says the stock “will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception.” “We created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders,” chief financial officer Susan Li said on Wednesday’s earnings call . “We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.” The filing says management’s forecasts “showed the Company’s need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026.” It also acknowledges the new stock “could substantially prolong the duration of Mr. Zuckerberg’s voting control of our Company.” Class A shareholders did not vote, because Zuckerberg “has the ability to unilaterally approve” the change. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
