events.title: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns
events.summary: Published 23 October 2026, 00:04 BST The lights will stay on this winter, the body in charge of Britain's electricity network has said after concerns were raised by some of its engineers. The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months. However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation. NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days". It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine. "While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO. In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables. The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears. The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations. Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas. However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator. Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced. It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult". The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership. Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said. The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run". One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June. This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation. Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right". Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them". "I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added. events.title: High Court orders car dealer to pay rival $300k after failed suit over Ferrari deal
events.summary: The dispute involved a Ferrari 296 GTB plug-in hybrid (pictured), as well as other luxury cars including Lamborghinis and a Bentley. High Court found Ong falsely claimed a $920,000 Ferrari buyer, but Wu won no damages because he could not prove his losses. Wu must pay Ong $300,000 over an aborted Lamborghini deal, while Ong still owes Wu $250,000 under a separate Ferrari sales agreement. Justice Kristy Tan said Ong’s stance was unreasonable and urged both sides to “act fairly and sensibly” in the dispute over luxury cars. SINGAPORE – A car dealer was found by the High Court to have falsely claimed he had found a $920,000 buyer for a Ferrari, but he still escaped paying damages because the man who sued him failed to prove his losses. In an unusual twist, the claimant, Wu Chong, the sole proprietor of Allmotoring.sg, was ordered to pay the defendant, Ong Bee Hong, the sole proprietor of Trusty Leasing, $300,000 in a counter-claim arising from a separate dispute over an aborted Lamborghini transaction. This was despite the fact that Ong still owes Wu $250,000 under the Ferrari sales agreement. Justice Kristy Tan, in a written judgment on Oct 22, described Ong’s refusal to allow the $250,000 to be deducted from the award as unreasonable, and urged him and his lawyers to “act fairly and sensibly”. The dispute involved a Ferrari 296 GTB plug-in hybrid, as well as other luxury cars, including Lamborghinis and a Bentley. Wu had a 20 % stake in the Ferrari. The remaining 80 % belonged to a man identified in court documents as Toh Wee Keong. Toh wanted to sell the car in January 2025 and asked Wu to market it, initially targeting a price of $980,000. Wu also approached Ong to help find a buyer, saying the desired price was between $920,000 and $980,000. On or around Jan 15, 2025, Ong told Wu that he had found a buyer for $920,000, although this was not true. Wu then provided documents and prepared sales paperwork for the transaction. The documents recorded a sale from Allmotoring to Trusty for $250,000 for the car body only. This agreed price between dealers for an unregistered car excludes taxes such as the additional registration fee . A second agreement recorded a sale from Trusty to Orizon Motorcycles for $260,000, also for the car body only. The Ferrari was delivered on Jan 27, 2025, to a house in Jalan Tani. Wu said he believed it was the ultimate buyer’s residence and felt pressured by Ong’s requests to deliver the car there. The property was, in fact, the home of Lim Soon Heng Terence, Orizon’s sole director and shareholder. The car was later registered in the name of Ong’s girlfriend Pee Hwee Kim on Feb 11, 2025, with a $348,000 hire-purchase loan. Ong told the court the Ferrari was actually his. He used Pee’s name because he had previously been bankrupt and it was easier to obtain financing that way. He added that he paid the loan instalments. In October 2025, Pee sold the Ferrari to Atoll Discovery for $878,000. After the loan was redeemed, $557,946.62 in net proceeds went to Pee. She transferred $400,000 to Ong and retained the remaining $157,946.62 to partly offset a personal loan of $180,000 that Ong owed her. Wu later sued Ong, Lim and Pee, alleging deceit, misrepresentation, conversion, conspiracy and unjust enrichment. Justice Tan found that Ong had falsely claimed in January 2025 that he had found a buyer willing to pay $920,000 for the Ferrari. She found that Ong made the claim to get Wu to act on it, and that Wu had relied on it when handing over documents and transferring the car. But she dismissed Wu’s claims because he could not establish the loss required to obtain damages. He did not identify any other potential buyer who would have paid at least $920,000, nor did he provide sufficient evidence to establish what the Ferrari would have been worth had the alleged wrongdoing not occurred. Justice Tan noted that even Ong and Pee had eventually sold the car for $878,000. The judge cited a Court of Appeal reminder that a claimant must prove both the existence and amount of damage. Otherwise, even a claim that might otherwise have succeeded could fail, and the claimant could find that, after incurring legal costs, “the game has not been worth the candle”. In the lawsuit, Ong had counter-claimed for $300,000 paid to Wu as a deposit for an orange Lamborghini Urus in a transaction that was later aborted. Wu argued that the sum had been offset by money Ong owed him from other vehicle transactions involving another Lamborghini and a Bentley, but the judge found that Wu had not established the alleged set-offs. Ong therefore succeeded in his counter-claim for the full $300,000. However, the judge noted that both men accepted that the $250,000 Ferrari sales agreement was genuine and legally binding. Ong consequently remained legally obliged to pay Wu that sum. Tan asked Ong’s lawyer whether the $250,000 could be deducted from the $300,000 award, leaving Ong with a net recovery of $50,000.

events.title: Volvo Cars to cut 2,500 jobs as third quarter swings to loss
events.summary: Volvo Cars will cut 2,500 jobs, mostly in Sweden, amid competition from Chinese automakers and weaker US sales. Volvo Cars will cut 2,500 jobs, mostly in Sweden, as it faces weak demand, tariffs and fierce competition from Chinese automakers. The company reported a third-quarter adjusted operating loss of 3.7 billion kronor, down from a 5.8 billion kronor profit a year earlier. Volvo will cut another 5 billion kronor in costs by end-2027, after scrapping full-year guidance and warning of a tougher market. STOCKHOLM – Volvo Cars said on Oct 23 it would cut a further 2,500 jobs, mostly in Sweden, after plunging to a much bigger-than-expected third-quarter operating loss, sending its shares down almost 30%. The company, majority-owned by China’s Geely Holding, has struggled with uneven demand for electric vehicles, mounting tariff pressures and deteriorating market conditions in China. The automaker reported an operating loss of 3.7 billion Swedish kronor (S$476.7 million) in the quarter, down from a profit of 5.8 billion kronor a year earlier. Citi analysts said the consensus forecast was for a loss of 724 million kronor. “The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs a decisive reinforcement,” chief executive officer Hakan Samuelsson said. Volvo said that, in addition to previously announced 23 billion kronor cost-cuts , it would reduce indirect spending and variable costs by a further 5 billion kronor, with the savings expected to be realised by the end of 2027. The latest measures will affect about 6% of Volvo’s workforce, including around 2,000 jobs in Sweden, through the termination of consultant contracts, natural attrition and targeted exit packages. The cuts come on top of 3,000 job reductions announced earlier. Samuelsson told Reuters the latest cuts should be completed by mid-2027, although he did not rule out further measures if the turnaround plan falls short. Volvo, which earlier in October scrapped its guidance for full-year sales volume and cash flow, said it would prioritise margins over market share in China rather than engage in aggressive price competition with domestic rivals. It plans to take a similar approach in the US. Volvo’s gross margin, a metric closely watched by investors to gauge the impact of tariffs and discounting, came in at 14.7% in the third quarter, compared with 20.4% in 2025. The group’s share price hit a record low this week and are down more than two-thirds so far in 2026 . REUTERS

events.title: FIFA President Infantino’s re-election endorsed in U-turn by Asian football
events.summary: Support crucial from president of 47-nation AFC, who had been a critic of Gianni Infantino over his failed private investment plan. The head of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says the body is endorsing Gianni Infantino for another term as FIFA president. The AFC has 47 member confederations. Even if all the members do not follow Friday’s direction from Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, those that do could be key to guaranteeing another mandate for Infantino, who leads the governing body of world football and is seeking a fourth term. list 1 of 4 Can Harry Kane end England’s 25-year wait for a Ballon d’Or winner? list 2 of 4 Real Madrid’s complaint over La Liga chief’s Nazi slant sent to tribunal list 3 of 4 Maradona doctor was made ‘scapegoat’ for his death, Argentinian court told list 4 of 4 Man United captain Fernandes slams Carrick’s tactics after Como hammering The FIFA election is in March. The deadline for candidates to file against Infantino is November 18, and so far, none has filed. Sheikh Salman, speaking at the AFC’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement. “We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling, and I think your commitment is clear as well.” Addressing his remarks to Infantino, Sheikh Salman indicated not every AFC member would go along with the endorsement but most will. “My feeling is, I’m sure, the feeling of most of my members,” the AFC president said. “And I’ve said that to you.” This is an abrupt turnaround for Sheikh Salman. Just over two months ago, the AFC joined the football governing bodies of Europe and that of North and Central America in saying Infantino had committed a “ fundamental breach of trust ”. Infantino apologised last week in Zurich to FIFA’s 37-member ruling council, which he chairs, for “mistakes” he made in assembling a now-scrapped $4.2bn plan to sell a stake in FIFA events, including the World Cup, to private investors. Sheikh Salman referenced the differences with Infantino in his speech but glossed over any details. “Gianni, I want to make it clear: Yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past,” Sheikh Salman said. “But let’s not relate the two things together. I think the last few days we met in Zurich, you made it clear that there’s a true understanding between us.” “The past I’m sure is part of our history,” he added, “We’ve all, I’m sure, learned important lessons from it. What matters now is how we move forward together. I think everyone has questions, and I’m sure the answers will be available, whether to us in Asia or the rest of the world. ” Infantino’s electioneering around the globe FIFA’s media office has been promoting Infantino’s travels around the world, seeking votes in exchange for millions of more dollars in financial support for small and large football countries. “Thank you for being here,” Sheikh Salman said to Infantino. “I know you have been everywhere. I don’t know how you can do it. But I’m sure that you set a record for being in almost every country.” Sheikh Salman then joked that, perhaps, Infantino had a “clone”. That drew a laugh. But the largest applause came at the end of his brief address when he again repeated his support for Infantino. “As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni,” Sheikh Salman added. “I want to make that clear today.” Infantino took the podium after Sheikh Salman and kept his remarks light. But he did acknowledge some errors. “When you do many things, you do – hopefully, as we did, many good things – you do some mistakes as well,” Infantino said. “The important, however, is, as you said, to learn, to learn always from the experience, from the mistakes, to apologise, to move ahead, to come together, to unite, to build for our future, for your future.” The largest applause came as he mentioned how, under his leadership, millions more are flowing to FIFA’s patronage network. “Before I started as FIFA president, each of you – some of you are still [here] and still remember that time – each of you was receiving $1m every four years” Infantino said. “As of the first of January of next year, it will be $25m.”

events.summary: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick is under growing pressure, but club legend Wayne Rooney takes aim at players. Manchester United great Wayne Rooney has labelled the current squad “babies” and “selfish” after a humiliating Champions League capitulation and post-match criticism by Bruno Fernandes of manager Michael Carrick. Carrick’s men are 13th in the Premier League before Sunday’s visit by Bournemouth and could drop into the bottom three if results go against them this weekend. list 1 of 3 Can Harry Kane end England’s 25-year wait for a Ballon d’Or winner? list 2 of 3 Real Madrid’s complaint over La Liga chief’s Nazi slant sent to tribunal list 3 of 3 Ballon d’Or: Which countries and players have won the most awards? With the club beset by infighting and off to their worst domestic league start for decades, Carrick was left clinging to his job after the 4-1 defeat at Como on Wednesday. events.title: EU entering winter with lowest gas reserves on record, IEA boss warns
events.summary: Al Jazeera interviews Fatih Birol in Berlin as the Iran war disrupts global energy supplies. Berlin, Germany – Europe is entering winter with historically low gas reserves and cannot withstand further supply shocks, Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, has warned, as the US-Israel war on Iran disrupts global supply chains. Speaking to Al Jazeera on the sidelines of an international conference in Berlin on Wednesday, Birol said all regions are being hit by energy disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but that Europe is particularly vulnerable and will likely face rising costs of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in the coming months – even if peace returns to the Gulf today. list 1 of 4 Qatar warns global energy shockwaves from Iran war have yet to peak list 2 of 4 US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack list 3 of 4 As Macron visits Gulf, can France forge its own energy-for-security future? list 4 of 4 EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows “The best day for a ceasefire would have been yesterday,” the energy economist, whose agency advises wealthy member nations and coordinates emergency responses, said. “Normally before the winter, European countries have a lot of gas stocks, but the gas stocks we have while we are entering this winter are much lower than historical averages,” he said, adding that Europe’s gas is competing with that of Asian countries, which are even more dependent on the Middle East. “I think if we have a harsh winter, we may see higher prices of natural gas in Europe,” Birol said, adding that the increasingly political nature of energy adds to the uncertainty. “Life will not be easy for Europe this year and also next year.” European nations have long relied on imported gas to generate electricity for industries and warm homes in the freezing winter. Nearly a 10th of the continent’s LNG transited through the Hormuz Strait before the war. However, Iran’s attacks on vessels have plummeted imports. As the winter chill settles, the European Union’s natural gas storage is only 72 percent full, down from the usual 90 percent. The shortfall is equivalent to the energy needed to power 10 to 12 million homes, analysts say. EU energy ministers are now mulling over whether they should ask households and businesses to ration consumption, according to news reports. Birol said he had long thought about the dangers of relying on the Strait of Hormuz. In fact, he said, his standard question to recruits seeking to join his agency was often: What would they do if the strait shuts down today? The fallout has hardly come as a surprise. The flare-ups in the alternative Bab al-Mandeb strait, he added, have only worsened things. “World leaders, how do they think?” Birol, who was born in Turkiye, said in his usual measured tone. “I am really disappointed that governments didn’t take the necessary measures. Now, everybody is in a hurry, taking measures; the Middle East countries are building new pipelines, expanding the new pipelines that are bypassing the Strait of Hormuz … but in my view, these efforts should have been done much earlier.” Europe’s historical over-reliance to blame The EU, whose ageing refineries have processed less crude in recent years, also faces shortages of imported refined products such as the diesel that powers the bloc’s trucking, agricultural and industrial sectors. Birol said Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were also behind a looming diesel scarcity. About a third of Russian deliveries have stopped coming, he said. When the Group of Seven (G7) nations agreed to push 400 million barrels of crude and diesel from their strategic reserves in March, it was Birol who coordinated how those emergency stocks reached global markets – the third time he has had to oversee emergency stock releases since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. For years, the energy economist said, his agency warned that the bloc was too tethered to Russia’s fuel, and that it had turned away too early from nuclear-generated power, which gave countries domestic leverage. When Russia invaded Ukraine, his warnings manifested after Moscow cut gas supplies in retaliation for sanctions. The EU plans to permanently phase out Russian gas, but amid the Gulf crisis, members like France have again stepped up orders. Industry experts say emergency reserves that hit the market have limited use, as some estimate only a few months will be covered. But Birol argued that his agency recorded real impact – a $20 drop in soaring oil prices immediately after the G7 countries agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel earlier this month. Prices are, however, on the rise again. Gas has surged by 140 percent since February, and Brent crude is trading well above $100. Whatever happens now, the war will be felt for months, Birol pointed out, adding that it has irrevocably altered how energy will travel around the world.

events.title: ‘We’ve lost a basic sense of politeness’: UK readers reveal daily reality of public transport
events.summary: Regular users detail their frustrations – and question whether Andy Burnham’s crackdown on antisocial behaviour will actually work Andy Burnham has announced a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport, including “headphone dodgers” who play loud music . “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone,” Burnham said in a statement. “It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.” Six people share their views on Burnham’s new campaign and recount their experiences of antisocial behaviour on public transport. ‘It saddens me that we have lost a basic sense of politeness’ I live in London and commute daily on the tube. Even yesterday, sitting next to me was a guy playing videos out loud, which is the most common issue. I’m interested in what has caused a sudden change to our social contract that allows people the psychological safety to completely disregard others. It’s not top of the list of worst behaviour; it’s in the same bracket as leaning on poles so no one can hold them, leaving your bag on the only seat left, leaning your arm on the fold up chair, or man-spreading. It mostly saddens me that we have lost a basic sense of politeness. I’m not sure Andy Burnham’s announcement will do anything. If you’re already playing very loud videos in public, presumably you don’t care very much about what you should be doing. You never really see police or “safety officers”, so who would enforce it? I’m glad they aren’t making the tube workers or bus drivers try to enforce it though; it would make their days hell. Claire, 41, London ‘Almost every bus or train journey has someone blaring music’ I get the train five nights a week to work and nine times out of 10, there is somebody taking phone calls on speakerphone, blasting videos or music, even in the so-called quiet carriage. Everyone’s too scared to ask them to move to a different carriage or turn it down, so it’s a regular occurrence. It makes my journey a nightmare. No one enforces anything. I doubt this new law will change this. It should include phone calls too and people putting calls on loudspeaker. It doesn’t go far enough. Margaret, 49, Weston-super-Mare ‘Commuters shouldn’t have to put up with it’ I think this is a great step to protect public spaces as shared spaces, and to show people the boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour. The last time I asked somebody who was playing reels aloud to use their headphones I was called “a piece of shit” and decided not to ask anybody that again. But commuters shouldn’t have to put up with it. Of course, the question is whether and how this will be enforced consistently. Ben Ellis, 38, Edinburgh ‘I’m sick of being the bad guy who points it out’ I’ve always challenged this behaviour by asking people if they have headphones. If they say no, I ask if they can turn the sound off. Most of the time this is OK, but I have had repeated incidents where people refuse. I’m stubborn and confident, so I’ll explain that it is not normal or socially acceptable to subject other people to jarring video scrolling. Only once in this situation did a train guard ask someone playing football at full volume to turn it off. And I can’t blame them. You’d be arguing with idiots for 90% of your shift if you did. I’m sick of being the bad guy who points it out. It seems like people of all ages have forgotten basic decency and consideration. I had a run-in with a teenage kid who was watching TikTok or something, and he said, “What do you mean? If you were watching Netflix on your phone, wouldn’t you have the volume on?” So there’s a range of understanding of what people think is appropriate behaviour in a public place. John, 43, Sheffield ‘Football fans on the trains can be difficult to deal with’ One of the bigger issues that never gets addressed is football fans on public transport. I’m a football fan myself, but fans on trains can be extremely offensive, oppressive, aggressive and difficult for people to deal with. One time that springs to mind was a bunch of fans on a two-carriage train. They were drinking, singing loud, offensive songs regardless of the fact that there were kids on the train, banging on the ceiling of the carriage, making a hell of a racket. There were no police or staff. There was a bunch of people waiting at the railway station at the other end, but it’s too late at that point. It’s become almost like an accepted thing that if you go in on a train, this is what you have to put up with. I’m glad to see that [Burnham] recognises that behaviour on public transport is an issue that needs to be addressed. Do I think this will address it? Not at all. How do you get to someone on a train? Will this be app based? Only instant reporting and action will work, but how does that square with a public transport network with significant coverage gaps?

events.title: SGX CEO Loh Boon Chye to step down in 2027
events.summary: Loh Boon Chye, who joined SGX as CEO in 2015, said there will be “ample time” for a smooth handover. SGX CEO Loh Boon Chye will step down in 2027. SGX has started searching for a successor, and Loh said there will be “ample time” for a smooth handover. SGX posted record 2026 results. Revenue rose 13.9% to $1.5 billion, and adjusted net profit rose 24.6% to $759.5 million. Loh said SGX will keep growing as a multi-asset platform. Plans include gold clearing, physically deliverable gold futures, and tokenisation of securities collateral. SINGAPORE – The Singapore Exchange (SGX) has begun its search for a new chief executive, as current CEO Loh Boon Chye will step down from his role in 2027. Loh, who took the helm of the SGX Group in July 2015, announced his decision at the company’s annual general meeting on Oct 23 at the Marina Bay Sands Expo and Convention centre . He said that the bourse’s strong performance and foundation presented an opportunity to be “equally thoughtful and deliberate about the leadership that will take SGX into its next phase of growth”. He said he had shared his intention to plan the CEO transition with SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee before the AGM, and the two executives would work together to find his successor. Loh, whose contract runs until mid-July 2027, said: “We are doing so from a position of strength – with a clear strategy, strong momentum and a highly capable leadership team. “This gives us the opportunity to plan thoughtfully and with confidence for the future. “To me, this is part of building a strong and enduring institution; one that continues to grow, evolve and achieve greater success in the years ahead.” No date has been set for the transition yet. Loh noted that the bourse will have “ample time” to plan the transition and ensure a smooth and seamless handover, with continuity in SGX’s strategy, business and relationships with its stakeholders. SGX recorded all-time highs in revenue and net profit for the 2026 financial year ended June 30. Revenue rose 13.9% to $1.5 billion, while adjusted net profit reached $759.5 million, up 24.6%. Loh had described 2026 as an “exceptional year” for the stock market, marked by improving participation, liquidity and trading activity. Retail participation hit a five-year high, with net revenue from cash equities up 28.1% to $502.9 million, accounting for 34% of total net revenue. Securities daily average value also increased 34.9% to $1.8 billion, while the total securities traded value rose 35.5% to $455.7 billion. In his address to around 400 shareholders, Loh also cited SGX’s multi-asset strategy as a key driver of the bourse’s performance and said it will continue to expand its product suite to build the bourse with multiple engines of growth and resilient earnings. This includes a platform for clearing gold trades, as well as a physically deliverable gold futures contract. Responding to a shareholder’s question, he added that SGX is looking to implement the tokenisation of securities collateral, which could entail issuing digital tokens to represent ownership of traditional securities such as stocks and government bonds. “My ambitions for SGX are greater than ever. I want us to accelerate our growth, expand our global reach and take SGX to a new level. That is what I intend to drive forward. “We have built something strong together, and I genuinely believe our best opportunities are still ahead of us,” said Loh . Koh said Loh stepped into the role in 2015 “in the middle of a crisis” as the bourse had been hit by a number of outages that led to trading halts. “Being at the top of a company like SGX comes with a tremendous amount of pressure,” Koh added. He credited Loh with stabilising the situation by strengthening its information technology capabilities, which was instrumental in transforming SGX from a cash equities market to a global multi-asset platform. Citing SGX’s strong financial performance and rising share price, which is up by more than 21% since the start of 2026, Koh said the company has seen a significant track record under Loh’s leadership and described his decision to step down as a “bittersweet moment”.

events.title: Premier Coal gives employees redundancy forms ahead of move to close night shifts
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts WA government seeks clarity from coal miner as operations set to wind back Premier Coal operates outside of Collie in WA's South West. ( ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry ) The WA government says one of the state's last remaining coalmines is planning to go to day operations only. The ABC understands Premier Coal told staff today and canvassed for voluntary redundancies. The WA government stands by its self-imposed deadline of ending coal-fired power by 2030. The Western Australian government says it is disappointed that one of the state's last remaining coalmines will shift to day operations only. The ABC has received confirmation from the government about Premier Coal's decision to reduce operating hours. The government is seeking more information on the matter. Transitioning to day shift operations would result in job losses at the mine in Collie, 200 kilometres south of Perth. The ABC understands Premier Coal has told workers night shifts will end in the coming months and there will be a three-week planned shutdown over summer. WA Premier Roger Cook speaks on ABC radio on Thursday. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) "Premier Coal's decision to move its operational workforce to day shift is very disappointing," a state government spokesperson said. Premier Coal did not respond to questions from the ABC. Unions said the move would mean the axing of about 40 per cent of the workforce, or about 150 jobs. Management today handed out forms for workers to nominate for voluntary redundancies. A form asking for voluntary redundancies was handed out at Premier Coal in Collie. ( Supplied: AMWU ) The decision comes as owner Yancoal has been embroiled in a tumultuous period of enterprise bargaining with workers as they try to negotiate their final agreement before the government's planned shutdown of coal-fired power generation by 2030. The workforce, which is more than 90 per cent unionised, has taken several hours of strike action since July, including refusing to load coal onto trains. Unions say the proposed offer from Premier Coal could leave workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off each year. ( ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden ) Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union Secretary Steve McCartney said the impacts of the decision were not just about staffing. "It looks like about a 40 per cent reduction in workers," he said. "That's a lot of people that would be looking for a job where there isn't one at the moment. In April, Premier Coal announced the loss of between 70 and 100 jobs at the Collie mine site. Energy analyst Tim Buckley, from Climate Energy Finance, said the night operations shutdown would not cause rolling blackouts. Premier Coal's open pit is near Collie in WA's South West. ( ABC News: Anthony Pancia ) "Customers of WA can be confident there's not going to be significant impacts to the energy grid from this," he said. Coal generated 24 per cent of all electricity in WA in the past 12 months, while renewables contributed about 40 per cent. Mr Buckley said the decision by Premier Coal came sooner than the government was prepared for, but renewable projects across the state were steaming ahead. In a statement, the state government said it was confident Premier Coal's decision would not affect the state's power supply. Taxpayer money has been pouring into Collie since the government made the announcement about shutting coal production in 2022 . The WA government's $230 million Collie Industrial Transition Fund has laid the groundwork for several new industries, but few have reached a final investment decision. Last month, $58 million in funding was announced for rehabilitation, road infrastructure and workforce transition initiatives in Collie, including targeted voluntary redundancy measures. In May, the WA government also flagged Collie as a potential home for a new manufacturing defence hub .

events.title: 'I live in the dark': How rising bills are shaping daily life
events.summary: Errol McGuiness says he has changed his daily routine to cope with higher household bills As evenings grow colder and household budgets come under renewed pressure, 79-year-old grandad Errol McGuiness has developed a routine to keep costs down. The pensioner collects rainwater, spends much of his time in a single room and piles on extra layers rather than turning up the heating. "I keep lots of clothes on, but don't tell my daughter," he said. His most striking money-saving measure comes when night falls. "You don't need a light on to watch telly. You don't need a light on when you go to bed. You know the way to the toilet and the kitchen, so you don't need a light on." Errol admits he has a health condition and says his daughter regularly reminds him to switch the heating on. But he is far from alone in trying to cut household costs. New figures published this week showed inflation rose to 3.5% in September, its highest level for almost a year, while higher fuel prices have pushed up living costs for many households. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised measures aimed at easing pressure on household finances, including removing standing charges from gas bills. Four years into the cost-of-living crisis, almost two-thirds of low-income families say they struggle to afford essentials such as food, heating and clothing, according to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. Almost half said they had skipped meals or reduced portion sizes to save money. Melissa Baydilly says many people seeking help are struggling with the rising cost of essentials Among them is 83-year-old widower Bryan, who says he now lives largely in a single room to keep bills down. "I put a cardigan on and whatever it is you put on to keep yourself warm, shut the door, put the fan heater on to warm the house up," he said. "When you see the price keep going up, I think,' well, I'm sitting in one room'." At Affordable Foods in Blurton, Stoke-on-Trent, centre manager Melissa Baydilly says stories like Errol's and Bryan's are becoming increasingly common. The organisation runs a food bank, social supermarket and outreach service helping people with debt, benefits and employment issues. "Every supermarket you go into, everything's gone up," she said. "There isn't a place where you would go now and not say there's at least a 25% to 30% hike on prices." She believes pensioners are among those feeling the strain most acutely. "I don't believe, in this day and age, our seniors of the city should go to the supermarket, look at the fruit and veg and think, 'I can't have apples and oranges this week, I've got to pick'. "Should they be doing that in their 60s and 70s, when they've worked all their life?" events.title: What is Warhound, Palmer Luckey's war dog startup that just emerged from stealth?
events.summary: Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm have launched a startup to genetically engineer military dogs. JAVIER TORRES/AFP via Getty Images Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm have partnered up for a new startup. Their startup, Warhound, aims to create a new league of highly capable military dogs. Warhound announced that it had $200 million in its seed round. "Man's best friend deserves man's best tech." That's what Palmer Luckey said about his new startup, Warhound. The Anduril cofounder, along with Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm , raised $200 million in seed funding for the startup that aims to genetically engineer high-performance military dogs. Warhound said in a Thursday press release that it wants to rebuild the US's supply of working dogs for military forces, law enforcement, and emergency first-response teams. It added that most of the military dogs currently working in the US are acquired from Europe, and many are eventually deemed unfit for service. Colossal Biosciences is a biotechnology company that uses gene-editing tools to protect endangered species and revive extinct ones. It will help produce healthier dogs suited to demanding missions, with Lamm telling TechCrunch that this involves enhancing the dogs' speed, agility, and ability to sniff out bombs. Anduril's contribution to Warhound is the external hardware to keep the dogs and their handlers safe, such as eye and ear protection. Warhound's $200 million seed round was backed by several VC firms, including In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, ARK Invest, and Franklin Templeton. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, said in the release, "Palmer, Ben and the Warhound team are exceptional. Sequoia is proud to back them." Warhound will be led by CEO David Spirk, a senior counselor at Palantir and a veteran of the US Marine Corps. He was also a former data officer for the Department of War. The startup, based in Texas, has made commitments to animal welfare, saying in the release that it's certified by the American Humane Society, the US's first national animal welfare organization. It said that improving the health and training success of the dogs will limit the number who enter unnecessary intensive training and enable safer missions. events.title: Singapore’s core inflation eases to 2% in September
events.summary: Singapore’s core inflation fell in September due to lower inflation in services, retail and other goods, and private transport. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s core inflation dropped in September, due to lower core inflation and private transport inflation. Core inflation – which excludes private transport and accommodation to better reflect household expenses – eased to 2%, down from 2.2% in August, according to data from the Singapore Department of Statistics on October 23. Overall inflation fell to 2.2% in September from 2.3% in the previous month owing to lower inflation in services, retail and other goods, and private transport. DBS senior economist Chua Han Teng wrote in an Oct 23 note that the data for September suggests “initial fears of a significant acceleration in inflationary pressures have not really played out”. Referring to the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Oct 14 decisions to narrow its 2026 inflation forecast ranges and leave its exchange-rate-based monetary policy unchanged, Chua said the authorities expect underlying price pressures to remain slightly elevated in the immediate future, before moderating discernibly from mid-2027. “This suggests that policymakers see core inflation as nearing its cyclical peak, as imported cost pressures and commodity supply disruptions ease in the second half of 2027 alongside muted domestically driven price pressures,” he wrote. Private transport inflation slowed to 7.1%, down from 7.5% in August and 8% in July, due to a more gradual increase in car prices. Meanwhile, accommodation inflation went up to 0.9% in September from August’s 0.8% as housing rents increased at a faster pace. Services inflation dropped to 1.7%, from 2% in August, due to a smaller increase in point-to-point transport service costs and a larger decline in telecommunication service prices. Retail and other goods inflation dropped to 1.2% in September from the previous month’s 1.8%, as furniture prices declined and clothing prices rose at a slower pace. Food inflation increased slightly to 2.4%, from 2.3% in August and from 2.2% in July, due to higher inflation in both non-cooked food and food services. Electricity and gas prices inflation remained unchanged at 8.7% for September, as electricity prices rose at a similar pace as in August. Mr Zavier Wong, market analyst at trading and investing platform eToro, said the cooling of goods and services can be read two ways: “Either businesses have little room left to raise prices, or shoppers are pushing back on higher prices.” Wong said it is likely the latter, as the 17% jump in electricity tariffs from July left households with less to spend in the shops, and retail trade was the one part of its sector group that did not expand in the third quarter of 2026. “Furniture prices fell in September, and clothing prices rose more slowly. The oil shock has inevitably pushed up retailers’ costs, and shoppers holding back simply adds to the strain,” said Wong. “It’s a double whammy for margins we’re seeing, and with Brent now back above US$110, the pressure to raise prices is only going to build from here.” Alyssa Woo is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. She writes about how retail and work spaces are used and evolve with the times, as well as personal finance stories for the Invest section.

events.title: NSW's second-largest national park created to protect koalas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Great Koala National Park established after more than a decade of campaigning Protecting koalas is the focus of a new national park. ( ABC News: Donal Sheil ) The NSW parliament has passed legislation that will officially create the Great Koala National Park. The federal Clean Energy Regulator announced the registration of the land to generate carbon credits yesterday. Environmental campaigners have hailed the park's creation as a "big step forward" for protecting native forest. After a marathon parliamentary debate, the state government has established New South Wales's second-largest national park. The Great Koala National Park (GKNP) will take in 478,000 hectares of land between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast, following a key promise from Labor during the 2023 state election . It will comprise a patchwork of existing national parks and more than 178,000 hectares of state forest and Crown Land. The Great Koala National Park covers land between Kempsey and Grafton. ( Supplied: NPWS ) The legislation passed today after more than 14 hours of debate in the Legislative Council, which considered approximately 160 amendments. NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe hailed the GKNP as a win for the environment that would protect more than 100 species of flora and fauna. "This is a defining moment for conservation in NSW," she said in a statement. "After more than a decade of campaigning and years of detailed assessments, consultation and planning, we have cleared the final hurdles to delivering our biggest environmental commitment. "We are protecting extraordinary forests … while ensuring future generations can enjoy these incredible places." Penny Sharpe welcomes the passing of the legislation to create the national park. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) For conservationist Ashley Love, the park's creation is the culmination of more than a decade of campaigning to protect koalas and their habitat along the Mid North Coast. "We're extremely grateful that the government has decided to protect native forest," he said. "Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward." Mr Love began lobbying for what would become the Great Koala National Park after hearing multiple reports from residents that koalas in the region were not as common as they once were. "It became too much to ignore," he said. "We proposed a reserve over the Crown land covering [the region], and that was a basis for the proposal for the Great Koala National Park." Ashley Love helped lobby for the Great Koala National Park for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Emma Rennie ) The NSW Labor Party unsuccessfully took the proposal to the 2015 and 2019 state elections, before winning government in 2023. Mr Love said despite the passing of the legislation, he would continue to push for more areas of the surrounding forest to be protected. "We still have to keep working on those elements that were not included," he said. Key to the establishment of the park was the approval from the federal government to generate carbon credits for ending native forest logging in the park's state forest areas. On Thursday, the federal Clean Energy Regulator announced it had registered the project, with more than 117,000 hectares designated for carbon protection. A moratorium on logging on the proposed area of the GKNP was introduced last year, and a transition package was offered to affected workers. Andrew Hurford says many mills now have no wood to process in the region. ( ABC Landline: Cameron Lang ) Timber New South Wales president Andrew Hurford said the logging ban has had a "creeping impact" for the industry along the Mid North Coast. "Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. "All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter." In July, state forest manager the Forestry Corporation of NSW (FCNSW) announced it would cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour related to the impacts of the GKNP. The government said impacted FCNSW staff would be appointed to suitable roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service.

events.title: Long John Silver’s Woodlands outlet to shut down following string of recent closures
events.summary: A closure notice at the Woods Square outlet in Woodlands on Oct 23. SINGAPORE – Fast food chain Long John Silver’s will be permanently closing its Woodlands outlet from Oct 31, on the back of a string of recent closures in Singapore. A notice seen by The Straits Times at the Woods Square outlet stated that the outlet’s last day of operations would be Oct 30. When ST visited the outlet on Oct 23, it was teeming with customers during lunchtime. “I didn’t know this outlet is closing. I eat here maybe once every two weeks. But I won’t really be sad when this outlet closes,” said Wilson Cheng, 40, who works in facilities. He was having lunch at the Woods Square outlet. Peggy Lim, 39, a long-time patron of the fast-food chain, said she would be sad if the outlet, which is the nearest to her, closed. “I didn’t know that Long John Silver’s was closing so many outlets. All the food and beverage places seem to be closing this year,” the supply-chain planner said. “My two favourite fast-food places are McDonald’s and Long John Silver’s. But the outlet near me is still open, so it’s okay for now,” Lim added. Staff at the Woodlands outlet told ST that they were unsure whether they would be redeployed to other outlets after the closure. This marks the latest of several closures in 2026 for the chain , which is known for its fried seafood. Its Jurong Point outlet shut on Oct 19, and checks show that at least four other locations closed earlier in 2026 as well. Based on social media posts and media reports, these were in Suntec City, Admiralty, Commonwealth, and Tampines. It also used to have a store in Westgate Mall in Jurong East, but it is unclear when that outlet ceased operations. When ST visited Bishan’s Junction 8 outlet on Oct 23, the shopfront had a hiring notice up. The outlet also had a busy lunch crowd. Currently, Long John Silver’s website lists 11 outlets. This is down from the 17 outlets reported by CNA in July 2025. The brand traces its roots in Singapore back to the 1980s, as part of the wave of US fast-food chains that entered the local market. Today, it is run by Zensho Food Singapore, a subsidiary of Japanese conglomerate Zensho Holdings Group , which is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange . The parent group manages a global portfolio of popular food and beverage brands, including Japan’s leading beef bowl restaurant chain Sukiya and Ichikokudo Hokkaido Ramen, which both have a presence in Singapore. Zensho Food Singapore currently manages all Long John Silver’s outlets in Singapore. Corporate registry checks show that the entity was registered in 2012 and has a paid-up capital of $29.3 million. The entity’s profit before tax for continuing operations was $422,132 for the financial year 2025, up from $85,134 for the previous financial year ending March 31, 2024. Revenue for FY2025 was about $34.3 million, up from about $32 million the year before, according to financial statements filed with the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority. ST has contacted Zensho for more information.

events.title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter
events.summary: Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen. Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports. The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing. National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut. The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted. In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies. Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent. Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years owing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision to approve the new Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month. Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter. The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July. The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid. Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed. National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels. Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”

events.title: Britain’s gas security needs reinforcement. Last-minute deals with Belgium are not a proper fix
events.summary: The UK still imports 60% of its gas and, even with Jackdaw, its energy supply and resilience problems are not going away A fter the overdue approval of the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur. To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high. Equally, though, the “high-impact” bit matters: we’re talking about having enough supplies to run gas-fired power stations at full pelt if necessary to keep the lights on. You don’t take chances. In short, 10p a month will be added to bills to cover the cost of paying Interconnector Limited, the Belgian owner of the pipeline, to maintain the compressors needed to shove big volumes of gas to Britain in a hurry if required. Without the arrangement, the company had already warned it would cut capacity, in part because the big pipe was not used much in practice last year. The first conclusion – the comforting one – is that the deal sounds like decent value for money. As insurance policies go, £1.19 a household a year is not much. The second, however, is that risks to Britain’s gas security are plainly mounting. The Ofgem document describing the Belgian deal says it was “the only currently available intervention identified that both addresses the immediate security of supply position for winter 2026/27 and provides continuing security of supply benefits over the following four years”. It was Belgium, plus any future deal on the Dutch pipeline, or nothing. Nor is the Belgian shuffle a cure-all. “The agreement does not remove the need for further measures led by government that are likely to be required to support security of supply and wider gas system resilience over the medium and longer term,” says Ofgem. The government should take that line as a heavy hint to get a move on. Do we need more gas storage, more LNG terminals, or both? And post-Jackdaw, what’s a realistic appraisal of how much will be sourced from the North Sea? It is now almost a year since an alarming report from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) warned of an “emerging risk to gas supply security” in 2030. The government promised to “do whatever it takes” to avert a crunch but one cannot say it has actually done much. An interim response to the Neso report came in August but no timetable was given for choosing what kit or arrangements were needed and by when. The final response isn’t due until next year. Read the “winter outlook” report from National Gas, published on Friday, and a few points stand out. Yes, it’s good news that, with the help of the Belgian deal, this winter’s outlook is positive. But the company also says that, even as annual consumption drifts down slightly, the peaks for demand remain as high as ever, driven by the role of gas-fired power generation when renewables output is low. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Like Ofgem, National Gas says “continued progress on government plans to reform security of supply arrangements will be vital to address enduring challenges in the years ahead”. It is becoming a theme. The obvious answer is more gas storage to address Britain’s skimpy current levels. That could mean Centrica’s Rough facility in North Sea (currently due to close next spring), the Bains development led by dCarbonX off the north-west coast of England (which may happen anyway), more on-shore salt caverns or any combination. Or, perhaps, German-style forward-buying deals on LNG. But something has to happen soon. None of this infrastructure gets built quickly and that 2030 potential crunch is getting closer. Certainly, the government cannot agonise for as long as it did over Jackdaw. Eleventh-hour deals with Belgium are not a permanent fix for Britain’s gas security headache.

events.title: Youth mobility scheme may be delayed to ensure success of UK-EU summit
events.summary: Visa quotas, university fees and NHS surcharges remain sticking points ahead of post-Brexit negotiations next month A deadline for a youth mobility scheme between the EU and the UK could be deferred by six months in a bid to ensure Andy Burnham has a successful “reset” summit on 20 November, diplomats have said. EU ambassadors in Brussels on Wednesday heard that the UK was still insisting on international tuition fees, quotas and an NHS surcharge for EU students. This has fuelled fears the summit could fail, just as the prime minister is promising to unveil a new vision for Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU. Sources say the UK also continues to push for a cap of about 50,000 a year on the numbers of EU citizens allowed in the country for work, travel or study under the mooted youth experience scheme (YES) visas. Some EU member states want the cap much higher, at up to 500,000. Others want no cap at all. The UK is also insisting that any YES visa holders pay the £1,035 NHS surcharge to cover potential doctor or hospital visits, although it is understood that a 25% discount has been suggested. Negotiations on two other issues – a food and drink trade deal and the emissions trading system – are almost complete but views on the youth mobility scheme remain divided . Sources say there is near-agreement on demands from the National Farmers’ Union that crops grown using fungicides yet to be approved in the EU could be sold in the bloc under a transition arrangement in the sanitary and phyto-sanitary agreement . “A lot of member states were in favour of keeping the trio of issues together and not breaking the agenda up, but there are others that think it is acceptable to decouple them and there is no agreement yet on which approach to take,” said one diplomat. But the reciprocal youth experience scheme designed to allow under-30s from both sides to work, travel or study in each other’s countries remains deadlocked. Talks on a fourth issue, in relation to the reintegration of the UK into the EU’s energy market, will also, as expected, continue after 20 November. More time is needed to resolve significant barriers that have emerged, such as state aid and oversight frameworks, including a role for the European court of justice. Tuition fees remains the thorniest problem, with UK universities putting pressure on the Labour government to maintain full international student fees for EU citizens – which can run to £69,190 a year at Oxford. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day One diplomat said there was an “emerging consensus” at the meeting in Brussels around a European Commission proposal to take tuition fees out of the package altogether, with wording in a joint statement on 20 November committing both sides to negotiating a solution by May 2027. It was thought that the landing zone was somewhere between home fees of £9,790 and the average international fees, but universities outside the elite 24-strong Russell Group have told the UK government they cannot afford to drop fees for EU citizens. According to several diplomats, the bloc is still divided on whether to remove tuition fees from the table. There are also divisions over how a cap on numbers would work amid fears in the UK that voters – particularly in “red wall” constituencies – would see it as opening the gates to workers coming from economically less wealthy countries such as Bulgaria. A proposal to cap the figures per country has been suggested, although how that would work in practice has not been detailed. Some countries such as France are still arguing for an “all or nothing” approach, with all three topics on the table, arguing if the UK cannot agree tuition fees now, 17 months since the last EU-UK summit, “why would they do so in six months?”. Others say with pressure to move on from three “significant but modest” issues to the bigger issues of deeper economic, security and defence ties, they cannot risk a failure on 20 November. “YES is politically, emotionally and diplomatically very important. But if we can get an agreement at the summit by removing one element from the agenda it is a price worth paying,” said one diplomat.

events.title: Wealthy Chinese move offshore money to U.S. banks as Beijing’s tax net widens
events.summary: More wealthy Chinese are opening U.S. bank accounts to move offshore assets there, keeping them out of Beijing's reach. Lawyers suggested a U.S. bank account may shield income from Beijing's watch for now, but it does not excuse the obligation to self-declare for individuals deemed tax residents of China. SINGAPORE — Wealthy Chinese rattled by Beijing's widening hunt for overseas wealth are turning to a once-familiar refuge for their money: the U.S. Private bankers and lawyers who work with Chinese clients say inquiries about opening U.S. bank accounts have grown in the months after Beijing imposed retroactive taxes on offshore wealth in July, moving assets previously stored in Singapore or Hong Kong there to stay further away from Beijing's reach. "It has become relatively prevalent," said Keith Tan, CEO of Singapore-based Golden Acacia Capital, who is helping Chinese clients manage their offshore portfolios. His clients began planning exits to the U.S. in July, and some have the accounts set up in less than two months. "The hurdle is not that high for Chinese clients to open American accounts and transfer assets there." Wealthy clients tend to choose large private banks while smaller accounts go to regional banks or online brokers, Tan said. The rush has gained urgency with China's new tax regime on offshore trusts. Authorities said in July that income and gains from overseas trusts owned by Chinese tax residents would be taxed at 20%, setting off a scramble for cash and alternative structures . Lawyers in Singapore and Hong Kong have been working to tally how much tax their clients owe, facilitating trusts' unwinding, sales of shares in listed companies or applying for loans to meet the outsized tax bill. Meanwhile, the U.S. sits outside the Common Reporting Standard, or CRS, the OECD framework under which more than 100 jurisdictions automatically share financial account data. While banks in Singapore and Hong Kong are supposed to report China-linked accounts to Beijing, American banks have no such obligation. Non-resident clients who open foreign bank accounts in the U.S. can also find investment vehicles with reduced or no tax-filing obligations to the Internal Revenue Service, said James Wang, CEO of Blue Brick Consulting Group, a private-client tax advisor. But China's latest regulations require people classified as Chinese tax residents to self-declare worldwide income to Beijing, Wang said. Banks in New York are seizing the opportunity to offer a solution that could shield Chinese customers from their country's tax man. U.S. banks are straining to keep up with the rise in demand, according to a New York-based wealth-planning advisor who works with Chinese family offices. "With inquiries surging, some banks have shortened the timeframe for clients to meet required minimum capital commitments" before the accounts are subject to closure, said the advisor, who requested anonymity to speak about bank processes. Chinese families with offspring holding U.S. green cards have also used foreign grantor trusts – structures treated as owned by their non-American founder – to shield them from some tax exposure in the U.S., Tan said. Low-tax states such as Nevada and Florida have become popular choices, he added. "They are gambling on not being disclosed, because the U.S. does not share information as part of the CRS system; they can dodge tax authorities," said Clifford Ng, a partner at Zhong Lun law firm in Hong Kong. Ng also expects that some with Hong Kong or Singapore residency whose trusts have not yet been flagged to Beijing may unwind those structures and transfer the money out. Lawyers caution that though the route works for now to avoid disclosure, it may be temporary. Money held offshore has probably already been reported to Beijing through the CRS and would "have shown up in China at some point," Ng said, so a transfer from a Singapore or Hong Kong bank to a U.S. one would be visible on its way out. "They may still be in breach of the rules because they have an undisclosed offshore account that's making money and they're not declaring it onshore," Ng said. "Hiding is not tax planning." Washington's Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act requires foreign banks to report American clients, but so far there's no matching automatic flow from U.S. banks to Beijing. Cris Cao, Beijing-based partner at W&H Law Firm, agreed on the risk of Beijing's ability to tax money moved to the U.S. "Even if they move all the money out of the CRS-reported accounts and into U.S. bank accounts, that doesn't naturally reduce or wipe out the tax authorities' right to tax, or their obligation to pay," he said. "There was a record of it being transferred out," Cao said, and "that alone is enough for the tax authorities to levy tax." What's more, the window of opportunity may have closed. Moving money that is already offshore around is relatively easy, but getting capital out of mainland China has become increasingly difficult.

events.title: SK Hynix puts US IPO of chip unit Solidigm on hold after Seoul authorities raise concerns
events.summary: A listing of Solidigm had been under consideration to help fund a new US factory and meet surging demand for chips in AI data centres. SK Hynix has paused its planned US IPO for Solidigm after market volatility and South Korean regulators raised shareholder concerns. Solidigm, a NAND flash and SSD unit, was meant to fund a new US factory, AI chip demand, and possible buybacks, with reports of a US$15 billion raise. SK Hynix will review future funding plans instead; the move may affect US chip policy talks and reflects wider fears over AI stock valuations and dilution. SEOUL – SK Hynix on Oct 23 put on hold a planned US listing for its Solidigm chip unit due to market volatility – a move which also comes after the South Korean authorities raised concerns that the deal could undermine shareholder interests. A listing of Solidigm, a former Intel business that specialises in NAND flash memory and solid-state drives, had been under consideration to help fund a new US factory and meet surging demand for chips in artificial intelligence data centres. It could also have funded share cancellations and buybacks, SK Hynix said in a statement. People familiar with the now-suspended initial public offering plans had said that the share sale could have raised US$15 billion (S$19.1 billion) valued the unit at US$150 billion. The South Korean chip giant, which became dual-listed with a debut on the Nasdaq in July, said it plans to continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm’s expansion and enhance shareholder value, including reviewing the timing, scale and financing of future investments. “This decision does not reflect any change in Solidigm’s growth prospects or investment needs,” it said. It was not immediately clear how the decision would be received by the Trump administration, which has put pressure on foreign chipmakers to build new facilities in the US and which has been holding discussions with SK Hynix. According to sources familiar with the matter, SK Hynix has sought to use the prospect of a potential factory in the US as a bargaining chip, linking it to hoped-for approval from Washington that would allow US chipmaking equipment to be exported to China to increase production there. The South Korean authorities have said they are discussing semiconductor investments in the US with Washington as part of broader bilateral talks, but they are not part of negotiations about a US$350 billion investment commitment South Korea made to the US in 2025 in exchange for lower US tariffs. Seoul’s dual-listing rules recently tightened Across the globe, sentiment towards AI and chip-related stocks has retreated sharply as investors increasingly fret over whether rising interest rates will mean that companies involved in building out the AI supply chain will make sufficient earnings to repay their debts. At the same time, in South Korea, concerns also have mounted that a listing of Solidigm in the US would dilute the interests of SK Hynix shareholders. Financial Supervisory Service governor Lee Chan-jin told a parliamentary hearing this week that regulators were examining whether Solidigm’s potential US IPO would require a review under the country’s dual-listing restrictions, which were tightened in July to strengthen shareholder protections. In addition to broad concerns about the AI sector, worries that a Solidigm IPO could dilute SK Hynix shareholders’ interests have weighed on the chipmaker’s shares, which have tumbled 31% since news of the potential listing emerged in late September. That compares with a 20% decline in the benchmark KOSPI index over the same period. The Korea Corporate Governance Forum, an independent body, welcomed SK Hynix’s decision. Instead of a US listing for Solidigm, the chipmaker, which has made massive earnings gains on the AI boom, could instead inject capital through its AI Company entity, even if Solidigm requires tens of trillions of won in capital expenditure, it said. Citing average estimates from South Korean brokerages, it said SK Hynix’s cash holdings were projected to reach 456 trillion won (S$439.9 billion) by the end of 2027. SK Hynix shares were up 1.4% in afternoon trade, outperforming a 1.4% decline in the KOSPI. REUTERS

events.title: Grenade exercise sparked deadly fire at Canada military base, army says
events.summary: High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more. A fire that killed four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a military official said. The deadly fire broke out on a grenade launcher range during military exercises on Saturday, with high winds propelling it across the base, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, commander of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group, told reporters on Thursday. “A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity,” she added, with the flames spreading to a training area at the Wainwright military base in Alberta. Due to the blaze being in the “permanent danger area” of the range, firefighters were unable to directly combat it, Hanrahan added. The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. The military base lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees. About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area. Four soldiers died and 39 were injured, with 27 requiring hospitalisation. The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military. The soldiers and reserve members were participating in exercises ahead of a planned deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation. The Wainwright base is one of the largest bases operated by the Canadian Armed Forces. It regularly hosts training exercises involving military personnel from NATO countries. During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.
