events.title: Gary Vaynerchuk knows where he'd start if he were 16 and launching a business today
events.summary: Gary Vaynerchuk has some advice for aspiring young entrepreneurs. Chelsea Guglielmino/Getty Images Gary Vaynerchuk shared what he'd do as a young entrepreneur starting out today. The first investment should be time spent making content and learning AI, he said. He said AI could be a once-in-a-generation opportunity for young founders — one as transformative as the internet. Gary Vaynerchuk , 50, says aspiring entrepreneurs should spend every spare minute mastering AI and content creation. During a Thursday appearance on the " Nude Project " podcast, Vaynerchuk shared how he would approach starting a business today as a 16-year-old with 1,000 euros in capital. The podcast is hosted by Bruno Casanovas and Alex Benlloch, founders of the Spanish streetwear brand Nude Project. "I would make content ," Vaynerchuk said. "The dollars don't scare me at all because it takes no dollars. I would spend every ounce of time learning AI. Like, from what OpenClaw is to Claude Code , to using it to think and ponder my ideas." Vaynerchuk said he understood why people were still weighing AI's enormous potential against its possible drawbacks, but believes it will be a missed opportunity "to not take advantage of how profound this technology is." "Much like the internet, much like computers, much like electricity, there will be pros and cons to big technologies. That is the story of man. That is life," Vaynerchuk said. "This is the most opportunistic technology that has ever been invented," he continued. Vaynerchuk then pointed to the founders' own success as proof of the internet's power, and said that younger generations often underestimate its impact because they have never known a world without it. "For 7-year-olds right now, they will never understand how profound AI is," he said. Vaynerchuk added that young people should use their free time to learn content creation, strategy, app-building, and how to use AI throughout their lives. He said AI tools and agents could automate chores, save money, and find sold-out items at the best price. If he were 16 today, he would fully immerse himself in learning tools such as Grok, Gemini, Nano Banana, and Higgsfield. "Everything, everything, everything. All of it," Vaynerchuk said. The entrepreneur has long been optimistic about AI's potential . In 2023, he said the technology was "coming fast" and that he believed workers could adapt to the disruption it'd bring. AI tools are lowering the barriers for startup founders and small-business owners to create marketing content, build early product prototypes, and automate routine tasks that once required a bigger budget, specialized expertise, or additional staff. At the same time, as those tools become more accessible, creativity may be the defining factor in standing out. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Senate control hinges on unwanted nominees
events.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) are living out their midterm nightmares — with nominees they didn't want and former colleagues they no longer control. Why it matters: Together, Schumer and Thune are stuck with five Senate races in which their party establishments thought they had a better chance of winning with someone else. 🤠 Texas: Thune's efforts to stop Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from winning the party's Senate nomination failed. Now Republicans are spending more than $329 million to defeat state Rep. James Talarico— and it's still a nail-biter. 🍑 Georgia: GOP leaders couldn't convince Gov. Brian Kemp to run. The eventual nominee, Rep. Mike Collins, has struggled to keep pace with fundraising juggernaut Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). GOP money is in retreat. 🦞 Maine: Schumer endorsed Gov. Janet Mills, but Graham Platner's implosion left Democrats with backup Troy Jackson against Sen. Susan Collins. ⛴️ Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens and made a name for himself nationally. But he won by just one point even though primary polls showed him up by double digits. He's now polling within the margin of error against the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers. 🏈 Minnesota: Peggy Flanagan ran as a progressive, said she would not support Schumer as leader and bested establishment-backed Rep. Angie Craig. But Cook Political Report moved her race against former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya toward Republicans even as it shifted other races toward Democrats. To make matters worse, Thune's and Schumer's former colleagues are creating fresh headaches by boosting candidates across the aisle. Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who flipped to independent in 2024 after being elected as a Senate Democrat, is campaigning for Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), as Semafor reported. Former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema , who also flipped from Democrat to independent before leaving office, is boosting Republican Jay Feely in her home House district. She even voted for him in the GOP primary, as Axios scooped. Former Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.) endorsed Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) in his reelection this summer. The other side : In two red states, Schumer landed arguably the best candidates he could get. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has all but put North Carolina to bed, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is keeping it too close for Sen. Jon Husted's comfort in Ohio.

events.title: Keeping Madhubala alive: The fight for Karachi’s captive elephants
events.summary: Karachi’s last two African elephants remain in captivity. Their sisters are already dead. Will they survive? At Karachi Zoo, Jude Allen sang, You Are My Sunshine, to an elephant he could not save. Noor Jehan, the 17-year-old African elephant, was suffering. Allen recalls massaging her legs, nursing her bedsores and spending her final days beside her. She died on April 22, 2023, surrounded by a few activists. Allen, 45, had held various corporate jobs while volunteering as an animal caregiver since an early age. But Noor Jehan changed something in him, he said. “The day this wild African elephant rested her painful forehead on mine, and I hugged her for the first time – it all made sense,” he tells Al Jazeera. Now three years later, Allen has turned the grief of Noor Jehan’s loss into care for one of her sisters, Madhubala, who also faces major health challenges. He is part of a growing campaign of Pakistani and international activists and doctors trying to save Madhubala, a victim, her carers say, not just of medical conditions, but also of a system that is simply unable to give animals in captivity the attention and facilities they need. In 2009, four elephant calves captured in Tanzania were brought to Pakistan, allegedly through an animal trader. Two of them, Noor Jehan and Madhubala, were kept at the Karachi Zoo, while their sisters Sonia and Malika were taken to Safari Park, a larger facility also in Pakistan’s largest city that has both a zoo and other viewing spaces for visitors to watch animals up close. Then, in 2020, Pakistan was gripped by the story of Kaavan, an Asian elephant that had spent 35 years in the capital city of Islamabad, eight of them alone after his companion Saheli died. Four Paws, an international animal welfare organisation, helped move Kaavan to an animal sanctuary in Cambodia , where he now lives with other elephants. That episode also shone a light on the Karachi sisters. At the time, Allen was helping a friend with another animal shelter, and came to know Four Paws was in town. He reached out to them, and they led him to Noor Jehan and Madhubala. By 2021, Noor Jehan’s tusk was infected. She suffered from malnutrition and stress, too. Allen and the other activists couldn’t save Noor Jehan, but the campaign had turned into a wider cry, demanding care and justice for captive animals in the urban jungle of Karachi, the coastal home to 20 million people. One animal in particular became the focus of attention. Named after an iconic Indian film actress from the mid-20th century, Madhubala was now the only African elephant at the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation-run zoo. She was alone, banging her head against the gate of her enclosure, Allen recalls. “She didn’t have a friend.” Allen says she needed company – she wanted a friend. Tragic reunion, and a slow recovery Allen, along with Four Paws, helped prepare her for a move to Safari Park, so she could join her sister elephants, Sonia and Malika. Four Paws assessed the elephants and found that they needed better diets, enrichment and medical treatment. The organisation recommended reuniting them. The reunion came in November 2024. Four Paws documented the meeting between the siblings at Safari Park. Sonia approached Madhubala first. Malika followed. The three touched one another with their trunks and drank together. But days later, on December 8, Sonia died, aged about 19, after collapsing in her enclosure. The park’s director initially described an apparent heart failure. Subsequent findings, reported by Four Paws, identified a severe bacterial infection associated with an advanced abscess on her foot. Amir Khalil, a Four Paws wildlife vet involved in the elephants’ care, told The Associated Press at the time that “such infections don’t spread in one day”. Four Paws linked her death to prolonged unsuitable living conditions and malnutrition. Meanwhile, Madhubala and Malika were both diagnosed with tuberculosis, although recent examinations reported by her veterinarian have indicated that Madhubala is no longer testing positive. Now Madhubala, 22, is recovering after losing more than 200kg (440 pounds) and becoming too weak to get up safely after lying down. Khalil, who has also rescued wild animals from multiple conflict zones, is one of the carers who has taken charge of Madhubala’s recovery. He told Al Jazeera that Madhubala had recovered 85 percent of her ability to walk, and was a good patient: “She really wants to follow the standard operation procedure and to adhere to the programme that I put in,” he says. That includes a “water massage for the leg with high-pressure water”. He says the required medication needs to be administered properly, and treating all the wounds – and they were getting better when he left Pakistan a few days ago. For Allen, the work began with Noor Jehan. While she was unwell, he says he visited the zoo daily, checking that the elephants received their food on time and in the right quantities.

events.title: Russia's new type of 3D printed missile will make jet Shaheds look like a 'small problem,' Ukraine's drone gurus warn
events.summary: A photo of debris from the Filin cruise missile, as posted by Sternenko and Beskrestnov. Screenshot via Telegram/Serhii Sternenko Russia looks to be moving toward 3D printed cruise missiles for its next era of air attacks on Ukraine. The threat could be so major, turbojet Shaheds would seem like a small problem, one drone guru said. GUR recently posted details of the Filin, a cheap Russian missile reported to fly as fast as 500 mph. Russia's next big bet in the air war will likely move past jet-powered Shaheds to a deep arsenal of new cruise missiles, two of Ukraine's most prominent drone experts warned on Thursday. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov and Serhii Sternenko wrote separately on their Telegram channels about the Filin, an 11-foot Russian winged cruise missile that Ukraine's military intelligence service recently unveiled. These cheap weapons possess superior capabilities that would easily overshadow the threat posed by the Shahed, according to the pair, both former drone advisors to Ukraine's defense ministry. "The mass use of this type of aerial attack weapon is what awaits us very soon," wrote Sternenko, who runs a major foundation that crowdfunds for Ukraine's military, in a Telegram post. "Then we will remember the jet Shaheds only as a small problem compared to this," he added. Beskrestnov, a drone analyst, said he had "long predicted that our adversary is betting on cheap cruise missiles for the future, not on jet Shaheds." He wrote on his Telegram channel that the Filin can fly faster, maneuver better, and carry a heavier payload than Russia's current turbojet drones, "They do not need drone ports, many of them can be launched from helicopters and UAVs. And most importantly, they can be produced from Russian components," Beskrestnov added. A strike at nearly 500 mph for cheap On Wednesday, Ukraine's military intelligence agency, GUR, released extensive details on the Filin, which it said Russia had begun deploying at the end of summer 2026. The Filin, it said, is the "continuation of the trend of the Russian military-industrial complex to develop inexpensive air attack weapons with jet propulsion and ground launch." The ground-launched missile can carry a 100kg warhead, and Russia has said that it can fly at speeds of almost 500 mph at a range of 745 miles. By comparison, the Kremlin's most advanced jet-powered drone deployed so far, the Geran-5 , is known to fly at a maximum speed of 370 mph. The Filin can also fly at "ultra-low altitudes" and as high as 3.7 miles, GUR said. Similar to Russia's Shahed drones, the Filin features a carbon and fiberglass fuselage, with some of its parts produced via 3D printing, the intelligence service added. And as with turbojet Shaheds, GUR also said that the Filin is filled with foreign electronics in its flight controller, inertial navigation system, equipment control unit, and counter-jamming hardware. The agency listed 35 components from the US, including transistors and converters; 22 from China; and 13 more from Japan, Switzerland, Taiwan, and the Netherlands. Notably, GUR said the Filin's engine is Russian-made, compared to the Chinese engines used on many of Moscow's turbojet drones . The same engine has been found on other recently unveiled Russian missiles, such as the air-launched Kover and Monochrome. Much of Russia's ability to reduce the cost of its new cruise missiles is owed to its use of commercial engines and components. Another high-profile Russian missile that also uses civilian tech is the Banderol, which emerged in the spring of 2025 and has been straining Ukraine's air defense networks in the last few months. The Banderol flies more slowly and has a shorter range than the Filin, but it still reaches a max speed of 435 mph, making it much harder for Ukraine to intercept with drones. Its estimated price is $150,000 per unit — about a sixteenth the cost of a traditional Kh-101 cruise missile — so it's easier to mass-produce. The frequent use of weapons like the Banderol over the summer has led to fears that Russia will lean into its tactic, often nicknamed "missile spam," to keep pushing Ukrainian air defenses. "What is the Air Force command doing now to build up countermeasures in advance?" Sternenko wrote on Wednesday about the missile threat. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn. In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring. Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market . The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year. “Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.” Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing. One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart-ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors. Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S. Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations. “Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.” Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air. Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung , RingConn , Circular , and Zepp Health . Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products . The dispute emerges as the smart-ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors. The lawsuit also comes just weeks after Oura shelved its $2.2 billion IPO , citing “uncertainty” in the market. The company has continued to add features to its smart rings, introducing new fitness metrics earlier this week that help users track how workouts affect their cardiovascular health. In September, Ultrahuman raised $70 million from investors including Qualcomm Ventures and Labcorp, valuing the startup at about $365 million. The startup is also working with Qualcomm on a new smart ring that could run more software directly on the device, as it looks to expand beyond health and fitness tracking into areas such as AI interactions and gaming. The article has been updated to include comments from Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

events.title: Israeli military kills 2 in Hebron gun battle as tension soars in West Bank
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Violence flaring as Israeli pogroms heighten tension across Palestinian territory. The Israeli military said it has killed two Palestinians in a gun battle in the city of Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. The military said it had killed two gunmen on Friday after they had attacked a reserve battalion near the illegal settlement of Telem. Israel’s ambulance service reported that at least six Israeli soldiers were injured, with two in critical condition. list 1 of 3 In Israel election, Palestinian citizens weigh fear against disillusionment list 2 of 3 Outposts, violence, impunity: The anatomy of Israeli settler land grabs list 3 of 3 Israel frees suspects in two settler attacks as West Bank pogroms intensify The gun fight comes amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory, with Israeli settlers and soldiers engaging in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife, with aggression on the rise ahead of next week’s Israeli election. Israeli sources report that the Palestinians were driving a car with an Israeli licence plate before shooting towards the soldiers near one of the many military checkpoints surrounding Hebron. Witnesses in the area said the shooting lasted for 20 minutes, which complicated the process of evacuating the injured. Images shared by the AFP news agency appear to show a man holding a handgun during the fight, and later lying on the floor surrounded by Israeli soldiers. Reports from Hebron said that the Israeli military has arrested two Palestinians and locked down the city. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has cancelled a series of election-related engagements planned for Friday and is expected to speak later on the shootings. Far-right national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir responded by calling for Israel to take full control over the occupied West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements, which are illegal. “We have to act before it’s too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” he said in a statement. Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim noted the precarious situation in the territory as settlers and Israeli security forces maintain pressure on the local population. “This is coming at a time of great tension, not just before the Israeli elections, but there has been a ramp-up in attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank,” she said. Israeli forces arrested 36 Palestinians during raids across the occupied West Bank on Thursday, as attacks on Palestinian farmers and their lands during the olive harvest season ramp up. In Jenin governorate, Israeli forces raided towns and villages, arresting 10 Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing data from the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society. The town of Tuqu in the Hebron governorate was also raided by soldiers, who arrested former prisoner Shorok al-Badan, along with five others from other parts of Hebron, according to Wafa. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said that Israeli forces also arrested 14 people in Khirbet Jawaya village of Masafer Yatta in Hebron, while Wafa reported that three other Palestinians were arrested across the Hebron governorate, citing a security source. In Nablus and Jerusalem, three more Palestinians were arrested during Israeli raids in the village of Burin, the town of Awarta, and the Qalandiya refugee camp. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it documented 17 pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers on Thursday against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest. The incidents were recorded across occupied West Bank governorates, including Hebron, Qalqilya, Nablus, Ramallah and el-Bireh, Jenin and Salfit. According to the Commission, the attacks included assaults on farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, theft of crops and agricultural equipment, damage and burning of olive trees, as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire. The Commission says the pattern represents an escalation in attacks targeting the olive harvest and undermines Palestinians’ ability to access and cultivate their land and maintain their livelihoods. Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers garnered international attention and condemnation. US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained on Wednesday by the Israeli military with a warning while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank.

events.title: Companies laying off staff this year include Meta, Amazon, and Visa — see the list
events.summary: Verizon is one of the latest companies to announce job cuts. Bloomberg/Getty Images Companies including Meta, Amazon, and Visa have said they're trimming staff this year. Many firms, like Wix, have cited the rise of AI as a reason they need fewer staff. See the list of companies letting workers go in 2026. More than 40 companies have laid off employees so far in 2026, continuing the trend of significant workforce reductions across a broad range of industries, including tech, media, finance, and retail. Some, including Block , Coinbase, and Standard Chartered, have cited the impact of artificial intelligence as a key reason for the layoffs. Target, meanwhile, is shifting resources from its supply chain into stores as part of the new CEO's turnaround strategy to improve the shopping experience and return to growth. More than 100 other companies have filed legally mandated WARN notices about job cuts to come in 2026, according to WARN Tracker. Some of the cuts are part of previously announced reductions. The moves come as artificial intelligence, public policy, and broader economic conditions are driving sweeping changes in the business landscape. A World Economic Forum survey last year found that some 41% of companies worldwide expected to reduce their workforces in the next five years because of the rise of artificial intelligence. The survey also found that jobs in big data, fintech, and AI are expected to double by 2030. Last year, Business Insider tracked layoffs at around 65 major companies, including Amazon, Meta, Paramount, and Starbucks. In 2026, we'll continue to track additional job cuts based on company announcements, WARN notices, and our own reporting. Here are the companies with job cuts underway in 2026, listed in alphabetical order. Amazon is laying off thousands of employees Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images Amazon said in January that it would eliminate around 16,000 corporate roles globally. Beth Galetti, senior vice president of people experience and technology, described the January move in a company memo as part of broader efforts to cut back on bureaucracy inside the company. The cuts followed mass layoffs from October 2025, when the tech and retail giant shed 14,000 roles. In May, Amazon's Selling Partner Services team slashed additional jobs as it continued to reshape its organization. "Following a recent review, we've made the difficult decision to eliminate a relatively small number of roles in our Selling Partner Services team," a spokesperson told Business Insider. Angi is cutting 350 jobs Donald King/AP Angi, the popular contractor listing site once known as Angie's List, said in January that it was cutting around 350 jobs "to reduce operating expenses and optimize the organizational structure in support of long-term growth." The company also said it's making the cuts "in light of AI-driven efficiency improvements." In a January 7 SEC filing, Angi said that the cuts would save between $70 million and $80 million in annual spending. The layoffs will cost the company between $22 million and $30 million, according to the filing. Atlassian is cutting 1,600 employees Atlassian Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Atlassian, the enterprise software company and maker of Confluence, said on March 11 that it will be cutting about 10% of its workforce as it invests in AI to reshape its organization. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes said in a statement that about 1,600 employees will be affected by the cuts. "We fundamentally believe people and AI create the best outcomes. Our approach is not 'AI replaces people,'" Cannon-Brookes said. "But it would be disingenuous to pretend AI doesn't change the mix of skills we need or the number of roles required in certain areas. It does." The company expects to incur $225 million and $236 million in restructuring charges, according to an SEC filing. Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs KHemaz/GVN via Getty Images Barclays, the British financial institution , disclosed plans to cut around 5% of its workforce. Anna Cross, the Group Finance Director of Barclays, said on an October 22 earnings call that the company expects more than GBP 1 billion in efficiency savings in 2027, which will involve reducing its head count by 5,000 full-time employees. Cross said that 60% of affected workers are related to "support functions, including fewer developers as AI makes our people more productive." The company reported Q3 pretax profit of GBP 2.3 billion — about $3 billion — up 12% from the same quarter a year earlier. Barclays CEO, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, said that the company is moving to "drive even greater cost efficiency through deep technological transformation, reducing the unit cost of product, manufacturing, service and innovation." British American Tobacco cuts 9,000 jobs Illustration by Timon Schneider/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images British American Tobacco said it will cut 9,000 jobs by the end of the year, about one-fifth of its workforce. The cuts will not impact the US arm of its business. "We are building a future-ready organisation that is more agile, cost disciplined and technology enabled," CEO Tadeu Marroco said in the statement. The company, whose cigarette portfolio includes brands like Lucky Strike and Dunhill, has stepped up its push in recent years into smoke-free alternatives, such as nicotine pouches and vapes. Citi's job cuts continue this year Citibank will continue to cut jobs in 2026. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Citi will cut more jobs this year as part of its plan to reduce its workforce by 10%, or 20,000 employees. In a statement on January 13, the bank said that it will continue to reduce head count in 2026. "These changes reflect adjustments we're making to ensure our staffing levels, locations and expertise align with current business needs," a spokesperson for Citi said. The plan was detailed in the company's January 2024 earnings report and could save the bank as much as $2.5 billion. Cloudflare lays off 20% of its global workforce INA FASSBENDER / AFP via Getty Images Cybersecurity company Cloudflare on May 7 said it plans to cut roughly 20% of its global workforce, affecting more than 1,100 employees. In an internal memo , Cloudflare executives said the company's use of AI has climbed more than 600% over the past three months, and that the rapid shift has forced the company to reconsider its structure. "We want to be clear that this decision is not a reflection of the individual work or talent of those leaving us," Cloudflare executives wrote in the May 7 memo. "Instead, we are reimagining every internal process, team, and role across the company." The company's shares fell more than 14% in extended trading following the announcement. events.title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony.ai and Nvidia
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Ride-hailing company inDrive , known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027. The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China. Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal. Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system. The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London , where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner . Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East. inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves. “Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.” Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios. “Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch. The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday. The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June. Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads. Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems. “Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.” Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun. “We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.” inDrive operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries. The company has also expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: ‘They are trying to intimidate us’: Indonesia’s Prabowo remains defiant in the face of an MSCI double downgrade
events.summary: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto declared that Indonesia will not be “intimidated” by MSCI’s proposal to downgrade the Southeast Asian country’s market to “standalone” status, alongside Argentina, Nigeria, and Ukraine. “Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” Prabowo said during an address to his cabinet . “I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down.” “We have the strength, the courage and we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender,” he added. On Oct. 15, MSCI said it was considering downgrading Indonesia to “standalone” status, which would exclude the Southeast Asian country from its major global and regional indexes. The index provider cited “continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.” As many investors use MSCI’s indexes as the basis for their funds, a downgrade could lead to billions of dollars of investment fleeing the country. A final decision on Indonesia’s status will come by the end of June 2027. Indonesia has labored under the threat of a downgrade for most of 2026. In January, the index provider said it was c onsidering lowering the country to “frontier” status , one rung below the country’s current “emerging” status. That downgrade threatened to pull as much as $13 billion in passive investment flows from the country. The current MSCI proposal—which would downgrade the country below “frontier”—would likely lead to even greater outflows. The Jakarta Composite Index is down by more than 10% since MSCI announced its proposal. The benchmark index is down nearly 40% for the year so far. Mounting pressure The MSCI reclassification is only the latest challenge to Prabowo, now entering his third year in office. His approval rating has dropped to just 44.5%, according to a poll from Saiful Mujani Research and ​Consulting cited by Reuters , primarily due to public dissatisfaction over the state of the economy. The same pollster put Prabowo’s approval at 81% in November. More than six in 10 Indonesians say they are unhappy with Indonesia’s free meal program, one of the president’s flagship social policies. Seventy-one percent also doubt that his village cooperatives policy—which plans to establish hubs in roughly 80,000 communities to handle basic-goods distribution, savings, and other rural services—would succeed. Wildfires in Indonesia are also the source of widespread haze that’s blanketing much of the region and making Southeast Asian cities such as Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world’s most polluted. Singapore is now threatening to prosecute companies responsible for the wildfires. Prabowo recently admitted that he’s open to foreign help to control the fires. But he’s also bristled at criticism. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting. Indonesians are increasingly protesting Prabowo’s administration. Reuters reports that more than 9,000 police officers were deployed across Jakarta this week, ahead of events marking Prabowo’s second year in office. Diplomatic flashpoint The market turmoil is now becoming a diplomatic issue. Former trade minister Muhammad Lutfi—who served under presidents Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono and Joko Widodo—accused Singapore state investors Temasek and GIC of pressuring MSCI to trigger a sell-off, so that foreign investors could “scoop up our strategic assets at discounted prices.” Both entities denied the allegations, with a Temasek executive calling them “patently untrue.” The spat is forcing Indonesian market officials to play damage control. Jeffrey Hendrik, president director of the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), pushed back against the conspiracy claims on Oct. 20. “We have always believed, and continue to believe, that global index providers are independent,” Hendrik said. events.title: US tech stocks tumble as investors fret over AI spending
events.summary: Tech-heavy Nasdaq falls 2.6 percent as debate rages over whether AI is a bubble. US tech stocks have dropped sharply amid market jitters over the sustainability of companies’ enormous capital investments in AI. The Nasdaq Composite, which is dominated by tech firms linked to the AI boom, fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, its steepest fall since the index tumbled 4.2 percent on June 5. list 1 of 4 US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award list 2 of 4 Hundreds of Ethiopians cross into Kenya to flee regional fighting list 3 of 4 Almost all shallow-water coral reefs now face extinction risk, study warns list 4 of 4 UK Conservative Party leader responds to Al Jazeera investigation The broader S&P 500 slid 1.21 percent, the benchmark’s biggest drop since a 1.52 percent decline on July 29. Apart from Apple, each of the “Magnificent 7”, which make up more than one-third of the overall market, saw substantial losses. Meta dropped nearly 7 percent after it raised its projected capital spending for this year to $135bn to $145bn in its latest earnings report, even as the Facebook parent company’s net profit fell short of expectations. Amazon fell 4.6 percent, while Nvidia dropped 4.4 percent. Tesla and Alphabet both fell 3.1 percent, while Microsoft declined 2.2 percent. The sell-off extended to other major tech players, including Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, both of which fell about 8 percent, and Broadcom, which slid 4.3 percent. After the losses, the Nasdaq is about 5.8 percent off its all-time high, reached on October 6. Rising oil prices since February, due to the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, added to the downbeat mood. Brent crude futures rose 4 percent on Thursday and continued to climb on Friday morning, taking the international benchmark above $114.20 a barrel, its highest since May. Major stock markets in Asia opened lower on Friday, following the losses on Wall Street. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 fell more than 2 percent in morning trading before recovering some ground, while South Korea’s KOSPI dropped as much as 3.5 percent. The Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong fell about 0.5 percent. Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said the swings in the market appeared to be driven more by sentiment than underlying fundamentals. “In short, nothing has changed. Investors have just decided to be afraid this week. Everyone I speak to points to a different cause for the downfall … It’s just a giant wall of worry,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera. “There are legitimate concerns about the AI trade, but this level of shift in the markets is driven much more by investor sentiment than any tangible reason.” US tech companies’ huge investments in AI have stoked intense debate about whether a market bubble is forming similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash. While some Wall Street analysts view current levels of investment in datacentres and graphics processing units as unsustainable, others argue that AI will revolutionise society to a degree that justifies the eye-watering sums involved. Global AI investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

events.title: Venezuelans demand elections in first national protest in nearly two years
events.summary: No date has been set to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro after the former president was captured by US forces. Thousands of Venezuelans have taken to the streets in several cities to demand free elections and other political changes, in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years. US President Donald Trump and acting President Delcy Rodriguez have said there would be elections, but no date has been set for a vote to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro, after the former Venezuelan president was captured by US forces in a military raid in January. list 1 of 4 US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says list 2 of 4 Venezuela’s Rodriguez pledges elections, path forward in UNGA speech list 3 of 4 Venezuelans rally for opposition leader’s return and presidential elections list 4 of 4 ‘We are desperate’: Venezuela’s power cuts fuel growing public anger Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027. Her Vente Venezuela movement organised the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas and other cities, including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo. “Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible,” said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. “I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader and president, Maria Corina.” “I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added. Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV). PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture. After the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV remained in power with the support of the White House. US President Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president. His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms. Venezuela’s socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters, but government forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Thursday, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark. The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas’ Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location. Talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government , aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council ahead of eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time. The negotiations, backed by the US, do not include Machado’s political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress. Machado’s proxy Edmundo Gonzalez Urrutia claims to have won the 2024 election according to vote tallies by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country’s legal and electoral institutions. Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro, through alleged links to drug gangs, represented a direct threat to US national security. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.

events.title: The Taiwan Strait is not on the verge of war: The ‘2027 invasion’ countdown is a mirage
events.summary: The most striking feature of the September summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington was not what was discussed—trade, tariffs, technological competition—but what was not. Taiwan was not absent entirely—both sides touched on it in the low-key “agree to disagree” framing register that has come to define the issue—but it was conspicuously absent from the top tier of the agenda. Pundits continue to portray the Taiwan Strait as the world’s most dangerous flashpoint; the summit’s agenda suggested otherwise. That does not mean the Taiwan issue has disappeared. Taiwan remains the “core of core interests” for Beijing, and tensions across the Strait remain a central feature of U.S.-China relations. Precisely because the issue is so sensitive, both Washington and Beijing have strong incentives to preserve stability. For years, the Western world has been counting down to 2027. The year has acquired a talismanic significance for China watchers, military planners, and commentators who see it as the moment Beijing could move against Taiwan. The “2027” narrative distorts global priorities and triggers unnecessary panic. Countdowns shape budgets and deterrence postures—which is why getting the timeline wrong has serious consequences, for all parties in the relationship. The gap between those predictions and the reality on the ground suggests many observers have overstated the likelihood of war. I grew up in Fujian, the Chinese province directly across the Strait from Taiwan, when the shadow of military confrontation shaped daily life. Back then, war felt less like a possibility than an expectation. The Fujian coastline today tells a very different story. The province is in the middle of a civilian infrastructure boom: Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport—located just three kilometers from Taiwan-controlled Kinmen—is expanding. New high-speed rail corridors are running parallel to the existing coastal lines. Industrial parks, logistics hubs, and technology clusters are springing up.  Most of the money is government-led, but private capital is piling in alongside it. The construction is transforming what was once a coastal defense zone into one of China’s most prosperous regions. Fujian now ranks among the top eight provinces in total GDP and fourth nationwide in per-capita GDP. Such long-term investment is difficult to reconcile with the notion of an imminent military confrontation. The boom does not prove that conflict is impossible, but it does reveal the assumptions guiding Beijing’s planning horizon. States preparing for an imminent war prioritize military mobilization and strategic hardening; Fujian, by contrast, is being developed as a long-term engine of economic integration, innovation, and cross-Strait connectivity. That is why I have long been  skeptical of the much-discussed “2027 invasion scenario.” Beijing continues to modernize its military and to preserve the option of force. But the physical landscape of Fujian reflects a strategy calibrated for patience rather than urgency. Beijing is playing a patient game of chess, not checkers. Despite a slowing economy and domestic labor-market pressures, China continues to subsidize and incentivize companies in Fujian to recruit young Taiwanese to work in the province. The strategy pairs economic carrots with gray-zone pressure. If Taipei refrains from crossing the ultimate red line of declaring formal independence, Beijing appears confident in its long-term strategy of integration. That is not a fringe view: Many geopolitical analysts, economists, and scholars agree that Beijing will refrain from using force due to the immense political and economic costs of conflict. Trump’s second term has changed the tactical management of Taiwan. For this transaction-minded White House, the long-delayed $14 billion arms package to Taipei is treated less as an ideological tripwire than as a bargaining chip for a “better deal.” One historical barometer of the Washington-Beijing-Taipei triangle is how Taiwanese leaders are treated when transiting through the U.S. Periods of closer U.S.-Taiwan political engagement have often been accompanied by more visible and politically significant transit arrangements. By contrast, recent restrictions or delays suggest a greater emphasis on managing relations with Beijing and avoiding unnecessary escalation. For example, in the summer of 2025, the Trump administration reportedly declined to greenlight a high-profile transit stop in New York—and a second in Dallas—for Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te, prompting Taipei to call off the trip, even though Taipei denies that was the reason for the cancellation. None of this means the U.S.-Taiwan security relationship has collapsed. As Taiwanese friends joke to me over coffee, spend enough time in the lobbies of Taipei’s five-star hotels and you will cross paths with American defense contractors, executing the logistical and bureaucratic work tied to ongoing arms sales. Yet these quiet preparations reveal a strategic paradox: Washington and Beijing are both preparing for a conflict that they are actively trying to avoid. Taiwan remains the most explosive issue in the relationship—and its very danger is what creates the mutual incentive to keep it stable. Taiwan’s central role in the global semiconductor ecosystem is another reason to doubt the countdown. Conventional analysis treats chip dominance as a source of instability. Yet we should take opposite argument seriously: That the economic and technological costs of disrupting Taiwan’s chip industry create powerful reasons for restraint for both Washington and Beijing. Call it “Silicon Mutual Assured Destruction.” The term is imperfect, but the logic is straightforward: neither side can easily disable the semiconductor ecosystem centered on Taiwan without inflicting severe damage on its own economic and technological future. Skeptics will object that none of this changes Beijing’s ultimate objective. They are correct. Chinese leaders have never abandoned the goal of reunification, and no one should dismiss the possibility of force. Economic integration, semiconductor interdependence, and diplomatic engagement also do not eliminate the possibility of miscalculation. Still, the evidence for an imminent conflict is much weaker than the predictions suggest. As 2027 approaches, the Taiwan Strait remains fraught. But the countdown to war that dominates so much public commentary looks like a mirage. events.title: US lifting sanctions on 'dark fleet' not expected to solve tanker crisis
events.summary: Lifting sanctions on “dark fleet” or shadow fleet vessels is not expected to solve the tanker crisis engulfing oil markets while the Iran war continues and owners remain wary of sailing through the Strait of Hormuz and risking crews' safety. The US move “could provide some relief, particularly around the Arabian Gulf where tanker availability has been strained, but I wouldn't expect it to solve the current tanker crisis”, said Salih Yilmaz, senior industry analyst of energy at Bloomberg Intelligence. The administration of US President Donald Trump this week authorised the sale of sanctioned oil tankers in a move to allow the vessels to start legitimately shipping crude and ease pressure on oil prices that have surged since the outbreak of Iran war in February. “A large share of sanctioned vessels appears to be already operating in Russian, Iranian or other restricted trades rather than sitting idle, so sanctions relief would mainly redistribute existing capacity into mainstream markets,” Mr Yilmaz added. Another big constraint is ship owner’s reluctance to operate in the Arabian Gulf as attacks on tankers continue, killing and injuring crew members. There have been 120 confirmed attacks on ships as of October 22, with 22 seafarer fatalities since the war began in February, according to the latest update from the International Maritime Organisation . Tanker owners are paying as much as $100,000 per month to ship's captains, along with a bonus of $50,000 for each trip, because of risks involved in sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a recent Financial Times report. “The bigger constraint today is the risk of operating around Hormuz. Owners are demanding very high compensation for exposing vessels and crews to attacks,” Mr Yilmaz said. The US government is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use them to transport non-sanctioned oil, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said at an event in New York this week. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet'," Mr Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more.” Wanying Zhang, a freight analyst at Vortexa, was also not optimistic about the US move increasing tanker availability in the markets. “Our analysis suggests that any easing of Ofac [Office of Foreign Assets Control] sanctions is unlikely to trigger a significant return of sanctioned tankers to mainstream trades,” she said. “A substantial share of Ofac sanctioned tankers remain subject to UK or EU sanctions, which could continue to restrict their access to European trades even if US restrictions are lifted.” Ofac is a financial intelligence and enforcement agency of the US Treasury Department that administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on US foreign policy and national security goals. It has been imposing sanctions on vessels linked to Iran and Russia for carrying crude to global markets. The relatively old age of these vessels could also delay their return to mainstream trade, given potential maintenance, inspection, insurance and commercial requirements. About 70 per cent of Ofac-listed tankers are at least 20 years old which limits the number likely to be accepted by mainstream charterers, analysts added. Ship broker Braemar said 170 very large crude carriers (VLCCs) were currently under US sanctions. It added that only 44 vessels are under 20 years old and acceptable to charterers, with 33 at least 25 years old and 92 between 20 and 24 years old. “Given the advanced age of most the ships sanctioned by the US, and the fact that a lot of the ships sanctioned by the US are also sanctioned by the EU or UK, we do not expect this move to lead to too many extra additions to the available tanker fleet,” said Mary Melton, senior tanker analyst at Braemar.

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. The trial of broadcaster Alan Jones has heard the mother of an alleged victim continued to ask the radio host for advice and assistance after he allegedly assaulted her son, despite agreeing in court that she was no longer "financially desperate". NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The woman has finished giving evidence in the NSW Local Court, where Alan Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. The woman's son, Complainant A, first encountered Mr Jones when he emailed the former 2GB breakfast host at 13 years old, asking for help for his mother. He alleges the broadcaster later kissed and touched him when he was 17. In a tense exchange with Mr Jones's defence team, barrister Claire O'Neill questioned the woman about her motives in continuing to speak to Mr Jones, and seek his assistance, at the same time as encouraging her son to report the alleged assault to police. The trial heard the woman emailed Mr Jones several times about a bill for legal services in 2017, after Mr Jones had put her in touch with a law firm to help retrieve money from her estranged ex-husband. "You suggested in this email that you were anxious and desperate about your financial situation?" Ms O'Neill asked. "I continue to be," the woman responded. "You had a house by the ocean…" Ms O'Neill put to the woman. "We lived in a battleaxe," the witness replied, before conceding her house was "a few hundred metres" from the ocean. The mother also agreed under questioning that she had a car, a job, was able to meet repayments on her house and had joined her son on a trip to Europe the following year. "You were not financially desperate do you agree?" Ms O'Neill asked. The woman admitted emailing Mr Jones to ask him to use his "influence" to get Complainant A's membership of the Sydney Cricket Ground fast-tracked through a waitlist, which she said Mr Jones did not do. She also agreed she asked him for "advice" about a repair bill she had received for her 4WD car, but denied she was insinuating that Mr Jones should pay for it. "Around the same time that [Complainant A] was speaking to police you were emailing Mr Jones about the cost of repairs to your Land Rover?" Ms O'Neill asked. "You were taking advantage of Mr Jones's generosity for as long as you could," Ms O'Neill put to the woman. "Absolute rubbish," the witness said. Complainant A's mother reiterated evidence she gave on Thursday, telling the court she was in a "web of dependency" with Mr Jones and that "everything was run by him", after he had assisted in having her home finished. The trial has previously heard that her son wrote her a note about 10 days after the alleged assault at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Falls property, saying "something sexual" had happened. Complainant A asked police not to pursue his complaint in 2018, but renewed the allegation in a 2024 police statement.

events.title: Chinese stocks bounce back from bear market on suspected state support
events.summary: CSI 300 wipes out losses of as much as 2 per cent as key ETF trading volumes surge, indicating possible state-backed buying Chinese stocks rebounded on Friday after a sell-off dragged the benchmark index into a bear market, as surging trading volumes in the nation’s biggest exchange-traded funds (ETFs) pointed to possible state buying and major companies at the centre of the artificial intelligence trade sought to reassure investors. The CSI 300 Index rose 1 per cent to 4,075.44 as of 2.06pm local time, reversing an earlier decline of as much as 2 per cent. Turnover in several key ETFs tracking the gauge surged, suggesting that Central Huijin Investment and other state-backed funds might have intervened to stem further losses. The benchmark technically entered bear-market territory a day earlier after sliding 20 per cent from its June peak. Technology stocks led the rebound. The ChiNext 50 index rallied 2.9 per cent after the nation’s top three makers of optical transceivers used in AI data centres either unveiled share buy-back plans or reassured investors that operations remained normal.

( Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff ) TT-Line has announced a $723 million accounting loss after major write-downs of its Spirit of Tasmania ferries and terminals. The state-owned company says it delivered a $1.5 million operating profit, and insists its long-term future is in good shape. Two new Spirit of Tasmania ferries will begin servicing Bass Strait from the end of the month as TT-Line tries to sell its two older vessels. The operator of the Spirit of Tasmania ferries has announced a $723 million accounting loss for the year, but insists the state-owned company's outlook is "very strong". The bulk of TT-Line's accounting loss in 2025–26 relates to a $646.9 million write-down of assets, including its four ferries and two terminals. A write-down is when an asset is reassessed as having a lower value to the company than what it was listed on the balance sheet as. "But it is non-cash, and it has no impact on our equity ask. It has no impact on our debt position. "And to that extent, it's really the accounting catching up with all the issues that have been well publicised for some time now." Union calls on MPs to stay out of schools unless premier apologises AI tool saves time but makes errors in police trial Second thylacine head hits UK auction house after years stashed under bed Topic: Endangered and Protected Species In May, it was revealed the company's much-maligned ferry replacement program had cost $717 million more than originally expected. In the same month, the government announced a $506 million equity injection into TT-Line , and later increased the company's borrowing limit by $410 million. Spirit of Tasmania I and II — from $174.3 million to $87.5 million Spirit of Tasmania IV and V — from $1.086 billion to $717.9 million Devonport terminal — from $416.8 million to $282.8 million Geelong terminal — from $311 million to $262.1 million Ken Kanofski (right) says TT-Line's lender TasCorp and state Treasurer Eric Abetz (left) have also approved changes to the debt repayment due dates. ( ABC News ) Like new car leaving showroom, chairman says Spirit I made its final voyage across Bass Strait on Thursday, and Spirit II will do the same on Friday evening. Bungled ferry replacement project cost $717m more than forecast The Spirit of Tasmania ferry replacement program has cost $717 million more than was forecast in the original business case, a parliamentary inquiry has heard. Mr Kanofski said several parties were interested in buying either one or both vessels. He said the significant write-downs for the older ships reflected decreased demand from buyers due to unrest in the Middle East, higher interest rates and the type of fuel the ships use. For the new ships, which begin servicing Bass Strait at the end of the month, Mr Kanofski likened their write-downs to the reduced value of a new car once it leaves the showroom. He also downplayed the revaluations of the Devonport and Geelong terminals. "Of course it's material, but it doesn't change anything," he said. "So we're not asking for more equity. It doesn't change the way we're going to trade. Along with the new ferries, Tasmania has invested in the construction of a new ferry terminal in Devonport. ( ABC News: Mackenzie Heard ) Mr Kanofski said TT-Line had recorded a $1.5 million operating profit last financial year. Buyer still wanted for Spirit of Tasmania ferries With their final voyage imminent, the future of ferries Spirit I and II is unclear, with no buyer yet and no local berths available to store them. While acknowledging the company still faced financial challenges, he insisted it was in good shape for the future. "I think the outlook is very strong," he said. "I mean, the reality is we've now got very, very good assets. "They're all brand new, the berths are brand new, the ships are brand new. "It's not unusual early in the life of large-scale infrastructure for the returns to be less than what you would hope for." He said the company's lender, TasCorp, and state Treasurer Eric Abetz had also approved changes to the dates its debt repayments were due. "We've been solvent at all times, and we remain that way," Mr Kanofski said.

events.title: Asian shares wobble as tech rout boosts bonds, dents rate hike bets
events.summary: South Korea’s KOSPI skidded 1.7%, on course for a 4.3% weekly decline. Asian shares fell as worries over AI funding hit tech stocks. Investors bought US Treasuries and safe-haven currencies, while hopes for more Fed rate hikes faded. Wall Street also dropped. Meta fell nearly 8% after its first cash outflow in over a decade, and Tesla cut 2026 capital spending plans. Treasury yields sank, with the US 10-year near 4.9591% after a big fall. Oil stayed high at US$114 a barrel, as Middle East tensions raised supply fears. SYDNEY – Asian shares fell on Oct 23 as concerns over the enormous funding needs of artificial intelligence hammered tech and led to the biggest daily rally in US Treasuries in more than three years, with investors fleeing to sovereign bonds and safe-haven currencies. Markets also sharply pared back expectations of further policy tightening from the US Federal Reserve, stripping out almost a full quarter-point rate hike for 2027 amid concerns a bursting AI bubble could derail the data centre investment boom and hobble the United States economy. A December rate rise is no longer fully priced, with the implied probability falling to 85%. That was despite elevated oil prices, with Brent hitting a five-month peak at US$114 a barrel on Oct 23. Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies as fears grow that the conflict in the Middle East could escalate sharply. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan fell 0.3% on Oct 23, bringing its weekly loss to 2.7% and marking a fourth straight week in the red. Japan’s Nikkei dropped 1.3% and was down a whopping 5% for the week. South Korea’s KOSPI skidded 1.7%, on course for a 4.3% weekly decline, with memory chipmaker SK Hynix down 2.5% on the day. Taiwan’s stock market was closed due to a typhoon. An index of mainland Chinese blue chips lost 1.1% on Oct 23 to hit the lowest level since July 2025. The index was down about 20% from its peak in late June. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.1% after dropping 3% on Oct 22. Charlie McElligott, managing director for cross-asset strategy at Nomura Securities International in New York, said in a note that AI is under sustained pressure. “US Treasury bonds are – gasp – working as your hedge again, as the market seems to be real-time repricing the probabilities of a US growth scare off the back of the AI reset.” On Wall Street, the Nasdaq slumped more than 2% as Meta shares lost nearly 8% after the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures, and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the technology. Tesla shares fell 3.1% as the electric carmaker cut its 2026 capital spending plans. “The question is whether selling accelerates or markets stage another familiar reversal,” said Chris Weston, head of Research at Pepperstone. “There’s nothing more emotive than a falling market where buyers refuse to engage. Sellers don’t need a fresh catalyst when deteriorating price action itself encourages more selling.” As equities tumbled, money flowed into safe haven US Treasuries, sending yields plunging across the curve overnight. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slid more than 19 basis points, the biggest drop since March 2023, before steadying at 4.9591% on Oct 23, back below the closely watched 5% level. That was also due in part to the ongoing sell-off in French bonds, whose benchmark yield climbed 6 basis points overnight to 5.0601%, the highest level since 2002. “The US 10-year yield gapped back below 5% with some conviction. We’re not convinced it keeps on going,” said Padhraic Garvey, ING’s regional head of research for the Americas. “We’re minded to expect it to snap back above (5%), as we still have inflation/fiscal deficit/AI boom underpinnings to navigate. And we have the US midterm elections approaching as an excuse for trouble. But it will need some degree of calm in the risk space first.” The two-year Treasury yield slumped nearly 19 basis points overnight and were last flat at 4.6566%. Government bonds in Asia also rallied. The yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds fell 9 basis points to 2.790%, while Australia’s 10-year yield dropped 10 basis points to 5.164%. In currency markets, safe havens such as the yen and Swiss franc gained. The dollar fell 0.2% to 156.44 yen on Oct 23, after slumping 0.9% overnight. The dollar also slipped 0.1% to 0.8196 Swiss francs, the lowest in a month, after an overnight fall of 0.5%. Gold failed to catch any safe haven demand though, and was flat at US$4,021.99 an ounce on Oct 23 after a nearly 3% drop overnight. REUTERS

US President Donald Trump has backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy amid controversy over an attack advertisement by the Ohio gubernatorial candidate against his Democratic rival. Trump said in a social media post on Thursday that Ramaswamy should keep running the advertisement that features Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother. list 1 of 3 One killed in US shooting near mosque in Columbus, Ohio list 2 of 3 Trump commits more than $400m ahead of high-stakes midterm elections list 3 of 3 Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio In the advertisement, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, disputes her daughter’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and ⁠⁠sexual abuse by her stepfather, urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton’s brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape. “Anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in office,” Trump said. The US president also attacked Republican Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who advised Ramaswamy to take down the advertisement, labelling him “disloyal” to the Republican party. At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time – my wife, Fran, saw the advertisement just run this morning on TV – I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.” Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, called the advertisement ⁠⁠a “desperate, disgusting attack”, while Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock called Ramaswamy’s decision to promote it “both despicable and entirely predictable”. Vice President JD Vance, campaigning on Wednesday with Ramaswamy ⁠⁠and US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican, had brushed aside ⁠⁠the blowback. Vance, a former senator from Ohio, expressed disgust with Republicans “whining” about the advertisement as low and in poor taste. Ramaswamy’s campaign said it was spending $4m to promote the advertisement. Opinion polls suggest Acton is narrowly leading Ramaswamy in a tight race to replace the term-limited DeWine.

events.title: Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming who in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
events.summary: A war of words has erupted over who is responsible for the restrictions on Starshield access in Ukraine A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration , officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink. The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials . Donald Trump said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning. Amid the diplomatic handwringing, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged , and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered. 1. Donald Trump The restrictions came as relations between the US and Ukraine hit their lowest point since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has accused Ukraine of driving up diesel costs for Americans through its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysis by the BBC found that the US-Israel war on Iran and resulting restrictions on oil exports from the Gulf have likely had a greater impact on global diesel supplies. Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO. Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.” Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man. The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything. Ukraine war briefing: Uncertainty over Kyiv’s Starlink access after Trump claims Musk restored service Read more The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”. He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk. However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”. 2. Elon Musk Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump. Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”. So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be. 3. Volodymyr Zelenskyy The Ukrainian president initially blamed the restrictions on “SpaceX and the United States”, saying on Wednesday last week that the move would “bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die”. Shortly after the systems failed, Zelenskyy said there were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in European Union countries and that they applied only to Ukraine. “In other words, this is a planned operation.” Zelenskyy said at the weekend that Musk’s SpaceX was ultimately responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starshield worked in Ukraine. “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed ... And technically, SpaceX did it.” Despite Trump’s insistence on Thursday that the service had resumed, a senior European official told the Associated Press that nothing had changed in the operation of Starshield. Prior to Trump’s comments, Zelenskyy ⁠said full Starshield speed had still not ⁠been restored ⁠for Ukraine, ​adding that he hoped for talks ⁠with Rubio in the ⁠coming days.
