events.title: Ilhan Omar plans to move out of her Washington DC home after federal raid
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Last week, US federal agents raided Omar’s home as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her home in Washington, DC, citing safety concerns following a recent raid of the property by US federal agents. In an interview with MS NOW on Wednesday, Omar spoke for the first time about the raid, noting that the incident has made her feel unsafe there. list 1 of 3 Epstein, Iran and ‘drain the swamp’: Have Republicans shifted before vote? list 2 of 3 Can Trump deport Congresswoman Ilhan Omar? list 3 of 3 Ilhan Omar home raid, Haines attack: Inside rise in violence on officials Last week, officers searched Omar’s home with what a Justice Department spokesperson described as a “judicially authorised search warrant”, adding that the raid was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation”. According to NBC News, which cited one person familiar with the matter, potential future charges against Omar may include conspiracy and making false statements in her immigration paperwork. Omar denies wrongdoing and accuses the administration of political intimidation . Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalised US citizen, said she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong”. The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of US President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies. Earlier this week, Trump called the congresswoman “sick” and “dishonest” and slammed her birthplace as a “real s—house”. For years, Omar, who is Muslim, has been the target of right-wing conspiracy theories about her immigration status, including allegations that she had married her brother. The Minnesota congresswoman has repeatedly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies”. In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for re-election in a deep blue district in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat. Omar recalled waking up at about 6am to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said. Omar came with her family to the US at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a US citizen five years later, in 2000. “It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I’m sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap,” she said in the interview. The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election. Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite”, logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

events.title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
events.summary: Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. Together, the ecosystem announcements below point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing — along with its growing demand for what comes next. The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships. Kazakhtelecom , the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale. AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them. More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute. Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications. Today’s announcements represent different layers of that stack — infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale. events.title: Fighting for the last hundredths
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] As Formula One moves from Singapore to Austin, Richard Mille and Ferrari show how innovation, performance and talent development can become powerful drivers of brand value. With the Formula One season entering a decisive phase following the Singapore Grand Prix, Ferrari remains one of the sport’s most closely watched teams. Whether through the performances of Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc, a long-time Richard Mille partner, and Lewis Hamilton on the track, or the engineering excellence that underpins every aspect of the Ferrari racing operation, the marque’s influence extends well beyond a race weekend. It is a philosophy shared by Richard Mille. When Richard Mille and Ferrari launched a multi-year partnership in 2021, it appeared a natural alignment between two performance-driven brands. Five years on, that meeting of minds has accelerated into an integrated platform spanning product innovation, motorsport, customer engagement and the development of future talent. Separated by around 600 kilometres, Richard Mille and Ferrari are united by a common way of thinking. From Les Breuleux in the Swiss Jura to Maranello, Italy, both share a relentless pursuit of innovation, performance and excellence. Bearing the names of their founders, they continue to embody the dreams and visions that shaped them. This meeting of minds is rooted in shared values, combining age-old know-how with cutting-edge innovation and a passion for pushing boundaries. What truly connects them is an obsession with fighting for the last hundredths. On the racetrack, that pursuit is measured in fractions of a second. In watchmaking, it may mean shaving hundredths of a millimetre from a movement. In both worlds, progress comes through relentless refinement. In many respects, the partnership brings together two different forms of mechanical excellence. Ferrari and Richard Mille both manufacture movements; the difference lies largely in scale. One powers a racing car, the other a wristwatch. Both demand the same commitment to precision, reliability and uncompromising performance. As Ferrari Chief Design Officer Flavio Manzoni explains, “anything that has a technical purpose can also be beautiful”. It is a philosophy Ferrari describes as functional beauty, where aesthetics emerge from performance rather than being applied afterwards. Richard Mille shares that approach, creating timepieces in which technicity dictates aesthetics. For both brands, technical excellence has become a powerful source of appeal among high-net-worth consumers who increasingly value achievement, innovation and authenticity alongside performance and craftsmanship. The first chapter of the partnership was written in 2022 with the RM UP-01 Ferrari, the first watch born from the collaboration. At just 1.75 millimetres thick, it represented a triumph of technical prowess and Richard Mille’s approach to watchmaking, in which technicity dictates aesthetics. Developed through more than 6,000 hours of development and laboratory testing, it demonstrated how a shared quest for perfection could produce genuine innovation and challenge accepted limits. The second chapter followed in 2025 with the RM 43-01 Tourbillon Split-Seconds Chronograph Ferrari. Developed through close collaboration between Richard Mille’s team in Switzerland and Ferrari’s design department in Italy, it reflects the deepening relationship between the two. Inspired by Ferrari’s engineering universe, it translates a shared pursuit of performance into a creation informed by expertise from both sides. Crucially, neither side sought to impose its identity on the other. As Flavio Manzoni, Ferrari Chief Design Officer, has noted, the objective was to build on common values rather than simply transfer design codes. The result is less a co-branded product than the expression of two engineering cultures working towards a common goal. That spirit extended throughout the development process. As Julien Boillat, Richard Mille's Casing Technical Director, observed: “The team from Ferrari worked very closely with our experts for two years on this new project ... it was incredibly stimulating to have Ferrari as our co-pilots on this adventure.” Together, both timepieces demonstrate how product innovation can be transformed into lasting brand value. Yet for Richard Mille and Ferrari, excellence is not defined solely by what is created today, but by how the next generation is prepared for tomorrow. The partnership’s most enduring impact may ultimately be found beyond the products themselves. Its scope extends across Formula One, WEC endurance programmes, Competizioni GT, Ferrari Challenge, the Ferrari Driver Academy and the fast-growing esports category, reflecting a long-term commitment to innovation and future talent.

events.title: With lockout looming, World Series could be MLB's last games for a while
events.summary: Major League Baseball faces uncertainty as owners pushes for a salary cap, threatening a lockout starting Dec. 2 MILWAUKEE -- On the eve of the World Series, there is a realization these may be Major League Baseball's last games for a while. Owners are pushing for a salary cap, and that could prompt a lockout starting Dec. 2 and result in canceled games in 2027. “It would be a real bummer to lose a season, that’s for sure,” Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen said Thursday ahead of the World Series opener against Milwaukee. “I think the industry as a whole is in way too good of a place.” This year's World Series is the first since 1991 between teams both in the bottom half of payrolls : Milwaukee ranked 19th as of Aug. 31 and Tampa Bay 25th. MLB says a cap is needed to help all teams compete more consistently, but players contend because of the method owners use to define expenses, a cap would lead to management taking a greater share of the sport’s revenue. “The system that’s being proposed, which is similar to other leagues in terms of revenue-sharing system, not only will help us compete, but more importantly all of the teams with lower payrolls, too, which is something also I think the fans want,” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said. MLB’s proposal would cap spending in 2027 at $245.3 million using figures for luxury tax payrolls, and limit a player to 15% of a team's payroll. Free agents would be capped at $265 million over six seasons — far under Juan Soto’s record $765 million, 15-year deal with the New York Mets . The players' association vows never to accept a cap. “If they’re going to sit there and wave their little magic wand at us saying they’re going to get a salary cap, it’s not going to happen,” Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill said. Negotiations for a collective bargaining agreement to replace the five-year deal expiring Dec. 1 could turn into each side trying to outlast the other. “My thought with it all is keep building on the former generations and build on what they gave us,” said Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski, who throws the first pitch of the Series on Friday night. “You don’t want to be the generation to send something backwards. You just keep building on what former generations have given you and hope for the best.” Attanasio said the Brewers ranked 11th in non-player baseball operations spending this year and the Rays were ninth. The owner said about 250 people report to general manager Matt Arnold. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Milwaukee is ranked 30th and last in market size in MLB and could become the first small-market team to win the title since the 2015 Kansas City Royals. “We have to keep an eye on the present and one eye on the future in every move that we make. Every trade we have to think about that,” Arnold said. “There are tradeoffs for what you can do to help the team today and what that looks like going forward.” Tampa Bay is the No. 15 MLB market. While the Rays haven't spent lavishly on major league payroll, they were among the bigger spenders on player development this year. The players' association filed a grievance against the Rays alleging the team didn't meet its obligation under the labor contract to use revenue-sharing proceeds to try to improve its performance on the field. The grievance, covering 2017, '18 and '19, was withdrawn in December. In a bargaining session Thursday, owners proposed to allow the use of cameras on catchers for broadcasts. events.title: Keppel DC Reit's nine-month DPU up 11.7% on organic growth, acquisitions
events.summary: Keppel DC Reit’s aggregate leverage rose to 36.2% as at end-September, up 220 basis points from three months earlier. SINGAPORE – Keppel DC Reit posted a distribution per unit (DPU) of 8.571 cents for the nine months ended Sept 30, up 11.7% from S$0.0767 a year ago. Distributable income rose 16.7% year on year to $228 million from $195.3 million, the real estate investment trust’s (Reit) manager said in an operational update on Oct 23. Revenue grew 13.3% to $365.3 million from $322.4 million a year earlier, while net property income rose 13.1% to $316.8 million from $280.2 million. The improved results were driven by stronger operating performance, positive rental reversions and escalations, as well as contributions from acquisitions including Tokyo Data Centre 3 and increased effective interests in Keppel DC Singapore 3 and 4. However, growth was partially offset by higher finance costs from acquisition loans drawn in the fourth quarter of 2025 and lease extension considerations for Keppel DC Singapore 7 and 8, as well as an enlarged unit base following a private placement in September 2026. For the nine months, the Reit achieved a portfolio rental reversion of about 14%, supported by renewals and new contracts secured in Singapore and Australia. Portfolio occupancy stood at 93% as at Sept 30, up from 92.5% as at June 30. Weighted average lease expiry by lettable area was 6½ years. Keppel DC Reit’s aggregate leverage rose to 36.2% as at end-September, up 220 basis points from three months earlier, due to a partial drawdown of yen loans to fund the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5. Average cost of debt stood at 2.6% for the nine-month period, with an interest coverage ratio of 6.5 times. On its outlook, the manager noted that data centre fundamentals remain resilient, with demand growth continuing to absorb new supply. Artificial intelligence adoption is expected to broaden enterprise demand, with AI workloads projected to account for half of Asia-Pacific data centre demand by 2030. Units of Keppel DC Reit closed 0.5%, or one cent, higher at $2.05 on Oct 22. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Rights groups are worried that the agency at the heart of Trump’s immigration crackdown could sway the vote on election day. Since returning to office for a second term, United States President Donald Trump has embarked on a campaign to root out and deport the country’s undocumented immigrants. Spearheading that campaign is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal agency housed in the Department of Homeland Security. list 1 of 3 Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls list 2 of 3 Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election security list 3 of 3 Homeland Security Secretary Mullin reiterates Trump threats about elections Under Trump, the agency has grown substantially, boasting 22,000 officers and agents as of January, a staffing increase of 120 percent. Thanks to recent spending packages, ICE is also considered the best-funded federal law enforcement agency in the US. But the agency, founded in 2003, has come under increased scrutiny for its aggressive tactics and expedited hiring techniques. Immigration agents, under the authority of ICE and other agencies, have been responsible for at least 25 shootings since the start of Trump’s second term, six of which have been fatal. At least 60 people have also died in ICE custody since January 2025. That track record has made democracy advocates and human rights groups worried about ICE’s activities in the lead-up to the November 3 midterm elections. Organisations like Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have voiced concern that the Trump administration could use ICE to intimidate voters. The threat of encountering ICE agents could also keep some voters away from the ballot box, the groups say. One national poll, conducted in September by the University of California, San Diego, found that 40 percent of respondents expected ICE agents to be present near polling stations on election day. Can ICE agents legally operate at or near polling stations? Federal law prohibits the use of armed federal agents at polling stations. Some states have similar provisions. The federal prohibition dates back to 1865. The law reads that it is illegal for anyone “engaged in the civil, military or naval service of the United States” to order or bring “any troops or armed men” to election sites. There is, however, a loophole if such force is needed “to keep peace at the polls” or “to repel armed enemies of the United States”. Another federal law prohibits members of the military from interfering with elections, and several other laws prohibit efforts to “intimidate” voters. Those measures have been tested this year. During the primary elections for the midterms, there were at least two incidents – one in San Antonio, Texas, and another in Ventura County, California – where ICE agents reportedly conducted routine operations near polling stations. In both cases, the ICE agents left after being asked to do so by local police. How has the Trump administration used ICE agents before the election? Though there are prohibitions against law enforcement near polling stations, advocacy groups say the Trump administration has nevertheless used ICE agents for election-related matters. ICE has different offices under its control, one of which is Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). In the months leading up to this year’s midterm elections, HSI has reportedly been ordered to prioritise its investigations of non-citizen voting, an illegal act. Only US citizens are allowed to vote in federal elections. Starting in August, the Department of Homeland Security deployed HSI agents for “field investigations” in at least nine states to probe questions of voter eligibility. Some have reportedly gone door to door, asking residents if they are citizens and if they plan to vote. This week, a federal judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to pause those investigations, citing the risk that a US citizen could be “wrongly swept up” and “subjected to intimidation”. The judge also noted a “high likelihood of error” in how the federal agents were identifying alleged non-citizens. Trump has pointed to non-citizen voting as support for his false claims of pervasive voter fraud. Experts, though, say such fears are unfounded, with tiny numbers of non-citizens actually taking part in elections, despite Trump’s depictions of the issue as a widespread problem. What has the Trump administration said about deploying ICE during the midterms? Trump officials have refused to rule out using ICE agents to stop illegal voting, an effort that could extend to election day itself. In May, Trump was asked by reporters: “For the midterm elections, would you send the National Guard or ICE to voting locations in November?” Trump declined to answer directly. “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.

events.title: Trump says Musk restored Ukraine’s Starlink access amid Russia war
events.summary: The US president has declined to comment on the process that led Starlink to lift speed and access restrictions on Ukraine. United States President Donald Trump has said that tech mogul Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s access to Starlink, a satellite internet service that plays a key role in Kyiv’s war effort and air defences. On Thursday, Trump declined to discuss a report from The Wall Street Journal that he had called Musk and instructed him to end restrictions on Ukraine’s connection. list 1 of 3 What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it? list 2 of 3 ‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal list 3 of 3 Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine The news outlet reported that Starlink services returned to normal following the call. “I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report. On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling. Though the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty. Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and the Trump administration officials trading blame. Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink. “Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk. “The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio said on Wednesday. But Musk has denied any responsibility , stating that Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said in a social media post on October 14, using the acronym for “president of the United States”. The Starlink speed caps and restrictions have also raised concerns that Trump, or the president’s right-wing allies, might seek to leverage such technology to pressure Ukraine into complying with US demands. Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly calling him “difficult” in comparison to his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin. Ukraine has been locked in a slow-grinding war with Russia since February 2022, after Putin launched a full-scale invasion of the Eastern European country. While Europe has backed Ukraine’s defence against the invasion, Trump has suggested Ukraine itself could be to blame for the conflict. In 2025, for instance, Trump blamed Ukraine’s ambitions of joining NATO. “ I actually think that that was the thing that caused the start of the war,” he said at the time. More recently, Trump posted on Truth Social that it was Zelenskyy’s fault the war had not yet ended. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote. As the war continues, Trump has been criticised by Democrats and some members of his own Republican Party for easing US pressure on Russia. Recently, his administration issued a series of announcements to buy Russian diesel and ease restrictions on Russia’s energy sector. Those decisions come as Trump is struggling with the political fallout of high fuel prices caused by his decision to join Israel in launching a war on Iran. He has also suggested he would be open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which would be a first for the three leaders.

events.title: 'Sell or put up with it': Changed regulations redraw housing battle lines
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Suburbs across Victoria are facing changes to their facade as election battle lines are drawn Under new planning laws, a developer intends to demolish five single-storey units and build a six-storey block of apartments in this street. ( ABC News ) Residents of a leafy Melbourne street are getting a glimpse of what the future could hold for their neighbourhood, and it's a dramatic departure from the low-rise streetscape they know. In Armadale, in the Liberal-held electorate of Malvern, plans have been lodged with the council for a six-storey development on Mercer Road, about 900 metres away from the train station. The developer intends to demolish five single-storey units and build a six-storey block of apartments. If approved, there would be 29 two-three bedroom apartments and two levels of underground parking. A render of an apartment development that is proposed for Armadale. ( Supplied ) Dave Corrigan lives in an apartment across the road and described the plan as outrageous. "[It's] enough to almost make me consider moving, to be honest," he told 7.30. "I could probably understand on a main road and High Street … but in the middle of Mercer Road, that's just ridiculous." Under Labor's new "deemed to comply" planning rules, Mr Corrigan's objections carry limited weight and his right to appeal has been stripped away. Dave Corrigan opposes the plan and the government regulations. ( ABC News ) "Deemed to comply" means that if a development meets a series of standards set out by the government, it can be approved without the usual scope for objections or appeals. The rules took effect in April, with Labor arguing it would reduce red tape, speed up housing approvals and give developers greater certainty. With the state election approaching, Labor's high-rise housing plans are becoming a political test: as residents push back against towers in their neighbourhoods and the Coalition pledges to scrap the activity centres and return planning powers to councils. Under the Victorian Labor government's activity centres plan, designated areas around major train and tram routes are being opened to more intensive housing development, including buildings of up to 20 storeys or higher in some locations. Armadale, in the City of Stonnington, is among 60 designated activity centres. Some residents in Armadale aren't happy about the new six-storey development. ( ABC News: Kathleen O'Connor ) Labor says Victoria needs an estimated 2.24 million additional homes by 2051, with at least 70 per cent targeted for established areas. The federal government has targeted building 1.2 million new homes nationally by 2030. State Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny says the existing planning system failed to provide enough housing in areas where people want to live. "We've acted to say that the status quo is no longer an option," Ms Kilkenny told 7.30. "We cannot continue to have a planning system that continues to lock out Victorians from living in places where they want to live." The policy has drawn fierce opposition from residents and councils who argue the changes will alter the character of established suburbs, while limiting their ability to influence what gets built. Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr said residents often assumed taller buildings would be concentrated around railway stations and major roads, but that was no longer the case and councils have been stripped of meaningful influence over decisions that would fundamentally change their communities. "Council's involvement is minimal because if they tick the government's planning boxes now, residents have no right to object, they have no appeal rights and council has very limited ability to make changes to those proposed developments," Mayor Sehr said. Box Hill: The future of high-rise Melbourne? East of Melbourne's CBD, Box Hill offers an example of what a shift towards high-density housing could look like. Danny Todica lives in a 30-storey apartment block, in Box Hill. ( ABC News ) Danny Todica lives there with his partner in a two-bedroom apartment in a 30-storey tower. The 52-year-old said the convenience of apartment living is hard to beat. "We have the highway just there, we have the shopping centre just around the corner here, so it's in walking distance of everything and the tram stop is just out there," Mr Todica said. Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years. He once campaigned against high-rise development but in 2016 bought an apartment in the 36-storey Sky One tower he had opposed. "If you can't beat them, join them," he said. Phil Ward has lived in Box Hill for 47 years.

events.title: Yen jumps as traders seek safety amid global flight from risk
events.summary: The Japanese currency rose 0.8% to 156.86 per US dollar and touched its strongest level since late September. The yen rose 0.8% to 156.86 per US dollar as weak tech and AI earnings, plus Middle East tensions, pushed investors towards safe havens. Treasuries jumped, the dollar slipped, and the Swiss franc also gained. The euro fell as French debt stress and higher energy prices hurt sentiment. Options traders grew more positive on the yen, but analysts said central bank meetings and US elections may stop a lasting rally. The yen surged, outperforming all its major counterparts on Oct 22, as a sell-off in global equities boosted demand for havens. The Japanese currency rose 0.8% to 156.86 per US dollar and touched its strongest level since late September. It gained 0.9% against the euro. A fresh round of disappointing technology and artificial intelligence-related earnings weighed on risk sentiment , along with escalating Middle East tensions, which boosted oil prices. Treasuries soared and the dollar edged lower. “Given that AI risk is US-centric, AI jitters have driven US yields lower, which in turn may have led to lower USD/JPY,” OCBC FX strategist Sim Moh Siong said. Other haven currencies also fared well. The Swiss franc gained 0.4% against the dollar. Meanwhile, the euro was marginally lower in the US afternoon as intensifying French debt stress together with elevated energy prices weighed on the common currency. “Foreign currency markets are reflecting traditional risk-off patterns, with the yen and Swiss franc outperforming, amid underperformance by the euro,” said Alex Cohen, a strategist at Bank of America. Options traders have also turned more optimistic on the yen as reflected in one-month dollar-yen risk reversals. The shift suggests investors are increasingly positioning for near-term yen gains, even as strategists debate whether the recent strength is being driven primarily by risk aversion or emerging domestic flow support. Still, analysts cautioned against reading too much into the move. “With central bank meetings coming up next week and the US midterm elections further ahead, I do not currently expect this to develop into a sustained yen appreciation trend,” said Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking. events.title: Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
events.summary: Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court. Thousands of people have protested in more than 20 towns and cities across Poland, calling for access to free and legal abortion services. list 1 of 4 A look at some of the world’s toughest abortion laws list 2 of 4 How women are resisting Poland’s abortion ban list 3 of 4 Poland’s ban on abortion forces many to seek help in Germany list 4 of 4 Women call for tougher EU stance on Poland’s abortion laws Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress. The demonstrations come days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the mostly Catholic country, but are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative President Karol Nawrocki. Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw. She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki’s veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women’s support to win elections next year. In the capital, Warsaw, about 1,000 protesters demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain. “Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36-year-old Emilia Niemiec, who manages the AboTak abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out a pharmacological abortion. Restrictive abortion laws have been in place in Poland since 1993, with Polish women leading calls for the legalisation of abortion ever since. In 2016, nationwide demonstrations took place, with women donning black as a sign of protest. But rather than being relaxed, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of foetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, with the overwhelming majority carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted. Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared with 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals. The tunneling venture was created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later. Boring Co. raised $3 billion in September, with backing from the United Arab Emirates. SpaceX said on Thursday that its stake in Elon Musk's The Boring Co. netted the company an investment gain of $561 million during the third quarter. The gain accounted for more than half of SpaceX's "other income" in the period and boosted its net income, which landed at just over $4 billion, the company said in its quarterly financial filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Created inside SpaceX in 2017 and spun out a year later, Boring Co. says its mission is to "revolutionize transportation" by creating underground tunnels with stations where passengers can board and exit. Last month, Boring Co. raised $3 billion at a $23 billion valuation, with backing from the United Arab Emirates and a roster of other longtime Musk supporters. Boring Co. has announced about a dozen city projects, but its only tunnels currently open for public use are in Las Vegas, where passengers can travel in Tesla vehicles between the downtown convention center and various casino resorts using its Las Vegas Convention Center Loop. In July of last year, Boring Co. struck a deal to build about 20 miles of tunnels in Nashville, Tennessee. The Music City Loop, as it's known, is being designed to carry paying passengers between downtown and the airport in Tesla vehicles. The fast-tracked project sparked a partisan feud when it was greenlit and has drawn new safety concerns over sinkhole risks this week. In the UAE, Boring Co. plans to build over 150 kilometers (93 miles) of tunnels, including a project announced in February of last year, the Dubai Loop. SpaceX also said in Thursday's filing that it purchased $151 million worth of Tesla's Megapack energy storage systems during the quarter. Musk said on SpaceX's earnings call on Tuesday that he thinks it would be a "good idea" for the two companies to merge, and said they've both created special committees to discuss a potential transaction. events.title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. “We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.” “Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt. The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.” When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring. “I’m wearing the Ring,” it announced. Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote. The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Tech Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said. The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump wanted a ‘Trump Ocean’ on Google Maps. He says CEO Sundar Pichai shut it down
events.summary: President Donald Trump has another body of water in mind for a name change: the Atlantic Ocean. But this time, he says, Google CEO Sundar Pichai told him no. “We seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean, and I called Google Maps, who were really great with the lake,” Trump said at a rally in Pendleton, S.C., on Wednesday . “No, no, no. This time, I’m not doing it,” Trump recalled Pichai saying. According to Trump, Pichai explained that oceans span multiple countries and urged him, “Please don’t ask us to do that.” “Should I pass on… I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean, right?” Trump asked the crowd. But Trump wasn’t finished with the oceans. He then floated renaming the Pacific the “American Ocean” and asked how Europe would feel about it, though no part of Europe borders the Pacific. It wasn’t the first time Trump had raised the idea. At a rally in Dalton, Ga., last Friday , Trump said he had asked Google about renaming either the Atlantic or the Pacific the “Trump Ocean.” “You know what they said? ‘We’ve had it. That’s enough. We’re not doing it anymore,’” Trump told the crowd. He said he was only kidding. He then added that he had sent Google “a little picture” labeled “The Trump Ocean,” and that the company called back to say oceans were different. “I said I was only kidding. That time I was,” Trump said. Trump first teased an ocean rename in August, when he signed the order renaming Lake Ontario in the Oval Office. Fortune asked Google to confirm Trump’s account of the conversation and whether it had received a formal request to rename the Atlantic Ocean. Fortune also asked how Google would handle a proposed name change for an ocean shared by multiple countries. Google did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Trump’s push to rename geographic landmarks began on his first day back in office. On Jan. 20, 2025, he signed an executive order directing the federal government to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. On Aug. 27, 2026, he signed Executive Order 14422 , renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, even though the lake is shared with Canada. Can Trump rename an entire ocean? For federal use, names of oceans and seas fall under the Foreign Names Committee, part of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. That’s according to a September report by the Congressional Research Service , Congress’s nonpartisan research arm. Trump could direct federal agencies to adopt a different name for the Atlantic or Pacific. That would not make the change binding anywhere else. Lake Ontario shows the limits. Trump’s order renamed it for U.S. federal use, but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the change , saying Canadians would keep calling it Lake Ontario “then, now and always.” Internationally, a United Nations resolution on geographical names says that when countries sharing a feature can’t agree on a common name, each country’s name is accepted. One country’s choice doesn’t override the others’. An ocean bordered by dozens of countries would be far harder to rename than a gulf or a lake. Google didn’t have to follow Trump’s lead. But it did. Google was not legally required to adopt either name change. The CRS report notes that federal naming decisions don’t bind private companies such as Google Maps and Apple Maps. Still, Google Maps adopted the Gulf of America and Lake America for U.S. users after the federal Geographic Names Information System was updated. Google said the changes followed its long-standing policy of reflecting official government sources and showing different names for bodies of water by country. For the Gulf, users in Mexico still see Gulf of Mexico, while users outside the U.S. and Mexico see both names. The Gulf decision carried a cost: Mexico sued Google over the label. For Lake Ontario, Canadian users continue to see the original name, and users outside the U.S. and Canada see both. Apple Maps made the same switch for U.S. users days later. Business Insider reported that Google was “ getting flak ” over the lake rename, facing backlash from users and Canadian officials. Meanwhile, rival MapQuest refused to adopt the new name, as it had with the Gulf. Its app climbed from No. 128 on Apple’s U.S. App Store on Aug. 28 to No. 1 overall by Sept. 1. The app recorded an estimated 632,000 U.S. downloads after Trump’s Aug. 27 order, according to Sensor Tower data reported by TechCrunch . From floating “Trump Strait” for the Strait of Hormuz to proposing “American Ocean” for the Pacific, Trump has no shortage of new names. But if his account of Pichai’s reluctance is accurate, an entire ocean may be one step too far for Google. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Oil tankers sailing US-China route are commanding US$60 million and it is crushing demand
events.summary: Asian refinery orders for American crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels in October sequentially. US crude exports to Asia are falling as tanker costs on the Gulf Coast-China route hit almost US$80 million, making long-haul trade far less attractive. Asian refiners cut November orders for American crude by about 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels, which could be a seven-year low if it continues. Freight costs, insurance, fuel, and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman are tightening tanker supply and squeezing US crude prices, Bloomberg said. NEW YORK – American crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost US$80 million (S$102 million). Asian refinery orders for American crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels in October sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly. If that pace of orders holds through the end of October, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the United States Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost US$60 million as at Oct 22, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Earlier in October, it touched US$79.6 million, an unprecedented ruction in a market where rates averaged less than US$8 million in the half decade before the conflict. As it stands, leasing the largest class of crude carriers for the 30-day voyage is equivalent to half the cost of building a brand-new vessel. Those eye-watering rates do not include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around US$100 a barrel. “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, Valero Energy’s head of oil trading, said during as conference call with analysts. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending US$30 to US$35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out in 2025, Hawkins said. To be sure, the end of the November trading cycle is not a hard deadline, which leaves some leeway for traders to snap up last-minutes cargoes. At least one market participant, who asked to remain anonymous, said Asia-bound US cargoes for November may recover to as much as 40 million barrels in post-cycle trades. Vortexa, however, is sceptical that such a turnaround is imminent. “We don’t currently see evidence of a near-term surge that would push those volumes significantly higher,” said Rohit Rathod, a senior Vortexa analyst. The drop in Asian demand appears to be rippling across US crude pricing. Export-bound Permian Basin oil was trading for 25 US cents above the benchmark futures contract at the Magellan East Houston hub as at Oct 21, down from more than US$3 six weeks earlier, according to Link Data Services. Medium sour export grade Mars, which is pumped from deep water wells in the Gulf of Mexico and is similar to Middle Eastern crude, has seen its premium to futures plunge to US$6 from US$17.50 in late March. Valero’s Hawkins said one factor hindering global tanker availability has been the increased use of smaller vessels to pick up crude in the Persian Gulf that are less likely to be hit by Iranian fire in Strait of Hormuz. Once they have traversed the waterway, their cargoes are transferred to larger vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. “The inefficient process of this ship-to-ship transferring that they’re doing of crude oil in the Gulf of Oman is really tying up global shipping and requiring more tankers to move the same amount of oil,” Hawkins said. Insurance rates and high fuel costs are also driving up freight costs, he added. “The primary factor remains high freight costs, which continue to squeeze arbitrage economics for long-haul routes,” Vortexa’s Rathod said. “The incentive for Asian buyers to source from the US Gulf Coast has diminished.” Bloomberg

events.title: Treasuries surge as worldwide worries spark rush to safety
events.summary: A French police officer extinguishing burning bicycles during a demonstration against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris on Oct 17. Treasuries rallied for their best day in more than a year, surging across the board as a deepening rout in AI-related shares , market turmoil in France and fresh Middle East tensions all combined to make US government debt the investment of choice for anxious traders. The gains on Oct 22 sent yields tumbling by as much as 20 basis points on some maturities, the most since August 2025, with the 10-year benchmark dropping back below the key 5% level for the first time in a month. Adding to the momentum was a wave of buying in Treasury futures, as traders rushed to unwind bearish bets and cover short positions. Mounting concerns around the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment – a major driver of US growth – and doubts about its eventual payoff have sent tech shares plunging from recent highs, leading some investors to hedge their bets by flocking to bonds. These worries are starting to spill over into unease about the outlook for the economy as a whole, leading traders to pull back on their expectations for an interest-rate increase this year. “There’s a change in the weather,” said David Robin, an interest rate strategist at TJM Institutional Services LLC. “Flight-to-quality is one thing, growth risk is something entirely different.” The rally powered on even as global benchmark Brent crude oil futures topped US$112 a barrel after deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns that escalating Middle East hostilities could hit supply. Increasingly, the inflationary surge in energy prices, a driver of bond losses that just weeks ago sent yields to multi-decade highs, is also being seen as another potential drag on growth. It is one reason traders are scaling back rate bets, fully pricing in a quarter-point hike for January, rather than December. On top of all this, there are the troubles in France , which sent French yields across maturities reaching multi-year highs and exceeding their German counterparts by historically wide margins. As French financial assets have been hit by mounting investor anxieties about its debt burden and the eruption of cost-of-living protests, US Treasuries have been a beneficiary. Robert Waldner, chief investment officer and co-head of Invesco Fixed Income, said they had been waiting for evidence of “something starting to break” after the surge in Treasury yields in recent months. “Treasury yields rose to extreme levels,” and AI worries means “for the time being that we have seen the peak”, he said. “Sentiment seems to be shakier these days as investors reconsider AI-related assets,” said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank. “With US yields still elevated by recent standards, investors may want to hedge off some of these risks by seeking safety in Treasuries.” A US$26 billion (S$33.2 billion) auction of five-year Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, was awarded at 2.367% – less than a basis point higher than the prevailing yield at the bidding deadline. It was the highest-yielding auction of the tenor since October 2023. A Bloomberg gauge of returns on Treasuries climbed about 1.2% in October as of Oct 21, after rounding off its biggest monthly drop in almost two years in September. “Even though oil has been slowly rallying, Treasuries have been feeling some safe haven flows again,” said Kenneth Crompton, head of rates strategy at National Australia Bank. events.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s creative plan to pay California’s proposed billionaire tax without losing control of Meta
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of nonvoting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote. Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control. Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest being used for food assistance and education. The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes. The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class. The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August. The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says. That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake. When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.” It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax. Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize. “Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added. events.title: Etsy bans AI-generated recipes and patterns from its online marketplace
events.summary: Etsy said it's banning AI-made recipes, patterns and instructions from its online marketplace. The company also laid out clearer rules around AI usage on its platform, including barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. User confusion around AI content on the platform has emerged as a "top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy," the company said. Etsy said Thursday it will no longer allow merchants to sell AI-generated recipes and patterns on its online marketplace, as part of a wider push to set firmer rules around the use of artificial intelligence on its platform. In a blog post , Etsy said it's banning the sale of "functional guides" that are created using AI, including patterns, cooking recipes and instructions. The products are usually marketed as digital downloads, such as crochet or sewing patterns. Users then "put in effort to achieve a finished product," the company said. Sellers will also be required to show an actual item made using the instructions, not an AI-generated or simulated result, "so buyers know what to expect," Etsy said. Etsy said in a separate notice to sellers that it was making the changes as AI threatens to erode buyers' and sellers' trust in the platform. "Today, many active buyers say they can't tell which items involve AI-generated content," the company wrote. "It's become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy. And you, our seller community, have told us you're concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways, and that it's becoming harder for buyers to recognize your role in creating your items." As part of the move, Etsy said it's barring sellers from creating bot-generated listings without any human involvement. Sellers will also be required to include at least one unedited photo of the actual item they're selling. Etsy told sellers it will continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform as long as merchants "play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process." "Sellers must still disclose when an item is created using AI and cannot misrepresent AI-generated work as handmade or entirely their own creation," the company added. Founded in 2005, Etsy is known for its mix of craft makers and artisan goods. The company has been leaning more into that reputation as it has battled an influx of generic, mass-produced items from resellers and increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart , as well as newer e-commerce upstarts like TikTok, Temu and Shein. Misleading, AI-generated products or images present a new challenge for Etsy and other online marketplaces. Etsy has in recent years struggled to curb the proliferation of AI-made crochet patterns and other AI "slop." Amazon recently required sellers to label photos or videos that feature AI-generated people in response to recent legislation mandating the disclosure. While Etsy has cracked down on the use of AI in listings, it's been infusing the technology throughout more of its website. The company has used AI to build more detailed profiles of shoppers and surface relevant products in search results. Etsy has also partnered with OpenAI on shopping features, including launching a ChatGPT app for product discovery.

events.title: Judge: Federal government lawyers ‘barely defend’ giving Elon Musk’s DOGE illegal access to government data
events.summary: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) breached federal law by sharing sensitive government data with the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), according to a federal judge. In a 39-page ruling released on Tuesday, Judge Denise Cote said OPM violated the Privacy Act of 1974 , a post-Watergate law which prohibits the disclosure of certain records and outlines requirements for safeguarding others, and subsequently disobeyed its own cybersecurity practices. OPM failed to provide a credible reason for why DOGE would need access to personally identifiable information (PII) of tens of millions of federal employees, as well as applicants and retirees, according to Cote.  “The defendants barely defend its legality, relying instead on what has happened since to argue that the case is moot and that prospective relief is unnecessary,” Cote wrote in her ruling. Musk assembled DOGE in the first days of President Donald Trump’s second term, claiming the special advisory would root out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government. While DOGE claims to have saved the government $215 billion in cancelled contracts and the reduction of approximately 300,000 government workers , former federal employees, including former IRS acting Commissioner Douglas O’Donnell, have warned the sweeping cuts will have lasting impacts on the government’s ability to increase efficiency through updated technology. The Department of Justice (DOJ), which served as the legal team for OPM, argued in previous court filings that DOGE agents required access to sensitive data—including employee records, background checks, medical files, and banking information—as part of the group’s workforce modernization efforts. However, previous government modernization initiatives have not required access to such information, Cotes said, and the administration never made a connection between the access to data and DOGE agents’ responsibilities. Cotes also rejected the government’s argument that the lawsuit was moot because DOGE is no longer a centralized entity. While DOGE agents have had access to sensitive OPM data since September 2025, one former agent is not employed at OPM, Cotes said. She did not offer a final remedy for the case. OPM and DOJ did not respond to Fortune ’s requests for comment. Policy experts and federal workers share privacy concerns A coalition of unions, including the AFL-CIO, filed a lawsuit against DOGE and the Department of Labor in February 2025, challenging the special advisory’s access to private information.  At the time, Musk justified the increased access as a means to reconcile variabilities in how government data was stored and displayed. “These databases don’t talk to each other,” Musk said in a Fox News interview last February. “And that’s really the source of, that’s the biggest vulnerability for fraud, is the fact that these databases don’t talk to each other. So we need to reconcile the databases. It’s a, frankly, painful homework, but it has to be done, and will greatly improve the efficiency of the government systems.” Policy experts, however, have warned DOGE’s access to government data could present significant cybersecurity and privacy risks, such as private-sector engineers without clearances having sensitive information on personal devices, as well as the increased vulnerability of a centralized database to hackers. “Being able to amass all of that information will give the federal government unprecedented power and control to do with that information a number of things that we just haven’t experienced as a country before,” Elizabeth Laird, the director of equity in civic technology at technology policy nonprofit the Center for Democracy and Technology, told Fortune last year.  Even if the dissemination of the data was legally permissible, Laird argued, it would still be a threat to the security of the information.  “Something can be private, and something can be secure, and it can be legal,” she added. “And it can still be a bad idea.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: SpaceX in talks to access 80,000 cell sites for wireless network
events.summary: SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk has made no secret of his intentions to create a standalone wireless carrier from scratch. SpaceX is talking to tower owners, including Crown Castle, to access at least 80,000 cell sites across the US for a new wireless network. The deals could be worth billions and would help Elon Musk build a fourth nationwide carrier to challenge AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. SpaceX has bought low-band spectrum and won FCC approval for 15,000 satellites, but it still needs ground sites for reliable mobile coverage. WASHINGTON – SpaceX aims to secure a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the United States, and it is in talks with at least one major cellular infrastructure company to reach that goal, according to sources familiar with the matter. The agreements would solidify the rocket and satellite giant’s path towards building a fourth nationwide wireless carrier, said the sources, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. One of the companies they are in talks with is Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers. When asked on Oct 21 on an earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com or other satellite-based telecom providers, chief executive Chris Hillabrant said: “You can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” He declined to discuss specific customer details. American Tower declined to comment. SpaceX and Vertical Bridge did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the US to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T, Verizon Communications and T-Mobile US typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it is more cost-effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared. The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has made no secret of his intentions to create a standalone wireless carrier from scratch, threatening the existing dominant providers with increased competition from a well-funded and politically potent new rival. While the prospect requires significant investment, Musk is ploughing ahead. SpaceX recently acquired low-band spectrum that will help it parlay its Starlink satellites and other elements into what Musk described as a “major mobile carrier”. The company won US Federal Communications Commission approval to launch 15,000 satellites designed to provide mobile service directly to phones. Wireless tower sites are another key component that SpaceX must assemble to establish reliable links with users on the ground. “We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there’s broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate,” Musk said during SpaceX’s earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition “will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US”, he said. Crown Castle’s Hillabrant said SpaceX’s acquisition of the low-band spectrum is a “huge milestone” in being able to provide broad mobile coverage. Tower companies’ share prices rose on the news of SpaceX’s latest spectrum purchase earlier in October, suggesting that the market anticipates major business coming their way as SpaceX seeks to build larger-scale infrastructure to implement the new airwaves. SpaceX has already said it plans to use its home internet equipment to emit mobile signals in the areas surrounding customers’ installations. Those sites are located where subscribers are, however, and not necessarily where they are needed to provide consistent coverage for a network, according to the research firm MoffettNathanson. events.title: Palmer Luckey teams with dire wolf billionaire Ben Lamm to launch $200 million Warhound, unleashing genetically engineered clone dogs of war
events.summary: The Colossal and Anduril founders want to clone, gene-edit and armor America’s working dogs, and bring the supply chain home from Europe. The U.S. military’s oldest autonomous system has a supply-chain problem: most of its dogs come from Europe. Fewer than half make it through training. And the Pentagon is bidding against foreign governments for the ones that are left. Ben Lamm is the co-founder and CEO of Colossal Biosciences, the Dallas de-extinction company that announced in April 2025 it had brought back the dire wolf, a predator that died out more than 10,000 years ago. What Colossal actually produced was three pups, Romulus, Remus and Khaleesi. Its scientists took gray wolf cells, edited about 20 sites across 14 genes to match DNA recovered from ancient dire wolf remains, cloned the pups from those edited cells and had domestic dogs carry them to term. Lamm and Anduril founder Palmer Luckey think the same tools, plus defense hardware, can fix that. Warhound, a defense tech startup the two came up with, is coming out of stealth with a $200 million seed round, Fortune can exclusively report. David Spirk, a former Marine and the Pentagon’s former chief data officer, is CEO. The company is based in Texas. The backers are In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, ARK Invest, Franklin Templeton , 8VC, USIT, Bob Nelsen, Breyer Capital, CAZ Investments, Neogenesis, Builders VC and Lux Capital, among others. “A dog is the oldest autonomous system there is,” Lamm said in emailed responses to Fortune ’s questions. “For thousands of years, dogs have gone into danger ahead of the people they protect.” Importing the good boys The Army set up the K-9 Corps in 1942. Today the Department of War’s Military Working Dog Program has more than 2,200 dog teams, according to the company, and more than 80% of U.S. military working dogs are bought from Europe. Lamm cited a Senate Armed Services Committee warning that “due to the finite number of breeders overseas, as well as rising market demand, the cost… to procure whelped military working dogs from Europe is skyrocketing.” He also cited the American Kennel Club’s assessment that “there is now a shortage of even mediocre quality foreign dogs available.” The U.S. is “competing against other country governments” for the same animals, Lamm said, China and Russia among them. The losses after purchase are expensive, too. According to the company, fewer than half of the dogs bought are judged fit for service after a roughly three-year acquisition and training pipeline. That means the U.S. has to buy and train about 200 dogs today to field 100 working animals later. Biobank, clone, edit Lamm described the plan in stages. Warhound will find top dogs that have finished training and biobank their genetic material. It will then clone those proven dogs, though Lamm said “training and environment will always influence performance.” Alongside that, it will work on targeted gene edits. The first group of dogs has already been biobanked and is being edited now, Lamm said. He expects to deliver the first dogs in about two years. “Breeding and raising a dog takes the time it takes,” he said. Warhound will screen out known harmful variants tied to muscle degeneration and other inherited diseases, so that “no dog enters service carrying genetic markers known to cause common career-ending conditions.” Lamm said the company is still working out which other traits are “scientifically and responsibly actionable.” Even so, he said Warhound is “planning future genetic enhancements to improve their already exceptional performance.” Anduril is supplying equipment including eye and ear protection, body armor, and integration with its Eagle Eye system, so that “dogs, handlers, and autonomous systems operate as one team.” The release announcing Warhound calls these “cybernetic Augments.” Lamm said the dogs are not a step toward robot dogs, nor a hedge against them. “No machine today matches a dog’s nose or its judgment in complex environments,” he said. No contract, no price tag Warhound has no signed customers yet, as Lamm said the company is working with canine experts across the national security community. It also isn’t quoting a price per dog, because “a young dog, a partially trained dog, and a cloned dog of proven health with training and support through retirement are very different things.” Lamm said Warhound is discussing a “Canine-as-a-Service model,” in which the government would buy a steady supply of trained dogs instead of individual animals. Software companies have sold to the Pentagon by subscription for years, and now the model is coming to the kennel. Cloning working dogs isn’t new. South Korea’s customs service deployed six cloned sniffer dogs in 2009. A decade later, Chinese scientists said they had cloned a top police dog , a Kunming wolfdog named Kunxun, to cut training time, and talked about producing more. By that November, six cloned K-9s had joined the Beijing police . Nothing at the scale needed exists yet, Lamm said, so the company plans to build national-scale kennel and training infrastructure step by step, “starting with private capital.” It has hired what Lamm called “one of the top dog handlers ever to serve in the U.S. military” as director of canine operations. The American Humane Society will certify Warhound’s training programs and help reunite retired dogs with their former handlers. The Captain America dog program The company says Lamm and Luckey came up with Warhound after a conversation at Peter Diamandis’ Moonshots Summit. Lamm said Luckey “loved our dire wolf announcement,” and the two got talking about the military’s working dog programs: where the dogs come from, how many wash out and what it costs to replace them. “I’m all about origin stories, especially when we’re talking about the Captain America dog program,” Lamm said. In the comics, the super-soldier program took a scrawny Army reject and made him the best soldier in the service. Warhound is aiming at the dogs who don’t make the cut. Then the two founders mostly stepped back. “Palmer and I don’t describe ourselves as co-founders,” Lamm said. “We developed the concept.” Luckey “doesn’t even own equity in the business,” he said. “I decided to be the one of us to join the board and tap Dave Spirk to do this,” Lamm added, saying he knew him well, as Spirk had spent four years as an adviser to Colossal and had watched the de-extinction work up close. Spirk spent eight years in the Marine Corps and close to 20 more as a government civilian in the intelligence community and special operations. He was the first chief data officer of U.S. Special Operations Command and then of the Department of War, and he was a plank holder on Project Maven, the Pentagon’s AI targeting program. He also served as deputy associate director of national intelligence for Afghanistan and Pakistan. More recently he was a senior counselor at Palantir , a stint Lamm said Spirk calls his “Palantir dip
