events.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
events.summary: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures. The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture. That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic. A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t. The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost. Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency. Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance. GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive. The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat. Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements. For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value. Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances. That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy. Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset. EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable. Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes. The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale. This content was produced by EXL. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

events.title: Here's how to protect your information from the PHP flaw, according to cybersecurity pros
events.summary: Cybersecurity researchers say that anyone's personal information is at risk after OpenAI disclosed a vulnerability in a popular software language. Richard Drury/Getty Images Cybersecurity researchers say the PHP vulnerability has repercussions for normal people, too. Even if you don't own a website, hackers could use the vulnerability to steal your information. One quick fix: diversify your passwords. If you're still using the same password for everything, it might finally be time to get on that. While the major cybersecurity vulnerabilities that OpenAI agents helped expose on Wednesday primarily impact the owners and operators of websites, it could also give hackers the opportunity to hijack your personal information, researchers said. "Be extra careful visiting ANY web site in the next few days," Changpeng Zhao, the cofounder of cryptocurrency platform Binance, said on X. OpenAI said on Wednesday that researchers using its AI models uncovered two "critical" flaws in the infrastructure of PHP, a popular open-source programming language used on about 70% of the world's websites. Because digital commerce websites, for instance, can store personal shopper information in PHP systems, that information would be accessible to a bad actor exploiting the web provider's system if that provider hasn't updated it. The National Security Administration warned that hackers using one of the PHP exploits could "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network." "Even if you yourself are not building software and that's not where your core business is, a lot of your life does depend on companies that depend on those systems," Madeline Lawrence, cofounder of Aikido Security, an application security platform, told Business Insider on Thursday. "And they could be deeply, deeply vulnerable," she added. She said that one day after the disclosure, cybersecurity platform Cloudflare reported millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerability. If you do own a website, PHP has released updates it says will help shield websites from hackers. Instructions for applying those updates are available on PHP's homepage. For everyone else, here are a few tips cybersecurity researchers say you can use to protect your info. Don't reuse passwords; use a password manager. Check for security advisories from your bank. Use two-factor authentication on your devices and accounts — especially for email, banking, and your password manager. If your data has been breached, expect more convincing scams and phishing emails. Turn auto-updates on and restart your computer weekly. "You can ask your claude code to audit what on your laptop is out of date and needs updating," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, a bipartisan nonprofit that advocates for safety guardrails and federal oversight, added in a post on X. PSA: in light of recent cyberattacks and vulnerabilities, I recommend everyone: * use a good password manager (1Password) and do not duplicate passwords * use two factor auth for everything important (not via sms!! Google Authenticator or better yet YubiKey) * Auto-updates on,… — Peter Wildeford🇺🇸🚀 (@peterwildeford) October 21, 2026 Though Lawrence called the vulnerability "very severe," she cautioned against people running to close their bank accounts to protect themselves. "Assume that if you're getting a notification that your data has been leaked," she said. "Take action on that because you could have credentials or information floating around the dark web." events.title: Microsoft and the Public Library Association expand free AI literacy training
events.summary: Expanding AI literacy with the Public Library Association and community-based programs Oct 22, 2026 | Justin Spelhaug - President, Microsoft Elevate The people and institutions closest to a community understand their needs best. Libraries, small businesses, nonprofits, and schools see firsthand where AI can create opportunity and where people need support to navigate change. At Microsoft, our role is to help these trusted institutions lead by providing practical resources, training, and clear safeguards that strengthen local capacity and put communities at the center of AI literacy and adoption. Public libraries have served as trusted centers of community learning across the United States for generations. Today, we are announcing a new initiative with the Public Library Association, a division of the American Library Association, to expand resources and no-cost AI literacy and skills training for public library workers and their patrons. This work delivers on the commitment we made earlier this year through our Community-First AI Infrastructure initiative: to expand access to AI learning and opportunity by investing directly in local training. We’re committed to neighborhood learning through libraries, free literacy training, and certification opportunities, age-appropriate learning in schools and colleges, and support for nonprofit and small-business workforces. This new library initiative is the latest example of our broader work to help trusted local institutions serve as entry points for AI learning, skills development , and opportunity. This program comes alongside small business accelerator programs in TechSpark, our new Elevate for Changemakers platform connecting nonprofits to resources, and our ongoing national and statewide work to bring safe and responsible AI to education. Local libraries lead AI learning in their communities The Public Library Association AI literacy initiative we are announcing today, Building AI Skills and Agency Through Libraries , is designed to build practical skills, critical awareness , and the judgment to use AI safely and appropriately. It will pair Microsoft’s AI skilling resources with PLA’s national network of expert practitioners to support library workers and community patrons as they navigate this rapidly evolving technology. The initiative will expand practical resources and training for library workers, create opportunities to learn from one another through a Community of Practice, and offer free webinars and guidance to support their work with patrons. Library workers help people navigate information, find learning resources , and make informed decisions for themselves and their families. Supporting those workers is a practical way to bring AI learning closer to people, while respecting the independence of the institutions they trust. The approach reflects a broader view of AI literacy: people need more than instructions for using AI tools; they also need the knowledge and judgment to decide whether, when and how those tools should be used. The training will help library workers and patrons understand how AI works and expand their skills , while also evaluating potential risks, protecting personal and confidential information, critically evaluating AI-generated claims and sources, and better understanding considerations related to safety and bias. Equipping trusted local institutions to lead responsible AI adoption Last July, we launched Microsoft Elevate, a company-wide initiative that brings together our work to help people and institutions build the skills and capacity to navigate AI responsibly. Under the Elevate charter, each year, Microsoft supports nearly one million nonprofit organizations and education systems worldwide with technology, training, grants and discounts. Microsoft Elevate for Educators, our global community of over 100,000 teachers and school leaders, recently recognized our inaugural group of 20 Beacon Schools and School Systems that are leading examples of AI transformation in education, bringing together effective AI practices while keeping educators and students first. They are powerful examples of what happens when you combine committed educators, AI-powered technology, and intentional, no-cost staff training. In Washington, our Elevate commitment has included a $3 million, two-year investment supporting 10 school districts and 10 community and technical colleges with grants, coaching, and communities of practice. To date, the initiative has reached 29,375 educators, with early pilots in Kennewick and Everett helping teachers explore practical uses of AI while keeping professional judgment at the center. Skills and access must be matched by strong safeguards. In September, Microsoft joined the American Federation of Teachers to establish a national AI Safety & Privacy Standard for Schools , with enforceable protections for student and educator data, human oversight , and transparency for families. Beginning November 1, every US school district can request Microsoft to add these protections to a new or existing agreement, without waiting for renewal or renegotiation. That same commitment extends to nonprofit staff and leaders. The Elevate for Changemakers program has already supported over 18,000 learners, helping them build practical AI skills, connect with peers, and earn recognition for turning learning into tangible outcomes for their organizations. And today we are expanding the program and introducing a new, connected experience that brings training, resources, and community together. Together, these efforts reflect a simple principle: responsible adoption requires more than technology. Educators , nonprofit changemakers , and community leaders need time, training, trusted connections, practical support , and clear guardrails so they can decide when AI strengthens learning and , equally important, when it does not. Investing in locally led economic opportunity across all 50 states For nearly a decade, Microsoft has partnered with local nonprofits and small businesses across the U . S . through our TechSpark program. Through Fellows grants, TechSpark pairs local expertise with Microsoft coaching and a national peer network to help nonprofits expand their impact in their local community and drive accelerated innovation for local small businesses. Today, Microsoft is announcing the new 2027 TechSpark Fellows across all 50 states and releasing the 2026 Fellows Impact Report showing what a locally led model can make possible. Over the last three years, the Fellows cumulatively report access to more than $298 million in community funding, 59,600 people trained and upskilled in AI literacy , and more than 1,500 nonprofit partners mobilized to advance their missions within their communities. These numbers tell an important story: no single organization can create lasting opportunity on its own, and local context matters.

events.title: I'm a boomer who's not leaving my kids an inheritance. How do I break the news to them?
events.summary: The offers and details on this page may have updated or changed since the time of publication. See our article on Business Insider for current information. A reader (not pictured) asks how to tell their children that they don't plan on leaving them an inheritance. Curly_photo/Getty Images For Love & Money is a column from Business Insider answering your relationship and money questions. This week, a reader's kids incorrectly believe they're getting a large inheritance. Our columnist says to loop them into their plans, and to focus on the memories they'll leave behind. Dear For Love & Money, My husband and I are in our 60s, the baby boomer generation . Due to hard work over the course of our adult lives, we've been able to comfortably retire. Because my husband and I set them up for success, our two kids, now all grown up, are doing quite well. We paid for a considerable portion of their college costs , their health insurance, and their car insurance until they moved out. We drove them to all the extracurriculars that helped get them where they are today, and paid for a couple of decades' worth of food, clothing, and shelter. They also got to have amazing life experiences, such as a two-week European vacation when they were teenagers. Recently, we had them and their spouses over for dinner, and a lighthearted conversation came up about inheritances. Our kids joked about who the favorite child was and who was likely to inherit our wealth . Since they were kidding, my husband and I didn't feel at the time that we needed to set the record straight. But now we've been talking and are now wondering if we need to say more — because we actually don't plan on leaving any inheritances for our children. We plan to use our hard-earned savings for our retirement years. If we live the comfortable, adventurous lives we want to over the next 20 years, we don't expect there will be much left for an inheritance. We even plan to sell the house, which is paid off, to afford our final years when we need assisted living . I don't feel like we owe our children anything, and they don't seem to need anything. However, I'm starting to wonder if telling them our plans will be a problem. How do I tell my kids there isn't going to be any inheritance after we pass? Sincerely, Boomer Who Wants to Spend My Own Money For Love & Money answers your relationship and money questions. Looking for advice on how your savings, debt, or another financial challenge is affecting your relationships? Submit your question in this Google form . Dear Boomer, Maybe I grew up poorer than I realize, but in my experience, few middle-class people plan on receiving a financially meaningful inheritance. We expect to go through Grandma's basement and figure out what to do with a lifetime's worth of accumulated belongings . We hope our parents have life insurance policies to cover the costs of wrapping up a life and saying goodbye. But few of us truly envision future will readings where the black sheep laughs cynically about being cut out, the stepson throws a tantrum over not inheriting the Van Gogh collection, and the niece no one's ever met inherits it all. However, we've all seen that movie. Thus, we joke about our parents' wills, favorite children, and who will inherit Yellowstone Dutton Ranch when they're gone. You asked me how to tell your kids, "There isn't going to be an inheritance," but I don't think this is an announcement you need to make. For most people who hold no claim to great wealth, even if they are financially comfortable, estate plannin g is a family affair. You and your husband will still have the final say over your estate, but medical bills, inflation, health concerns, and all sorts of unknowns can easily complicate money matters. Your anxiety might stem from you second-guessing a dynamic you were comfortable with back when the reality felt far away. You might not have a fortune to bestow on your children when you pass, but you will still give them an estate to sort out and conclude. They will be the ones to carry out your end-of-life wishes and figure out memory care should the need arise. Your children are the ones who will need to present death certificates to close down your bank accounts and hold an estate sale should you stay in your house to the end, after all. Considering the enormity of this task, looping your children in now is a good idea. There's no need for this conversation to include a dramatic confession about how little you have to leave them; instead, it invites them into your plans and lets them know what to expect. It isn't too late to start investing a small amount and designating the returns for your children, of course. But remember that when your kids are playfully squabbling over inheritance , they are likely thinking of the possessions you will be handing down rather than money. For instance, my dad has a large library of floor-to-ceiling bookshelves packed with hardbacks written by writers like Louis L'Amour, Dean Koontz, and Agatha Christie. Neither my siblings nor I expect to receive even a tiny cash legacy, and we know the books hold little value, but you can bet we always argue — mostly in jest — over who will inherit the collection. Simply taking the time to thoughtfully divide your prized possessions and sentimental momentos and naming who gets what in your will is likely more of an inheritance than your kids expect, but one they will be very grateful to receive. In your letter, you listed all the ways you've set your kids up for success, but I didn't need the list to believe you. You have built a legacy where your adult children and their partners can sit around your dinner table joking with you and one another. This is the best legacy — one full of love and laughter. You did it. Rooting for you, For Love & Money An earlier version of this article was originally published in December 2024. Looking for advice on how your savings, debt, or another financial challenge is affecting your relationships? Write to For Love & Money using this Google form . events.title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds. Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber . Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview. Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles. Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over. Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028. “The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.” Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap. Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator. “For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.” It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.” Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable. Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1T pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day. Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said. “Especially when you think about validation, right? So that’s really the piece where you’re saying, ‘is the system good to ship?’” Philbin said. “And there, you really want to have a good sense of this sim-to-real gap, because to do that kind of hand on heart, you really need to trust that answer is in the positive. Otherwise, you’re measuring something that’s not representative of how it will actually perform in the real world.” This article was updated to include more quotes from Philbin and more details on Rivian’s automated driving strategy. events.title: Trump asked Musk to lift Starlink slowdown, WSJ reports
events.summary: President Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported. Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk, per the Journal. Trump has repeatedly denied involvement in the decision and said he does not know if Musk was behind it. President Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to ease restrictions he had imposed on the military-grade version of SpaceX 's Starlink system in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials. The Starshield system, which Ukraine depends on in its war against Russia, was "working more normally Thursday, shortly after" Trump spoke to Musk by phone, U.S. and Ukrainian officials told the Journal. Trump said later Thursday he did not "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk. "Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump told reporters outside the White House as he departed for a campaign rally in Iowa. "The bottom line, he put it back," Trump said of Musk. The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk, the founder and CEO of SpaceX and a critic of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had ordered the Starlink slowdown. Two unnamed sources in that report said Trump and Musk had discussed the decision to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, while one source said Musk had spoken to Trump prior to imposing the speed cap. "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved," Trump said Wednesday. The Starlink controversy, which drew bipartisan concern and criticism from lawmakers, emerged as Trump has ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy for continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure. At the same time, Trump has pursued a deal to ease sanctions on Russia so it can supply some diesel on the global market. Trump must sit for deposition in BBC lawsuit by Dec. 11, judge orders Virginia state Sen. Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle Sen. John Cornyn , R-Texas, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Wednesday that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House." Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the ranking member of the Senate homeland security committee's investigations subcommittee, on Thursday launched an inquiry into how SpaceX's satellite tech was "degraded for Ukraine without notice." "This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally not only put Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril, but raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," Blumenthal said in letters to Musk and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Thursday's report that Trump had asked Musk to lift the restrictions.

events.title: I made a rookie flight-booking mistake that cost me $3,000. These are the 4 things I'll do differently next time.
events.summary: One flight-booking mistake cost my family nearly $3,000 and a day of travel. Natalie Becerra I booked two separate flight itineraries on different airlines for a family trip to Ireland. I realized this was a mistake after the first airline diverted, and the second left without us. The fix cost my family nearly $3,000 in new tickets and a day's worth of touring. I'm a veteran traveler who has booked more long-haul flights than I can count. But earlier this year, I made a very expensive rookie mistake. While planning a trip, I came across a deal I couldn't pass up: a $317 one-way flight on Icelandair to Ireland with a multi-day layover in Reykjavik. It was essentially a way to take a trip within a trip without paying extra airfare. The catch? The flight departed from New York, not our home airport in Florida. I'd be in New York a few days early, but my family would need to fly up to meet me. Booking separate itineraries was far from ideal, but I figured a five-hour buffer would be enough. It wasn't. A storm in New York canceled my family's JetBlue flight from Florida, and their replacement flight then couldn't land and was diverted to Virginia. Their Icelandair flight to Europe was automatically canceled after they were marked as no-shows. On the night we were supposed to fly together to Iceland , my family was stuck states away, and I was scrambling to find a solution. With my family's original flight gone, we had to spend nearly $3,000 to get them back on track and navigate the complicated credit card trip insurance process. Here are 4 lessons I learned the hard way. Booking separate itineraries comes with a pricey risk I didn't account for enough time for flight disruptions. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Arriving in the city of your next flight at least 24 hours before may feel a bit extreme, but it's the minimum safety net you need. Being already in the right location for your flight can be a huge weight off your shoulders. It also allows sufficient time for rebooking should something go wrong with your flight. My last-minute whim to visit a few friends upstate turned out to be key. Those extra two nights in New York meant I was able to make the flight to Iceland. If I had booked my family of three on a flight the day before our long-haul flight, they would have made it too. My family made it to New York the next morning and ended up taking a replacement flight to Iceland that evening, getting in about 24 hours later than originally planned. I bought two basic economy tickets for $734 each, and one standard economy ticket with extra baggage allowance for $1,105. In total, I spent $2,573 on new tickets. The costly mistake made me realize that although an extra hotel night is an added expense and may mean using more PTO, it's a cheap investment compared to the cost of new international flights — and the cost of missed events — if things don't go to plan. This is especially worth it if you have definite plans right after your arrival, such as a cruise or a concert. Neither airline has to help in my scenario Neither airline was required to help my family make their flight to Iceland after the diversion. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When you book connecting flights on a single itinerary, the airline is responsible for getting you to your destination. If you miss that connection through no fault of your own, then the airline will put you on another available flight at no additional cost. When you book flights separately, you're responsible for making each connection — or buying new tickets if you miss one. And generally, regardless of reason, the airline operating your next flight isn't obligated to accommodate you if you miss it because of a problem with your previous airline. Our tickets to New York and Iceland were separate, so despite numerous calls to each airline, none were responsible for the missed connection. If you do miss a connection on a single booking, look up alternatives yourself and discuss them with the agent. It's not guaranteed, but they may be able to accommodate you on a partner airline at a more convenient time. And remember, it's not the staff's fault for the disruption. You get more bees with honey. I should have read the fine print It didn't make sense for me to pay to change my flight to wait for my family, so I took my original flight to Iceland. Michael Nigro/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images I didn't book the cheapest fare, but I didn't read the fine print either. When things started to go wrong, I was shocked to see there was a $250 change fee per person on my original flight and no refunds. Changing the tickets would have cost nearly as much as the original flight, plus the fare difference. At the time, it was uncertain when my family would actually arrive in New York and feasibly be able to catch the next flight to Iceland, so we didn't change the tickets. Missing the first flight on this stopover itinerary meant my family was marked a no-show and their onward leg to Dublin was canceled, which is standard airline policy. While there were other ways to get to Iceland , there were few nonstop flights from Iceland to Ireland — a one-stop meant at least four extra hours of travel — so the best option was to book a new stopover ticket with Icelandair. When I started booking the new tickets, I noticed that almost every fare class had punitive cancellation and change policies — and this time I was sure to be familiar with the terms of my booking. I need to better understand my credit card's trip protections I will better strategize which credit cards I use to book flights. OGI75/Getty Images Premium credit cards can have your back when flight plans go wrong, but they don't cover everything. We used the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business' trip cancellation and interruption protection for the original Icelandair tickets and were reimbursed $952. The coverage typically reimburses covered unused, prepaid expenses — but not the cost of buying new airline tickets. Trip delay coverage doesn't either, but it can cover other expenses for covered trips. However, credit card policies vary — and this is where I went wrong. We booked the flights to New York on an American Express Business Platinum Card but used a different card for the return flights. That meant the Amex trip-delay protection did not apply: its terms require the full round-trip fare to be charged to the eligible card. I had split the flights across cards to preserve Chase's bag-delay protection, but I didn't realize I was giving up the Amex protection in the process, so the $103 spent on dinner after the diversion wasn't covered. For future trips, I'll use only one credit card with good travel protections for all my trip expenses to reduce complications. Airlines may also provide some compensation for flight disruptions. events.title: Embracing the Experience Economy
events.summary: As CSTS Enterprises pivots from a 78-year history of traditional corporate travel into luxury experiences, global events and tech-enabled service, Group CEO and executive director Abel Zhao is betting that the future of travel and experience economy will be defined less by where people go and more by what they can do once they get there. When Abel Zhao thinks about the future of travel and live experience, he begins with a memory. As a high school student during the 1998 FIFA World Cup, Zhao was too young to enter the stadium. Instead, he stood outside with friends, listening to the roar of the crowd and absorbing the energy of thousands of people gathered from around the world. “We could only stand outside and hear the cheering, but that was already exciting enough,” he recalls. Decades later, that experience has become part of the strategic thinking behind one of Hong Kong’s most ambitious travel transformations. Following its acquisition of Connexus, one of Hong Kong’s leading travel agencies, CSTS Enterprises has repositioned itself at the intersection of travel, sports, entertainment, technology and major live events. Its ambition is to become “the world’s leading experience innovator” – connecting people, brands and cultures through travel and shared experiences. For Zhao, Group CEO and executive director of CSTS Enterprises, the transformation was prompted partly by necessity. Covid-19 severely disrupted the travel industry, and more than half of Hong Kong’s travel agencies disappeared, he says. “We needed to find a way to grow,” Zhao says. CSTS’ transformation began with a shift in how travellers define luxury. Premium flights, five-star hotels and expensive restaurants are no longer enough. Customers increasingly seek access, rarity, meaning and memorable experiences. “Traditionally, when people thought about travel, they thought about booking flights and hotels,” Zhao says. “But now it’s completely redefined.” Through Connexus, CSTS already had a strong B2B foundation, serving multinational corporate clients. That business provided trusted relationships, operational expertise and travel infrastructure. The next step was to apply those strengths to the experience economy, particularly global sports, entertainment and exclusive live events. Events such as the FIFA World Cup, UEFA Euro Championship and Formula 1 require much more than tickets. They involve logistics, hospitality, local knowledge, contingency planning and personalised service. CSTS therefore aims to become an “experience company” rather than simply a travel intermediary. For event customers, the experience begins “once they step onto a plane” and continues until they return home safely. Behind the scenes, multi-location teams coordinate suppliers, solve problems in real time and manage every stage of the journey. “Precision and personalisation,” Zhao says, are central to the model. The company also challenges the idea that luxury is defined solely by spending. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, CSTS served ultra-high-spending clients, including one family whose expenditure exceeded US$2 million. At the same time, college students saved money, flew economy and stayed in modest hotels to attend an iconic event in New York. “Premium or experience tourism does not just mean you spend more money,” Zhao says. “It is something that can be created with special content and something that has a significant impact on yourself.” CSTS’s role is to curate moments that customers cannot easily arrange themselves, from access to football legends and exclusive hospitality to entertainment and culturally significant cross-border experiences. Partnerships with major sports and entertainment organisations are central to the strategy. They provide access, expertise and a significant barrier to entry. “Working with some of the largest brands or IPs already creates a very high market entry barrier,” Zhao says. Technology is the other pillar of CSTS’s future. Zhao sees the technology evolution is necessary for improving corporate travel, analysing customer behaviour and making daily service more efficient. The company plans to apply those capabilities gradually to its newer, more bespoke experience businesses. The aim, he says, is to use technology to “significantly increase efficiency and create value for our customers”. However, Zhao does not believe technology will replace the human element of travel. On the contrary, as people spend more time online, they may place greater value on concerts, sporting events, cultural gatherings and other shared experiences. “The one thing technology cannot impact is the experience,” he says. “The more technology is adopted, the more people want to go out there and find a reason to sit in the crowd watching a football game with everyone else.” CSTS is building an international operating structure with core teams in New York, Hong Kong and Shanghai.

events.summary: These youth, aged 16 to 24, are known as the bedroom generation, for staying at home and living off parents. The transition to adulthood has never been easy. My own early twenties, about a decade ago, were a time of high anxiety, low self-esteem and steep learning curves. There were friendship group dramas, internships with bad bosses and the stress of in-person job interviews. But there was also plenty of social interaction: small talk at the office and big talk at parties. In fact, there was little true alone time in the spin cycle of university, work, house shares, dating and socialising that shaped me into the person I am today.

events.title: ‘They are here to sweep the market’: Minor Food chief sees more Chinese chains opening in S’pore
events.summary: Minor Food Group chief executive Dellen Soh believes there is still money to be made in F&B, but survival will increasingly depend on the ability to rework the business model. Chinese restaurant chains are entering Singapore faster, using efficient kitchens, low prices and strong concepts. Dellen Soh said they are here to “sweep the market”. Local F&B firms must adapt with tighter menus, faster service and better cost control. Soh said weak hawker stalls and older brands may disappear if they cannot compete. Minor Food is refreshing brands, testing food retail and watching the 2027 RTS Link. It is also considering a Singapore listing to support future growth. SINGAPORE – As the Singapore economy expands, more Chinese restaurant chains are likely to enter the Republic, bringing efficient kitchens, competitive prices and “beautiful” concepts that could leave older local favourites struggling to keep up, said Minor Food Group chief executive Dellen Soh. These operators are not just testing whether Singaporeans like their food. They are also bringing business models honed in China’s fiercely competitive food and beverage (F&B) market, with targets to expand across South-east Asia. “They are here to sweep the market,” Soh, a Singaporean, told The Straits Times in an interview. The influx of Chinese chains, from hotpot and grilled fish to coffee and tea, is reshaping Singapore’s dining scene and raising the stakes for local operators whose menus, staffing and prices have not kept pace. While Soh believes there is still money to be made in the business, survival will increasingly depend on the ability to rework the business model, with some local favourites inevitably disappearing from the scene. Minor Food is a subsidiary of Thailand-listed Minor International, whose businesses span hotels, restaurants and lifestyle retail. Soh, who also heads Minor Food Singapore – operator of about 120 restaurants across 24 brand s, including Sanook Kitchen, Poulet and Mamma Mia – predicts that some longstanding hawker stalls and local brands will eventually disappear. This comes as owners retire and successors prove difficult to find, while heavier operating models struggle to compete with efficient global chains. For many foreign chains, however, Singapore is a demanding but valuable testing ground, filled with busy malls and well-travelled consumers who dine out regularly and have a deep appetite for global cuisines. If these chains can operate profitably here with their focused menus, lean staffing, fast preparation and competitive prices while satisfying discerning diners, they will be better placed to expand into other regional markets, Soh said. “If you can make it in Singapore, you can make it anywhere else in South-east Asia.” Good food and service, fast preparation and a cost structure that makes commercial sense may seem basic, but they are essential requirements for F&B brands to survive in Singapore, Soh said. Menu engineering helps bring these together. A carefully chosen range of dishes can make a kitchen easier to run, reduce the number of cooks needed and help restaurants serve consistently good meals at competitive prices. Soh pointed to shrinking dim sum menus at some restaurants as an example. “Maintaining a team of skilled chefs to hand-make each basket of dim sum is costly.” Minor Food has applied that thinking to Xin Wang Hong Kong Cafe, which is part of its Singapore portfolio. While the brand offered about 300 dishes when it opened 22 years ago, its menu has since been reduced to just 80 to 90 items. Streamlining the menu also speeds up service, cutting wait time and boosting table turnover during peak hours, Soh added. Keeping costs down must go hand in hand with giving diners a reason to visit, said the F&B veteran, adding that he would accept a higher food-cost ratio if lower menu prices helped fill the restaurant. An impressive margin on each dish means little if the tables are empty, especially when around 80% of people in Singapore eat out, he said. “The key is to offer good food at prices that encourage diners to return regularly.” Rising rents are a common complaint among Singapore’s F&B operators. But Soh said businesses should know their commitments when signing a lease and develop operating models capable of covering the rent. “It’s only when you cannot do well, then the rental becomes expensive,” he said. Soh expects rents to keep rising, pointing to pressure on real estate investment trusts and listed mall operators to grow their returns. Rather than count on concessions, he urged business operators to put themselves in the landlord’s shoes. “Overseas chains bring fresh concepts, attract crowds and can afford rents that some established businesses cannot. events.title: These are the tech and product leaders who survived the Paramount-WBD merger — and the ones who are out
events.summary: Skydance's co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz. NYSE Skydance is cutting tech and product leaders after closing its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Four WBD technology executives are out, per a memo from Skydance chief product officer Dane Glasgow. Its new team will mostly feature Paramount execs who worked on its recent tech transformation. Consolidation is underway at David Ellison's Skydance just a few weeks after the company closed its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Skydance's chief product officer, Dane Glasgow, laid out the product and tech leadership structure of the combined entity in a memo viewed by Business Insider. Four top WBD executives are leaving, according to the memo. They include: Avi Saxena , Warner Bros. Discovery's chief technology officer Tyler Whitworth , chief product officer for WBD's streaming business Dave Duvall , WBD's chief information officer Trish Collins Weedon , WBD's chief information security officer (CISO) Duvall, Saxena, and Whitworth will stay on in an "advisory capacity as we undergo this transition," Glasgow wrote. The company is mostly keeping Paramount executives in charge of its combined tech and product organization. These leaders include: Lakshman Nathan , Paramount's chief information officer Carlo Joseph, its chief information security officer Jim Harrison, its executive vice president of infrastructure, broadcast, and distribution Nick Lee , Paramount's executive vice president of media systems A few WBD executives are staying on in Skydance's post-merger leadership, per Glasgow's memo. They include  Brinton Miller,  formerly WBD's media technology and operations lead, who will serve as Skydance's executive vice president of production and studio technology, and  James Crossland , formerly head of global content operations at WBD, who will serve as its EVP of global content operations. Skydance has spent the past year revamping its tech and product team, often recruiting talent from tech companies. Glasgow joined Paramount from Meta, while Lee joined from Microsoft's AI division . Other team leaders in its post-merger structure include head of design  Suzanne Pellican , formerly a Google exec;  Hugh Williams , a former Google, eBay, and Microsoft exec; and Barak Turovsky , who came to Paramount after serving as chief AI officer at General Motors and VP of AI at Cisco. Bringing technical expertise to Paramount has been a priority for Ellison, who wants to turn the century-old media brand into a modern, tech-forward business like Netflix. The company revamped its data and insights strategy in January, and merged some engineering teams in March to bolster its streaming tech. "We are building a product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley," Ellison told CNBC earlier this month. In his memo, Glasgow expressed gratitude for the work of both Paramount and WBD staffers, writing that he was "encouraged by the early collaboration, the bold new ideas you're bringing forward, and your openness to exploring new ways of working with your colleagues." He also acknowledged the structural changes could be disruptive. "I know a change of this scale brings questions, especially as we get to know new teams and colleagues," Glasgow wrote. "Your leaders will share more about their organizations in the coming weeks and we'll bring our teams together soon to keep building with and learning from each other." events.title: Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
events.summary: The Super Bowl used to be exclusive to broadcast networks. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Airing the Super Bowl on many platforms cuts into the viewership and associated advertising revenue for broadcast stations. Get the CNBC Sport newsletter directly to your inbox The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox. Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives . Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission . And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates. ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private. Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021 . The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna. Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million. Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally. An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers. About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter. Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming. There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees. This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee. For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past. Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game. Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI. Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts " of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats"). Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"- themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+. The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free. Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.

events.title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors
events.summary: OpenAI is close to finalizing an up to $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, according to people familiar with the deal. Investors from the United Arab Emirates and Coatue are leading the financing, the people said. The financing is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering . The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said. Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public." Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation. events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech selloff
events.summary: Traders at work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City. US stocks fell sharply as renewed doubts about AI spending hit tech shares, with the Nasdaq suffering its biggest drop since June. Meta and Tesla both fell after earnings, while chip stocks slumped and the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost about a quarter from its June peak. Oil prices rose after new Houthi strikes, adding inflation fears, while strong labour data kept the Federal Reserve under pressure to raise rates again. NEW YORK - US stocks tumbled on Oct 22 and the Nasdaq posted its steepest daily drop since June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race. The S&P 500 ended deep in negative territory. The tech-laden Nasdaq, dragged down by microchips, fell the most in the wake of a spate of high-profile AI-related earnings results. Meta Platforms’ results beat analyst expectations, but its stock tumbled after the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the nascent technology. Tesla shares fell even though the electric car maker unexpectedly posted positive free cash flow in the quarter and cut its 2026 capital spending plans. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has driven much of the current bull market’s gains, plunged. With the Oct 22 decline, the SOX has lost about one-fourth its value since its record closing high reached on June 22, yet it remains sharply higher for the year, well outperforming the S&P 500‘s year-to-date gain. “It’s a wonderful day on Wall Street,” said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest, in Elmhurst, Illinois. “The only part of the market that is really suffering here is technology, which has been the golden child of the markets up until about June.” “Investors are starting to realise that there are some holes in the AI story,” Nolte added. “And that’s having an impact on the indices because they’re so heavily weighted towards technology.” On the geopolitical stage, Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes against Saudi targets, sending crude prices to a five-month high. Investors worried that ongoing Middle East strife could keep inflation hot and force the US Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates. Data from the Labour Department showed initial claims for unemployment benefits kept drifting along near multi-decade lows. Signs of labour market stability will allow the Fed to focus on fighting inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in the probability that the central bank will raise its policy rate by another 25 basis points before year-end. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 92.40 points, or 1.19%, to end at 7,664.77 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 690.28 points, or 2.58%, to 26,008.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 17.51 points, or 0.03%, to 52,873.60. Third-quarter earnings season is well under way, with 111 of the companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 83% have beaten analyst expectations, according to the most recent LSEG data. Procter & Gamble warned that rising cost pressures would take an increasing bite out of profit, but beat analyst estimates, sending the stock sharply higher and supporting consumer staples. Blackstone advanced after the company said widening credit spreads on AI-related debt could present an opportunity to lock in higher returns. Lockheed Martin climbed after the aerospace/defence firm raised its annual sales and profit forecast. Spotify jumped after the Swedish music streaming firm forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates, betting on its AI-powered features to drive user growth. Union Pacific rose following the company’s quarterly earnings beat, which was helped by core pricing gains, although the railroad flagged a hit from rising fuel prices. Chipmakers Western Digital, Intel, ADM , Sandisk, and Marvell all posted steep percentage losses amid the broader semiconductor selloff. REUTERS

events.title: ASX ends slightly up, ABC's The Business to end this year — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASX edges up at close, ABC's The Business will be discontinued at the end of 2026 — as it happened The ASX has finished the trading day up slightly after US tech stocks tumbled, led by Meta as its plans to ramp up AI spending fuelled doubts about whether the investment will pay off. Brent crude topped $US113 a barrel after further Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and concerns about a fresh escalation between the US and Iran. ABC News director Simon Robinson told staff that The Business would not return to screens in 2027. Look back on the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog. Disclaimer: This blog is not intended as investment advice. ASX 200 : flat to 8,795 points (live values below) Australian dollar : -0.1% to 70.08 US cents Asia : Nikkei -0.6%, Hang Seng +0.8%, Kospi -0.2% Wall Street : S & P500 -1.2%, Dow flat Spot gold : -0.1% to $US4,021/ounce Prices current at around 4:39pm AEDT Live updates on the major ASX indices: Choose what information you see below by using filters We'll end our markets live coverage here and thank you for all the love for The Business and our team! We really appreciate your support (it always makes my day, personally speaking anyways 😊). You can catch up on today's developments below, or download the ABC News app and subscribe to our range of news alerts for the latest news. The team will be back next week with all the latest. Now, time to say goodbye and have a great weekend! Batteries lower evening peak prices Violette Mouchaileh, AEMO's executive general manager of policy and executive affairs, said it was a milestone. "Batteries continue to shift record amounts of renewable energy into the higher-demand evening period, when households and businesses typically need more power," Mouchaileh said. "Increased battery charging and discharging contributed to significantly lower evening peak prices, with batteries setting prices in almost half of dispatch intervals, up from 18 per cent a year ago." AEMO said the east gas market was relatively subdued during the third quarter, with prices averaging $10.77 a gigajoule, up slightly from the same time last year. Demand was marginally lower, as declining demand from gas-fired generators was offset by an increase in exports from Queensland producers. On the other side of the Nullarbor, demand went up by 1.6 per cent amid lower temperatures and greater heating needs. Gas-fired plants surged 27 per cent year-on-year to meet those needs on the back of lower wind output and coal plant outages. Prices, meanwhile, soared to uncomfortable levels in the west, where they were 30 per cent higher at an average of $117 a megawatt hour, a new record. Once other system costs were taken into account, they averaged a painful $175 a megawatt-hour. Power prices continue to drop as batteries flex their muscles The latest troubles to hit Snowy 2.0 come amid profound changes in the national grid. In its latest snapshot of the national electricity system, the Australian Energy Market Operator noted that demand for power was surging even while wholesale spot prices were easing. So-called underlying demand, which includes the consumption households meet themselves through rooftop solar, jumped 1.3 per cent to an average of more than 25,000 megawatts in the three months to September 30 compared with the previous corresponding period. According to AEMO, Victoria accounted for most of the growth, which was driven by the switch to electrification, high industrial demand, and the rise of power-hungry data centres. As well as this, the market operator noted renewable energy was meeting an ever-greater share of the market. Generation from renewable sources increased from 41.8 per cent to 44.3 per cent of demand during the quarter, which included winter months typically associated with relatively low output from wind farms and solar panels. Leading the way was the unstoppable growth of rooftop solar, which surged 13 per cent to an average of 3,200 megawatts, followed by rises in grid-scale solar and hydropower output. And, in a major shift, AEMO noted that batteries for the first time eclipsed the contribution of gas-fired power plants during peak hours in the evening. Grid-scale batteries, the agency said, met 8 per cent of total generation during those hours compared with 5 per cent of gas plants as the amount of storage installed tripled over the course of the year.

events.title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
events.summary: President Donald Trump defended a controversial campaign ad by Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race. Trump's defense of the Republican nominee's ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton has "lied her entire life." "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do," Acton said. "My mother is not well." President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton , his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar. Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur , was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur. In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life." "Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad . "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse." Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004. Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse." "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor." Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him. "The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday. Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing." "I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said. Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim. Trump must sit for deposition in BBC lawsuit by Dec. 11, judge orders Virginia state Sen. Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate. But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America." "The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts." Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets. Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad. Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do." "My mother is not well," Acton said. Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested. "Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants." Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down. "The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line.

events.summary: On October 13th, Brendan Carr's FCC gave itself a new power - it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security . events.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
events.summary: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business. V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers. Don't let the door hit you on the butt “However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” Read full article Comments

events.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
events.summary: CoreWeave's stock is down 36% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening. The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds. CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 36% this month after plunging 10% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 179% in the past year and 39% in October. It last stood at 1,145 basis points, or 11.45%. The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 33% this month, while IREN's stock is down 38%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft . That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing. Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options. "Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant." CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter." Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary? Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
