events.title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
events.summary: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires. The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November. The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes. He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure. California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group. The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% , external each year. Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board. It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed. In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal. Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings. Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value. The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California. Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence." The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii. After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring. Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers. Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools. With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company. Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion , external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres . Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year. It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in. And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work. The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday. Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

events.title: AI could displace one in 11 workers, Goldman says, but the layoffs are likely waiting for a recession
events.summary: The AI layoff panic that peaked this spring has gone quiet. Goldman Sachs thinks the layoffs are waiting for a recession. “Concerns of imminent AI-related labor displacement have cooled in recent months after hitting a fever pitch this spring,” Goldman economist Joseph Briggs wrote in a note published Thursday. Then he laid out what may be coming. Under the bank’s forecast that AI eventually lifts productivity by 15% in the U.S. and other developed economies, he found that up to 9% of workers could be “displaced during the AI transition,” with slower hiring weighing on employment by another 3%. That’s roughly one in 11 workers. The bigger finding is about timing. Briggs went back through decades of data on how technology has replaced workers and found that “automation-related labor disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns.” “AI-related labor disruptions could well amplify the broader business cycle,” he wrote. Goldman has now made this argument twice, a year apart, from two different teams. In October 2025, Goldman’s U.S. economists David Mericle and Pierfrancesco Mei called “jobless growth” the likely new normal, Fortune reported at the time . “The modest job growth alongside robust GDP growth seen recently is likely to be normal to some degree in the years ahead,” they wrote. Then came their warning: “History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits.” Briggs reached the same conclusion. “The timing and extent of automation and labor disruption will likely track the overall economic cycle,” he wrote. The pattern goes back decades. “Historically automation-related labor disruption is quite cyclical,” Briggs writes, “with companies tending to automate work and shed labor costs when the economy starts to slow.” Mericle and Mei cited a leading explanation last year: “Companies use recessions to restructure and streamline their workforce by laying off workers in less productive areas.” The chart that makes the case tracks the share of Americans in routine jobs: clerks, secretaries, factory machine operators, mechanics. That share “has remained stable during expansions but declined sharply during downturns,” Briggs writes. The line drops in steps for the recessions of the early 1980s, 2001, 2008, and 2020, and it doesn’t climb back to where it was. “Historically, most of the labor headwinds from routine job automation are concentrated in economic recessions,” he wrote. Mericle and Mei pointed to the same pattern last year with the “jobless recovery” that followed the dotcom bust. “During that recovery, despite a soft labor market, productivity growth remained elevated, and GDP growth rebounded earlier than employment growth,” they wrote. Looking industry by industry, Briggs found that “labor market displacement is more severe when the economic backdrop is less favorable.” The hit to unemployment from a technology-driven productivity gain was 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points bigger when the overall jobless rate was rising. Across 25 occupations that past technology upended, employment fell an extra 4% over five years for every point the national unemployment rate climbed. “A more concerning takeaway from our analysis is that a cyclical slowdown would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses, thereby amplifying the broader business cycle,” he wrote. How 6% became 9% Briggs has been raising this number for a while. In August 2025, he and Goldman economist Sarah Dong estimated AI could displace 6% to 7% of the U.S. workforce if widely adopted, within a range of 3% to 14%. That used the same 15% productivity assumption. By June, on Goldman’s Exchanges podcast, Briggs put the figure at about 9%, or 15 million workers over a decade. He first described them as workers who would be “reallocated to new positions.” Thursday’s note calls them displaced. That’s a long way from where Goldman’s U.S. team stood last fall. Mericle and Mei said then that they were “skeptical of the boldest claims that rapid technological progress could lead to very high unemployment,” citing Goldman’s global economics team, which Briggs co-leads. Briggs can square his estimate with that: He says the displacement is temporary. On the podcast he said that “even under our forecast for 9% of workers being displaced, we’d still expect that the unemployment rate increase in any given year would be less than one percentage point.” Part of the answer is in what Briggs counts. Thursday’s note measures gross job losses rather than unemployment, because the jobless rate hides people. “Some workers that are displaced may find jobs relatively quickly,” he writes, “while others may decide to exit the labor force.” Historically, each 1% gain in technology-driven productivity pushed the unemployment rate up 0.3 to 0.4 points at its peak, fading to zero after two years. Over the same stretch, it raised the cumulative gross job-loss rate by 0.5 to 0.6 points. Multiply the top of that range by 15 and you get 9. The occupation data shows how bad it can get in one line of work. Briggs looked at 25 jobs hit hard by past technology, including photo processors, movie projectionists, proofreaders, file clerks, and bank tellers. On average, employment in those jobs fell 25% in the five years after it started to decline, “suggesting that very large job losses are possible when technology makes labor redundant.” He calls those numbers “likely upper bounds” for AI, since he picked the cases where technology hit hardest. Most of the shrinkage came from people losing or leaving jobs, more than from employers hiring fewer people. Separation rates rose in 19 of the 25 occupations, by 3.8 points on average. Hiring rates fell in 13, by 0.7 points on average. That’s why Briggs says AI-related layoffs “should provide a good real-time guide” to disruption. He also lists reasons the 9% could be low. Displacement ran higher during the late-1990s/early-2000s productivity boom, “the period most widely viewed as comparable to today.” It also ran higher after unusually large productivity jumps, and Goldman expects AI’s boost to beat most past ones. “This pattern suggests more scope for displacement during the AI transition,” he wrote. Why it’s quiet now “Given that our estimates point to a significant amount of technology-related job losses to come, why has the impact been limited so far?” Briggs asks. For now, the layoff gauge reads low. AI-attributed layoffs in Challenger’s tracking have pulled back sharply from their spring peak. News coverage of AI-related job losses has fallen back to levels from the start of 2026. Job growth in the most AI-exposed industries has run about 10,000 below its long-run trend over the past three months, roughly offset by hiring for AI-related construction. “While these patterns suggest that a modest labor market headwind is emerging, the near-term headwinds remain smaller th

events.title: Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this: “ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?” Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?” I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising . Demo-Driven Development Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have. Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this. That website works great in the demo —under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process. Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it. What you can do about it Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage. Learn how AI models work . If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions. Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team. Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter. I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time. Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us. Don’t chase (too many) shiny objects Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that. —Brian We Need to Embed Ethics Into Our Engineering Courses The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework. Read more here . The U.S. Just Bet $1 Billion on Quantum Chip Manufacturing Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips? Read more here . Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company. Read more here .

events.title: Black October: why bugs discovered by OpenAI tech are creating a cyber emergency
events.summary: The websites you use every day may have been vulnerable to hackers for years because of hidden flaws in their code that AI only recently discovered. Why it matters: The code, called PHP, powers millions of websites, and the vulnerabilities could allow hackers to steal sensitive data or take control of affected servers. If exploited, the bugs could allow attackers to steal sensitive information, like your passwords and data, or take control of vulnerable servers. Driving the news: A potential attack exploiting flaws in PHP emerged on Wednesday, which prompted governments and companies to temporarily take their websites offline while they installed security patches. Dozens of websites in the U.S., U.K., and around the world were briefly taken offline to make the fix. The disruption put the National Security Agency and Europe's cybersecurity agency on alert. State of play: Security patches were released to fix the issues on Oct. 21, 2026. Cybersecurity firms urged anyone using PHP to install the security updates immediately. What they're saying: OpenAI's technology helped find the bugs, and the company called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory." "To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did," OpenAI said. The cybersecurity firm Wiz wrote in a blog post : "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history." Read more below. What is PHP? You've probably never heard of PHP, even though you've interacted with it for decades. PHP, which stands for Hypertext Preprocessor , is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known. It has been around since the 1990s to help build websites, taking data and generating content sent to a browser. It's still used today for a variety of websites, including Wikipedia, WordPress blogs and shopping websites. How it works: HTML determines what a website displays. PHP works behind the scenes to collect information and generate content. What was the PHP vulnerability, exactly? AI researchers discovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP that could have allowed an attacker to take control of a website's server without having legitimate access to it. Hackers could exploit the flaws, dubbed " php2shell " by cybersecurity firms, to steal information from those websites. Between the lines: The flaws went undetected for more than a decade because exploiting them required complex technical work that AI helped researchers discover, per Wiz. Why cybersecurity incidents are a big deal Thought bubble via Axios' Bradley Olson : The PHP vulnerabilities are so serious that the NSA warned website operators to take their sites down if they didn't have enough time to patch the bug. But the cybersecurity problems in recent days have extended far beyond that and include disruptions to developer platforms, data leaks on public schools, break-ins on public companies and more. A major Axios scoop also revealed that banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agent access inside customer accounts, a problem they are racing to contain. Cyber pros are calling the series of attacks "Black October" due to the sheer volume and the level of risk, although so far many organizations have mitigated the risk and avoided massive real-world harm. While defenders and AI companies have warned for months that a season of cyber emergencies would imminently arrive, they have also been working to secure some of the obscure software that still underpins much of the modern internet ecosystem. The bottom line: As attacks continue, experts have urged users to secure passwords, use a password manager and also to avoid panic. As with any cyber emergency, the true barometer of harm is the extent to which damage seeps into the real world, as it has done with ransomware that took hospital software offline or a pipeline system that disrupted fuel supplies briefly on the East Coast.

events.title: Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak
events.summary: People near south Wales river were told to keep windows and doors shut after thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site got into the water Oily slicks of kerosene still appeared to be leaking into the River Taff this week, several days after a breach of thousands of litres was spotted by members of the public. The breach into the Welsh river was identified last Friday, after people reported strong chemical odours emanating from it. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) officers arrived on site soon afterwards to identify the source of the pollution and were assisted by the south Wales fire and rescue service, which placed absorbent mats and booms to contain as much kerosene as possible. Residents along the Taff were advised to keep windows and doors closed last week, after it emerged that thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cynon Taf had entered the river. Four kilometres (2.5 miles) of waterway were affected, according to NRW. GE Aerospace is a US multinational company that designs and builds military and commercial aircraft systems and engines. Its site in south Wales is among the world’s largest maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for commercial aircraft engines, employing more than 1,350 people. In 2017 GE Aerospace was the recipient of £5m in funding from the Welsh government, intended to support innovation and sustainability in the aerospace sector. Despite early estimates of a volume of about 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled, NRW was unable to confirm what quantity entered the river, and could not comment on possible enforcement action while its investigation was under way and it gathered information. Public Health Wales advised that the community should avoid all contact with contaminated areas along the busy stretch of river, which runs parallel to many popular trails on both banks, including the Taff trail. People near the river had been complaining of sinus problems and headaches. “Kerosene vapours may be mildly irritating to the respiratory system. Our current assessment is that people who can smell kerosene may experience temporary irritation, particularly if they are exposed for prolonged periods,” said the health body. Sarah Llywelyn, who lives in a riverside home in Glan Y Llyn downstream from the GE Aerospace facility, was among those who reported the leak to NRW. “The smell was absolutely unbelievable. My eyes burned as soon as I opened our door into the garden. I knew it must have been huge because of the smell, and it’s a fast-flowing river – it was essentially unsafe from the point of contamination to Cardiff Bay. We moved here because of the river. What I want more than anything is for lessons to be learned. This should never happen again.” A visit by the Guardian to the site found oily slicks still leaking into the Taff five days after the incident began. NRW believes that the pollution has now been stopped from entering the river. An NRW spokesperson said: “Fuel that entered the drainage system before the leak was stopped by the operator could remain within parts of that network and whilst containment measures help reduce and capture pollution, they are not always able to separate all fuel from flowing water. Our work to investigate this incident and assess environmental impacts is ongoing.” Prof Steve Ormerod, from Cardiff University’s Water Research Institute, confirmed that the photos of the leaks appeared to show the kerosene still entering the waterway through the bunding (a secondary storage system, usually to catch overflows). “The Taff has been recovering from its grossly polluted past,” he said. “So this incident is a potential setback to clean water species such as salmon, dippers and kingfishers that have been recolonising the river. “Kerosene is a mixture of paraffins, naphthenes and benzene-like chemicals that risk direct toxicity to aquatic organisms, reductions in oxygen transfer across the water surface, and suffocation through impaired gill function in fishes or insects. Effects on feather waterproofing are also likely in the birds that have no choice but to enter the water to feed. Overnight rain was insufficient to raise river levels and flush the Taff, so kerosene will still be lurking in backwaters and eddies along the river.” Gerwyn and Jordan Lewis from Ynysgau farm, directly opposite the site of the main spill into the river, said they were advised by NRW that the river was unsafe for animals to drink from due to kerosene pollution, meaning that areas of the farm with access to the river could not be safely grazed. “We simply cannot take the chance of our animals becoming seriously ill or dying. Our winter feed stocks could now be depleted at an alarming rate, leaving us facing the possibility of having to purchase substantial additional feed at considerable expense.

events.title: The fight for MAHA's soul
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s alliance with health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. helped deliver Make America Healthy Again voters. But the movement Trump spent years cultivating is showing signs of splintering. Now the question is whether Kennedy could reconsolidate the same voters if he launches a new bid for the presidency. He’s lost battles over pesticides, failed to codify food safety efforts into durable regulations, and faced legal hurdles in his bid to reshape federal vaccine policy. “This administration has screwed over MAHA numerous times,” a former HHS official who worked on MAHA issues told me. “MAHA folks have started to become independent again, if you will, and they will no longer vote by party, but by whoever they think will advocate the most for them.” The departure of top Kennedy confidant Calley Means today leaves MAHA advocates without arguably their most vocal champion within the Trump administration. Means described Washington as a “corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo” in a text message confirming the news first reported by The Wall Street Journal. Vocal MAHA activists cried foul when the Trump administration advanced a directive on an herbicide that they said was too industry-friendly. Others say Kennedy hasn’t done enough to codify his work on food dyes so the restrictions will live on after Trump leaves office. An HHS spokesperson touted the administration’s “historic MAHA wins,” but for practical purposes, health policy is back up for grabs. Per lobbyist TJ Petrizzo: MAHA is intertwined with MAGA. Meanwhile, liberals are keen to win over the same voters — even if they are unwilling to court the anti-vaccine crowd. Democrats, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed, are going after voters concerned about corporate influence over food and pesticides. Vice President JD Vance (a noted fan of Kennedy’s sauerkraut diet ) will make his own bid for the voting bloc after appearing at events like the MAHA Summit. Kennedy is bouncing around Texas, New Hampshire, and Florida to tout the Trump administration’s work on chronic kidney disease, rural health efforts, and nutrition. Those are safe talking points for the midterms, but hardly the MAHA agenda Kennedy promised to deliver in Washington.

events.title: Only 10 artists have topped the Billboard chart with 10 different albums — here they all are
events.summary: Taylor Swift performs during the Eras Tour in Toronto. Emma McIntyre/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management The Billboard 200 is the definitive all-genre chart for album sales in the US. Only 10 artists in Billboard history have topped the chart at least 10 different times. The Beatles have the most No. 1 albums with 19. Taylor Swift and Drake are tied for second place. The Billboard 200 has tracked the best-selling albums in the US for decades. It's a major accomplishment to top the chart, especially when an artist manages the feat with multiple different albums. Only a handful of artists have crossed into double-digit No. 1s, including modern superstars like Taylor Swift , Drake, Jay-Z, and Future. They're listed below in ascending order. Editor's note: Although Elvis Presley is often credited with 10 No. 1 albums, a Billboard representative told Business Insider that most of his biggest releases predate the modern Billboard 200 chart, which launched in 1963. Madonna — 10 Madonna performs in New York City's Times Square in 2026. James Devaney/GC Images Madonna's 2026 album "Confessions II" became her milestone 10th No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Madonna is also the first artist with a No. 1 album in the 2020s to have already topped the chart in three other decades: twice in the 2010s ("Madame X" and "MDNA"), four times in the 2000s ("Hard Candy," "Confessions on a Dance Floor," "American Life," and "Music"), and thrice in the 1980s ("Like a Prayer," "True Blue," and "Like a Virgin"). Bruce Springsteen — 11 Bruce Springsteen performs with The E Street Band in 2023. Sergione Infuso/Corbis via Getty Images Bruce Springsteen's 11 chart-topping albums span over three decades, from 1980's "The River" to 2014's "High Hopes" — even though Springsteen has yet to score a No. 1 hit song on the Billboard Hot 100. Barbra Streisand — 11 Barbra Streisand performs at Madison Square Garden in 2019. Kevin Kane/Getty Images for BSB Barbra Streisand logged her first No. 1 entry on the Billboard 200 with "People" in 1964. Fifty-one years later, she set a record for the longest span between No. 1s when "Encore: Movie Partners Sing Broadway," her 2016 studio album, topped the chart. Streisand previously held the record for the most No. 1 albums among female artists until  Taylor Swift broke it in 2023. Kanye West — 11 Rich Fury/Getty Images for Coachella Ye, who still releases music under the name Kanye West , topped the Billboard 200 for the first time in 2005 with "Late Registration." He logged his 11th consecutive No. 1 album in 2024 with " Vultures 1 ," a collaborative effort with Ty Dolla $ign. Eminem — 11 Eminem performs during the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame induction ceremony. Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic When it was released in 2000, Eminem's "The Marshall Mathers LP" sold over 1 million copies in its first week, easily earning a No. 1 debut on the Billboard 200. Two decades later, "Music to Be Murdered By" debuted at No. 1, becoming Eminem's historic 10th chart-topper. He logged his 11th in 2024 with "The Death of Slim Shady (Coup de Grâce)." Future — 11 Future performs during the We Trust You Tour in 2024. Prince Williams/WireImage Future earned his first No. 1 album in 2015 with "DS2," which has since spent over 300 weeks on the Billboard 200. In 2024, Future's "Mixtape Pluto" debuted atop the chart — his third No. 1 album in just six months and 11th overall. Earlier that year, Future topped the chart with "We Don't Trust You" and "We Still Don't Trust You," collaborative efforts with Metro Boomin. The former is widely known for reigniting a feud between Drake and Kendrick Lamar . Jay-Z — 14 Jay-Z performs during the 2017 Meadows Music And Arts Festival. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images Jay-Z began collecting No. 1s in 1998 with his third studio album, "Vol. 2... Hard Knock Life." In 2017, he extended his total to 14 with his latest effort, "4:44." Jay-Z is also one of the most-awarded artists in Grammy history . Drake — 15 Drake performs at the Wireless Festival in 2021. Joseph Okpako/WireImage Since pivoting to music after starring on "Degrassi" as a teenager, Drake has racked up 15 No. 1 albums, from 2010's "Thank Me Later" to 2026's "Iceman." Drake's grand total also includes one mixtape ("Care Package"), three collaborative albums ("What A Time To Be Alive" with Future, "Her Loss" with 21 Savage, and " $ome $exy $ongs 4 U " with PartyNextDoor), and one project mysteriously billed as a playlist ("More Life"). Taylor Swift — 15 Taylor Swift performs during the Eras Tour in 2023. Marcelo Endelli/TAS23/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Only one of Taylor Swift's albums hasn't topped the chart: her self-titled debut, which peaked at No. 5 in 2008. Swift earned her first No. 1 later that same year with "Fearless," which has since been ranked the fourth-biggest album in Billboard 200 history. In the 2020s, Swift rerecorded four of her old albums and rebranded each new release as "Taylor's Version." All four of those topped the chart, too. Most recently, 2025's " The Life of a Showgirl " launched atop the chart with the biggest sales week in history, breaking Adele's record. It became her 15th No. 1 album, extending her record for the most among women. She is tied for the most among solo artists. Swift has also broken Elvis Presley's record for the most cumulative weeks spent at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a solo artist. The Beatles — 19 The Beatles gave their final performance together in 1969. Apple Corps Ltd The Beatles hold both records for the most No. 1 songs on the Hot 100 and the most No. 1 albums on the Billboard 200. The latter group includes classics like "Revolver" (1966), "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" (1967), "Abbey Road" (1969), and their post-band breakup compilation "1" (2000). As a solo musician, Paul McCartney has topped the Billboard 200 eight more times, while John Lennon managed the feat three times before he died in 1980. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance The current US administration is an obstacle, but public demand for protection will ultimately prevail O rganisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws. What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”. Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament. As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities. Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “ Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore. Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis. But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Working one job isn't always enough. Gen Zers and millennials are taking on side hustles and freelance work.
events.summary: A new study finds 80% of Gen Zers have worked outside their main jobs. LeoPatrizi/Getty Images Goldman Sachs Asset Management found 80% of Gen Zers have worked outside their primary jobs. People across generations said this was because they needed the money or for financial security. Not feeling secure can affect financial goals, like homeownership. Having a job doesn't always mean you have enough to cover daily living or savings goals. A July survey of Americans by Goldman Sachs Asset Management and the behavioral economics firm Escalent found over 60% of respondents have worked outside their primary roles, largely because they needed to. Twenty-seven percent of respondents said work covers their expenses, but it's tough to get ahead. "Employment remains essential for retirement security, but for many Americans, it is no longer sufficient," a Goldman Sachs Asset Management retirement report said. Gen Zers were most likely to say they earn or have earned money outside their primary job; millennials followed closely behind. The report said that's despite most Gen Z and millennial workers reporting their jobs provide financial stability. "Younger workers may feel stable in their main jobs while still seeing extra work as necessary," the report said. Throughout the generations, a majority said they're doing gig or side work out of necessity or for financial security. "The traditional full-time job may no longer be carrying the full weight of financial security," the report said. "For many, supplementing income appears to have become part of the baseline." Some Americans are living paycheck to paycheck or adjusting their budgets to cope with rising gas prices and other everyday expenses. It can be hard to get ahead when wage growth has been consistently falling short of inflation, and it's tough to find a new job to try to earn more money. Not feeling financially secure can lead to putting off savings goals. Eighty-three percent of Gen Z and 78% of millennials said they put major financial goals on hold. Forty-one percent of millennials have delayed emergency savings despite being employed, and 30% said they delayed housing or homebuying goals. For Gen Zers, the shares were 35% and 34%, respectively. Do you work more than one job? What's that like? Do you use the earnings to handle different expenses or financial goals? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com . While some people may be working a part-time side job, others are "overemployed" and working multiple full-time jobs. One millennial has worked five full-time remote IT jobs , earning over $700,000 annually. As Business Insider's Jacob Zinkula reported, overemployed people use their extra earnings for different reasons, such as retiring early or paying down debt. Having multiple income streams can also be considered a " portfolio career ," where people piece together different kinds of work, such as writing a newsletter, doing a side gig, and holding an office job. It can be one way to try " stability stacking " to feel more secure about your career if, for example, you were laid off and lost an income stream. "When you decentralize everything from one 9-to-5 and build a portfolio career, you protect yourself from the emotional and financial shock if and when business needs change at your 9-to-5," said career coach Janel Abrahami in a TikTok video. And sometimes, working a side gig can become a complete career pivot. Harlan Rappaport, in his 20s, turned his email marketing side hustle into a full-time career after working as an investment analyst at a financial institution. "I used to get really excited about the numbers, but over the last couple of years, I realized it's more about the freedom I've had in my life over the last couple of years as a freelancer," Rappaport said in an as-told-to essay. "I don't miss family events, can travel when I want, and can work from anywhere in the world." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump says he asked Google CEO to rename Atlantic Ocean on Maps
events.summary: Tech company previously complied with president’s demand to rename Gulf of Mexico as Gulf of America Donald Trump said Google rejected his request to rename the Atlantic Ocean after himself or America. Speaking at a rally in South Carolina on Wednesday, the president said he had called Google’s CEO, Sundar Pichai, to ask whether the company could “handle” his proposal. “I only like two oceans: the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two. So we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean, and I called Google Maps , who were really great with the lake … They’re still rattled from the Gulf. I said: ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean,’” Trump said. Trump referenced his previous executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, as well as his push to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid a trade feud between the US and Canada, for which he also signed an executive order requiring US federal agencies to use his new moniker. According to Trump, Pichai rejected the latest proposal. Trump described the Google CEO’s response by saying, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it … Oceans are different, sir. They cover … a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.” “So I’ll probably pass. Should I pass it?” Trump said, adding: “I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean.” The Guardian has approached Google for comment. Google has previously acceded to Trump’s demands for name changes, which triggered public criticism including from Mexico and Canada . On Google Maps, the locations themselves are labeled “Gulf of America” and “Lake America” for US users, while search results display the new names alongside the original names in parentheses. Users in Mexico and Canada, meanwhile, continue to see the original names. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Trump has also previously floated renaming the strait of Hormuz after himself. Last month, amid the US’s ongoing war with Iran, he wrote on Truth Social: “Should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!”

events.title: The Guardian view on England's north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on England’s north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution The prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. His government must redistribute wealth to close deadly inequalities A ndy Burnham’s call to abandon “ 40 years of neoliberalism ” rests partly on the damage that he says it has done to northern England. A new study – published in the Lancet this week – adds weight to his argument. It found that for adults aged 25 to 49, death rates in the north were 13% higher than in the south in 1981. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival? The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on. Deindustrialisation stripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales. Austerity then weakened support systems. These reasons also underscore Mr Burnham’s analysis that Britain’s economic model and concentration of power in London have failed its regions. The question for the budget is what will it do about these inequalities. The north has substantial levels of deprivation , lower rates of pay and fewer healthy years of life for its people. Among people under 75, the Lancet study found that mortality in northern England was 26% higher than in the south. To close these gaps means helping poorer households with the rising cost of essentials and sending more resources to deprived areas. Investment in, say, early years education and council budgets would help to deal with the social conditions underlying ill health. Reducing regional inequalities requires redistribution – not just devolution alone. Giving a poorer area more control over an inadequate budget does not increase the cash it can spend. Mr Burnham’s idea to let mayors retain locally raised taxes may help. But without a way to ensure each region gets enough resources to meet their needs, such a policy might simply preserve existing disparities. Researchers at Manchester and Liverpool universities and Health Equity North divided England into two roughly equal populations along a line from the Wash to the Severn Estuary. Closing the north’s health gap, they claim, could add £18bn a year to its economy. Regional policy plays a complementary role to redistribution by aiming to change where wealth is produced. However, in a recent paper, Steve Fothergill of the Industrial Communities Alliance warned that “the UK has moved away from a long‑established framework that explicitly sought to promote jobs and growth in its less prosperous places … the UK now deploys a weaker set of tools for regional economic development than at any point since the mid-twentieth century”. Mr Burnham needs to reverse this trend. The chancellor, John Healey, says that he wants a budget for “ bloody-minded entrepreneurs ”. But a richer northern England would not necessarily be a healthy or more equal one. During the 19th century, when Manchester became known as “Cottonopolis”, Friedrich Engels – bemoaning the city’s “disgraceful unhealthy slums” – was shocked to be told by a local businessman: “And yet there is a great deal of money to be made here.” Bringing investment and good jobs to economically weaker regions matters. But whether the resulting prosperity translates into secure incomes, decent homes, good public services and longer lives is just as important. Mr Burnham’s ambition needs to meet twin challenges: where wealth is created and what life it lets people enjoy. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC
events.summary: Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit. The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech. While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case. Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery. “We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom. The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself. “It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.” The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”. Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.” After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned to the BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition, after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about. While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule. Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order. “The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said. In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January. During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president. Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.” Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.” In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.

events.title: Tesla just laid out its transportation mission: World domination
events.summary: Elon Musk has said he thinks the world will switch over to autonomous driving tech. He ramped up that prediction on Wednesday. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images - Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Elon Musk has repeatedly said cars will drive themselves around the world. Now, he's making a bolder claim: Tesla will dominate that autonomy, he predicts. The only thing that could get in the way, Musk says: these pesky governments! Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously thinks bots will drive us around. On Wednesday, he took that long-running vision of autonomy a step further. During the automaker's earnings call, Musk predicted that Tesla itself would dominate how passengers get around — so long as pesky regulators don't get in the way. "I think Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely," he said. "And you can come back and look at this prediction, but I feel confident about this prediction." He said Tesla's biggest hurdle to world domination is foreign governments blocking autonomous tech "to protect a domestic industry." That is a bolder statement than Musk's prior autonomy predictions. During a January earnings call, he said the "vast majority of miles traveled" would eventually be autonomous and guessed that people would manually drive fewer than 5% of miles. That prediction left other autonomous competitors — Waymo, Zoox, Ford, GM, Rivian, etc. — in the fray. Vehicle autonomy is core to Tesla's valuation story. The company says its future lineup will include only one vehicle that drivers can operate manually: the high-priced Roadster . In September, the company started rolling out the steering-wheel-less Cybercab for ride-hailing in Texas. That rollout has had its fits and starts. While Tesla says it's ramping production and preparing to launch Cybercab rides in Florida, the NHTSA issued an audit inquiry hours after the car's public release to probe the automaker's self-certification. Musk, who has described his predictions as his "best guesses," has missed several recent timelines for Tesla's autonomy rollout — including a prediction that unsupervised autonomy would ramp across the US in 2025 . Now, Tesla has a new target date for the consumer launch of its full self-driving software. On Wednesday, Ashok Elluswamy, the company's VP of AI, said unsupervised FSD is coming "somewhere around Q2 next year." Tesla didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Palisades recovers damaged nuclear fuel assembly, but critics of restart escalate concerns
events.summary: A nuclear fuel assembly that had tipped over was successfully retrieved from the soon-to-be-restarted Palisades nuclear reactor in Michigan but controversy over the restart has been escalated to Congress. On Wednesday, owners of the Holtec International reactor said “technical ingenuity” would allow efforts to resume operations at the plant to continue. “When we encounter a challenge, what matters is how we respond,” said Fadi Diya, Holtec's chief nuclear officer. “Our team approached this recovery with the same commitment to safety, technical rigour, and teamwork that has guided our work throughout the restart.” The Palisades reactor, bought by Holtec after being decommissioned in 2022, has become synonymous with a US nuclear energy renaissance induced by the significant energy needs of artificial intelligence data centres. Efforts to restart the reactor in Covert, Michigan, hit a snag in August, when, according to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), one of the fuel assemblies tipped over during fuelling. The NRC said no radiation was released. However, it was another controversy linked to the Palisades reactor, which first went online in 1971. In 2012, an NRC report warned about the work culture at the plant, where it said safety concerns were routinely dismissed. In 2016, security staff were placed on leave, which was then owned by Entergy, for failing to properly follow fire prevention protocol. And in October 2025, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, though was not seriously injured. Most recently, the NRC sent a letter to Holtec following an inspection that determined that although Palisades maintained a safety-conscious work environment overall, “a chilled work environment” existed in the supply chain and quality assurance departments. “Employees in these two work departments are hesitant to raise safety concerns using all available avenues without fear of retaliation,” the NRC said. Last week, Patrick O’Brien, Holtec's director of government affairs and communications, told The National that Holtec was “taking actions to address these issues and will continue our work to maintain and strengthen a healthy safety-conscious work environment”. Arnie Gundersen, a nuclear engineer and expert adviser for the environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan, has criticised how the Palisades restart is being handled. “In the last four weeks, Palisades lost control and tipped a nuclear fuel bundle and couldn’t get it out, nine out of 15 licensed reactor operators failed their exam, and more than half of the people in their quality assurance and procurement departments feel they will be fired by management if they bring concerns forward,” he said, and yet “ironically … the NRC just gave them permission to begin loading fuel again!” Mr Gundersen recently told The National he has escalated his concerns about the Palisades nuclear restart to US Democratic Senator Edward Markey, a long-time critic of the nuclear industry. “The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has either ignored or rebuffed my safety concerns as an expert witness for the last three years,” Mr Gundersen's letter to Mr Markey reads. “Simply put, restarting the 55-year-old Palisades reactor is unsafe. Holtec is a rookie with no nuclear operating experience and has been entrusted with an incredibly complex, never-before-attempted undertaking.” Michigan's Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer has previously praised the Palisades restart efforts, however, and has shown no sign of reversing course. Meanwhile, Holtec on Wednesday insisted that safety is a priority. “Palisades will resume operations when all required work is complete and all applicable federal requirements and industry standards are met,” a press release from the company said. Yet despite taking a victory lap after the company retrieved the tipped nuclear fuel assembly, woes continue to darken the doorstep of Holtec. On Wednesday, according to Law360, a jury in New Jersey found that the company had violated whistleblower laws by firing it's former chief financial officer who said that he refused to make statements about Holtec that he thought were misleading. Holtec told Law360 that it didn't agree with the jury and planned to appeal.

events.title: The Ford Foundation, one of the world's largest grantmakers, will throw more weight behind democracy
events.summary: The Ford Foundation, one of the world’s largest private grantmakers, will overhaul its spending to counter what new leadership views as the mutually reinforcing rise of both autocracy and inequality NEW YORK -- The Ford Foundation, one of the world's largest private grantmakers, will overhaul its spending to counter what new leadership views as the mutually reinforcing rise of both autocracy and inequality. The New York-based philanthropy committed Thursday to driving more funds toward the basic building blocks of democracy. The new strategic direction comes less than one year into Ford Foundation President Heather Gerken's tenure at the helm of the social justice funder's $18 billion endowment. In a report to trustees, Gerken — widely recognized as a leading expert on constitutional law and elections — framed the changes in the context of an “emboldened strain of 21st-century authoritarianism." Seven new programs — focused on democratic governance, inclusive economies, trustworthy information, public safety, gender equality, global cooperation and racial justice — will be detailed throughout next year. Their impact, Gerken suggested, will reach beyond just issues of democracy. “If you don’t have a rule of law, if you don’t have an election system that functions, all the other values that Ford cares about, all the other projects that Ford has done over the years, fall apart," she told The Associated Press. "So, protecting marginalized communities, pushing forward on equality, protecting the climate, all of these depend on those basic building blocks.” It's the foundation's largest strategic refresh since immediate past president Darren Walker prioritized inequality in a 2015 overhaul. Already the nation's leading democracy grantor by some counts, the Ford Foundation sees this new approach as a necessary extension of that focus. The latest changes arrive in the heat of a midterm election cycle that has underscored the strains on American democracy . Republicans drove unusual levels of partisan redistricting this year and the Supreme Court hollowed out the landmark Voting Rights Act . Fewer U.S. adults said democracy is central to the country's identity in an April survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. International monitors have warned of a deterioration in political rights and civil liberties worldwide. Foundations have fielded recent years' tests to American democracy by increasing support. events.title: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan | Andy Burnham
events.summary: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval O n Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments. At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project. There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering. The simple truth is that even as we pursue our ambitious target of net zero by 2050 , we will need oil and gas for years to come as a bridge to that clean-energy future. And imported gas has a higher carbon footprint than gas produced at home. The transition to net zero is a process, not a moment. I want Britain to make that transition on our terms: reducing our dependence on foreign fossil fuels, supporting good jobs and growing our economy so we can help people with the cost of living. I know this news will be warmly welcomed in Aberdeen and by oil and gas workers across Scotland. Their jobs support families, businesses and entire communities. Yet, like many others, their industry has suffered from deindustrialisation, with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives. Our oil and gas workers have powered our nation for decades, and they will continue to play a key role for decades to come. Last week, I promised the Scottish people that we would reindustrialise their nation . I believe the transition to clean energy represents the best chance we will ever get of making that happen. I am determined to ensure that the next generation of energy jobs is created across Scotland and all nations of the UK. That is why, alongside the decision on Jackdaw, we are establishing an energy wealth fund – something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago. It will begin with an initial £2bn and allow us to convert future North Sea oil and gas tax revenues into clean-energy programmes across the country. This investment in renewable energy will enable us to substantially delink gas and electricity prices by the end of this parliament and bring down bills in the long term. This government is taking a pragmatic approach that supports our oil and gas industry today, while driving the growth of the clean-energy industries of tomorrow. We are also making a sustained effort to bring energy costs down over the next decade and in line with those of our European neighbours . I know, however, that people need breathing space right now. I will do everything I can to ease the pressure on household budgets in the short term. One of my first acts as prime minister was to remove VAT from electricity bills, and households have seen that reduction in their bills this month. I have now asked the chancellor and the energy secretary to look at removing standing charges from gas bills at the earliest opportunity. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more I will ensure the government continues to take action to reduce both gas bills and electricity bills as part of our fundamental changes to the energy system. The manifesto on which Labour was elected committed us to issuing no new oil or gas licences to explore new fields in the North Sea and to reaching net zero by 2050. I stand by both promises. Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires. More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations. There are two ways we can transition to clean energy. One way, the traditional Whitehall way, is to make people carry the burden of change while others take the rewards.

events.title: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK
events.summary: Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory F or the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war. But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK. Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting , opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks. Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract. Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months. Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.” The factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles). The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to the brutal new reality of drone warfare . But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower. “In Ukraine , we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening. He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad. The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds. These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028. The factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda. Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Telford investment followed an agreement in 2024 between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely. Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the “reindustrialisation” of Britain desired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems. Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine.

events.title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
events.summary: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw? What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally ? Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services. The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault. In the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked. The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included the Internet Archive, Wikipedia and 4Chan. The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties. Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug. However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.” The flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards. In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”. Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday. CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP. Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free. It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.
