events.title: Chip Scaling Moves Beyond The Transistor
events.summary: Key Takeaways: The semiconductor industry reached $1 trillion years early, but keeping pace with demand now depends on systems integration as much as transistor scaling. Packaging, photonics, power, and test are converging into one optimization problem, which means improving any one of them can move the bottleneck somewhere else. AI is shifting from the workload the industry serves to a tool it uses, and the open question is how much engineering and manufacturing authority it will be given. When SEMICON West gathered in San Francisco in 2023, the semiconductor industry was forecasting a path to $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2030. Three years later, the industry has already blown past that number. SEMICON West 2026 returned to San Francisco with a sold-out exhibit floor, more than 30,000 attendees, and an industry confronting a different question: How does it keep up with the growth it once aimed for? SEMI’s own projections show how steep that curve has become. In his opening keynote, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha forecast a market of more than $2 trillion by 2030, and potentially $3 trillion by 2035. At the SEMI Market Symposium, the association projected 300mm fab equipment spending of $149 billion this year, rising to $227 billion by 2029, with construction beginning on 20 new 300mm fabs or production lines in 2026 alone. AI infrastructure is driving much of that growth, but electrification, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation are adding semiconductor content, as well. What makes the current expansion unusual is the growing complexity of the systems those chips will enable, not the almost insatiable demand for chips. “We’ve started talking about how to re-engineer engineering because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys . “That’s at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?” Across presentations, panels, and discussions on the show floor, several issues kept converging around that problem. Advanced packaging is becoming part of system architecture. Photonics is moving closer to compute, while bringing new manufacturing and test challenges with it. Test, inspection and metrology have to follow more complicated assemblies and manufacturing histories. And AI is moving from something the industry builds to something it uses to design and manufacture. None of these technologies is new, but each is becoming harder to optimize independently, and that may be the clearest indication of what the industry will be working on in the coming years. Scaling becomes a system-level challenge The shift was apparent in conversations ranging from transistor scaling and HBM to advanced packaging, optical interconnects, and cooling, where improving any one of those can move a bottleneck elsewhere. More compute increases pressure on memory bandwidth and power delivery. Moving memory closer reduces data movement but concentrates heat. Disaggregating a large die can improve yield and allow functions to use different process nodes, but it creates more interfaces that have to be connected, powered, cooled, and tested. “Packaging is no longer simply the place where semiconductor innovation ends,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D at Intel Foundry . “Increasingly, it’s the place where system innovation begins.” That makes memory, data movement, power delivery, and thermal management part of the architecture rather than downstream considerations. “The challenge is not to co-optimize one component,” Immaneni said. “It is to co-optimize across the system from end to end between silicon, packaging, and platform.” Nitin Deshpande, Marvell’s vice president of advanced packaging, made a similar point during imec’s pre-show ITF USA program. “The package is really becoming a system where the compute, the memory, the interconnects, the power, the cooling, all of these things come together.” Making those pieces work together is only part of the challenge. Larger, more heterogeneous packages still have to become high-volume products with acceptable yield, reliability, and cost. “We can have very cool concepts, but if we cannot scale these into high volumes, if we cannot have a high-yielding, reliable process with a supply chain that can provide the parts in time, everything that we do cannot be converted into a business,” Deshpande said. Patrick Vandenameele, CEO of imec, noted that AI infrastructure can keep growing by adding accelerators and racks, but adding hardware isn’t scaling in the traditional semiconductor sense. “These data centers are true engineering marvels,” he said. “But at the same time, this is not what we semiconductor people call scaling. It looks a little bit more like multiplication.” That distinction helps explain why so many separate topics at SEMICON West kept leading back to the same place. The industry isn’t abandoning transistor scaling. It’s adding another level above it, where performance depends on how effectively different technologies can be combined into a functional system. Fig. 2: Redefining a system. Source: SEMI AI moves from assistant to operator AI was nearly impossible to avoid at SEMICON West, but the conversation is shifting. Machine learning has been part of design, process control, and defect classification for years, and generative AI added natural-language access to complicated tools and data. Agentic AI goes further, allowing engineers to hand an agent an objective and let it invoke other tools, models, or agents to reach it. “We started from an assistant copilot to generative capability to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome,” said Synopsys’ Ghazi. The appeal of agentic AI becomes clearer when looking at the size of the spaces engineers are being asked to optimize. “The space that we’re optimizing in has exploded,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research . “We’ve now gotten to a place where the parameter set is intractable.” A current Lam etcher, for example, can have a potential recipe space on the order of 10 23 possibilities, which is well beyond what any engineer can explore manually. “That’s really where AI is coming to the rescue,” Fried said. “It’s the ability to get through massive multi-parameter dimensional spaces, massive sets of intertwined sensitivities between a much larger parameter space, and a much larger spec space.” Acting on what AI finds is where the discussion gets more complicated. events.title: How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å
events.summary: As their dimensions continue to shrink, conventional gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors may face growing challenges, such as leakage, mobility, resistance, and manufacturing variability. A proposed self-aligned complementary field-effect transistor (SA-CFET) architecture addresses these constraints by vertically stacking N-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (NMOS) and P-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (PMOS) devices and using self-aligned modules to improve density and manufacturability. What is a CFET? A complementary field-effect transistor (CFET) is a transistor architecture that vertically stacks NMOS and PMOS devices. This configuration can reduce cell area, increase effective channel width, and improve electrostatic control compared with side-by-side device layouts. With SEMulator3D , the Semiverse Solutions team used digital twin process modeling to show that the self-aligned architecture can support static random-access memory (SRAM) and logic cells while delivering a 0.0094 μm² SRAM bit cell, a 52.7% area reduction compared with N3 technology, and at least a 10 nm overlay window across critical contact layers. Why transistor scaling beyond 10 Å is difficult Many experts believe that the currently most-advanced transistor architecture, silicon GAA nanosheets, may begin to have physics and manufacturing issues past the 10 angstrom (Å) node. These challenges include: Source-drain tunneling and increased leakage current as the gate length shrinks Mobility issues, surface scattering, and manufacturing issues as the channel thickness is reduced Contact and parasitic resistance issues as the transistor size decreases Manufacturing variability that may seriously impact yield beyond the 10 Å node With these challenges, it is becoming increasingly difficult to scale down the nanosheet device area or enhance device density by simply shrinking the active area, gate, or metal patterning pitch. Why CFET matters for sub-10Å scaling CFET architecture stacks PMOS and NMOS vertically to achieve significant area reduction, enhanced performance through larger effective channel width, and improved electrostatics. 1,2,3,4 However, CFET architecture faces its own critical integration challenges: metal gate isolation complexity and contact crowding that can cause electrical shorts or open circuits. These issues intensify at smaller dimensions, requiring innovative solutions for scalability. How the self-aligned architecture works To address these challenges, we propose a SA-CFET architecture with three key self-aligned modules: SA-BPR (buried power rail), SA-CT (contacts), and SA-TSV (through-silicon via). These process modules enlarge the edge placement error window and mitigate contact crowding, improving process margin. The architecture uses non-metal gate cut design and middle dielectric isolation (MDI) for work function split. 5 SA-CFET maintains compatibility with N3 specifications (42-nm CPP, 21-nm metal pitch), transforming overlay-sensitive steps into self-aligned processes for better manufacturability. Fig. 1: Key integration loops of the SA-CFET. Design implementation: SRAM and logic cells The SA-CFET design can be used to successfully build 6T SRAM cells and logic standard cells (NOT, NAND, NOR) with no metal gate split required within any single fin, simplifying the process flow. The complete interconnection network, validated through digital twin (process) simulation, demonstrates complex routing capability while maintaining self-aligned benefits. Fig. 2: 3D interconnection network architecture showing SRAM and logic cells (NAND, NOR, NOT) with complex routing validated through digital twin simulation. Performance results SA-CFET achieves a 6T SRAM bit cell area of 0.0094 μm²—a 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology 6 and 19% reduction versus state-of-the-art A7 CFET designs. Process robustness validation shows at least a 10-nm overlay window for all critical contact layers with no open/short failures, confirming robust process margin. Fig. 3: SRAM bit cell area comparison showing 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology. Fig. 4: Overlay window validation confirming robust process margin across critical contact layers. Conclusion This article describes an innovative self-aligned CFET architecture that employs multiple self-aligned processes. Using this architecture, we designed a process sequence for both a 6T SRAM device and for logic standard cells using digital twin (process) modeling. We found the proposed architecture shares similar or even more relaxed design rules compared to current or conventional semiconductor manufacturing. It also provides an area reduction from both existing N3 devices and state-of-the-art CFET architectures. More importantly, it avoids many of the scaling issues found in existing nanosheet architectures, achieving enhanced performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes. We believe that this work demonstrates a potential architectural solution to support CMOS scaling for transistors at 10 Å and beyond. Kükner et al., “Double-Row CFET: Design Technology Co-Optimization for Area Efficient A7 Technology Node,” 2024 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM), San Francisco, CA, USA, 2024, pp. 1-4. events.title: Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery
events.summary: By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Nicolas Butzen, and Vishal Javvaji The semiconductor industry has embraced multi-chip and stacked-die architectures as the primary path for continued performance scaling. As monolithic designs become more difficult and costly to advance, chiplets, advanced packaging, and 3D integration enable higher levels of performance, bandwidth, and functional integration for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Yet the success of stacked-die, multi-chip architectures has exposed a growing power delivery challenge. As more compute resources are integrated into a package, there is a sharp uptick in current density and the number of independent voltage domains, placing unprecedented demands on shared power delivery resources. To address these challenges, we discussed in our recent power delivery white paper how Intel Foundry is moving voltage regulation closer to the load. By enabling higher-voltage power distribution, integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) reduce current density in the package, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks. Intel Foundry’s portfolio spans package-integrated magnetic inductors, fully capacitive IVR chiplets, and advanced package integration technologies, providing multiple paths to improve power integrity, efficiency, and scalability. System-level consequences of stacked-die architectures Advanced packaging delivers significant gains in performance, bandwidth, and integration density. However, consistently distributing power through increasingly complex packaging and interconnect structures introduces new challenges in maintaining power integrity across the package. One consequence is voltage droop. As AI workloads generate rapid swings in current demand, the power delivery network must respond instantly. When it cannot, voltage can briefly fall below target levels, potentially impacting performance. To maintain reliability, designers often add voltage guard bands and operating margins. While effective, these safeguards can limit silicon from reaching its optimal efficiency and performance. Multi-chip and stacked-die architectures also intensify the tradeoff between signal density and power delivery. As more compute tiles, memory interfaces, and die-to-die links are added, routing congestion increases, creating additional resistance, tighter voltage margins, and growing power delivery constraints. Moving power delivery closer to the load As current density continues to increase, the industry is moving toward architectures that bring voltage conversion closer to the point of consumption, reducing power delivery losses while improving responsiveness to rapidly changing workloads. Intel Foundry is advancing several complementary technologies designed around this principle. FIVR with CoaxMIL: Intel was an early pioneer of fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs), which moves the last voltage conversion stage onto the processor. By shortening the distance between the regulator and the load, FIVR helps reduce distribution losses and improve transient response. To support rising current densities, Intel developed CoaxMIL, a magnetic inductor technology that delivers significantly higher current density than earlier approaches while requiring less area (see Figure 1). For customers building next-generation AI and HPC devices, this translates into improved power conversion efficiency, faster response to workload changes, and more efficient use of valuable package real estate. The result is greater performance potential without proportional increases in power delivery complexity. Fig. 1: CoaxMIL magnetic inductor technology. C2VR: Intel Foundry’s continuous capacitive voltage regulator (C2VR) takes voltage conversion in a different direction. Rather than relying on traditional inductors, C2VR uses high-density capacitor technology to achieve efficient voltage conversion in an extremely compact form factor. Because capacitors are integrated directly onto the voltage regulator chiplet, C2VR can deliver both high efficiency and exceptionally high current density. It can also respond rapidly to sudden current demands, helping minimize voltage droop during the bursty workload transitions common in AI accelerators. For customers, the benefit is improved power integrity, tighter voltage control, and a scalable solution capable of supporting future multi-kiloamp workloads. IVR chiplet architectures: These dedicated power management chiplets allow voltage conversion to be positioned closer to the compute die than traditional motherboard-based regulators. The primary advantage of IVR chiplet architectures is flexibility. Architects can position voltage regulation where it delivers the greatest benefit, whether on the landside, embedded within package layers, or beneath compute dies. This flexibility allows architects to optimize power delivery for specific applications while reducing distribution losses and improving overall efficiency. In advanced stacked-die systems, these architectures also open the door to vertical power delivery schemes that reduce distribution distance and improve power integrity. The future of power delivery As AI systems continue their rapid evolution, power delivery is becoming as critical to performance scaling as transistor and packaging innovation. The next generation of data center architectures will require a portfolio of solutions that move power conversion closer to the load, improve efficiency at extreme current densities, and maintain stable operation under increasingly dynamic workloads. Intel Foundry technologies are important building blocks, helping ensure that future compute platforms can continue scaling performance without being constrained by the power delivery network. This blog is the second in a two-part series on power delivery innovation. Part 1 explores how data center energy trends are affecting chip power delivery. Nicolas Butzen is a principal engineer at Intel. Vishal Javvaji is a process integration manager at Intel Foundry. events.title: What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel changes more than available area. Processes developed around wafer geometry, handling, and equipment have to be reconsidered at panel scale. Larger panels amplify dimensional change, warpage, and process history, making what happens at one manufacturing step increasingly important to the next. The most economical manufacturing flow may use different substrate formats at different stages rather than carrying one large panel through the entire process. Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel sounds, at first, like a geometry problem. Large AI and HPC packages are increasingly rectangular, while the 300mm wafer underneath them is still round. As the package size grows, more of that expensive processing ends up around the circle’s edges where nothing useful can be built. A panel gives that area back. It can fit more large packages into the same process cycle, and unlike a wafer, its dimensions don’t impose the same hard limit on the size of a square or rectangular package. For advanced packages that keep getting larger, the economics are difficult to ignore. But the semiconductor packaging sector has spent decades learning how to process wafers, not panels. Equipment, materials, recipes, handling systems, and process controls were all developed around the geometry and mechanical behavior of a round workpiece. “The risk of doing the assembly on the 600mm panel is high, and I don’t think we have all the equipment today to run the process,” said Teck Chong Lee, technical director of advanced fan-out development for HPC applications at ASE , in a recent presentation. “One of the options is, once you complete the interposer in large format in 600, then you divide it into four pieces to run the assembly and the C4 process. This is a much lower-risk approach.” The economics behind that compromise are substantial. In the same study, a 5.5×-reticle-size interposer produced 9 units on a 300mm wafer, compared with 16 on a 300mm panel. A 600mm panel divided into four 300mm pieces produces 64, while processing the full 600mm area intact raises that to 72. In pure utilization, the intact panel produces 8 times as many units as the wafer, a gain well beyond the roughly fivefold difference in raw area, because the rectangular panel wastes almost nothing at its edges. The flow therefore takes the area advantage where it can use it, then gives some of it back before assembly because the manufacturing infrastructure isn’t ready to follow the larger format all the way through. That compromise exposes the larger transition underway. Moving packaging from wafer to panel isn’t simply making the process bigger. It is discovering which parts of the process were dependent on the wafer dimensions all along. The process was built around the wafer The utilization advantage grows as the package does. In one comparison, Intel Foundry used a 510 × 515mm panel and showed that a roughly 4× reticle package would produce about 10 units on a 300mm wafer and approximately 48 on the panel. Eventually the wafer imposes a harder geometric limit, since the largest square that fits on a 300mm wafer is only about 210 × 210mm. “For certain form factors, we believe a wafer is more economical,” said Tarek Ibrahim, senior principal engineer at Intel , in a conference presentation. “However, when you go beyond a certain form factor, you can see quickly that the panel becomes more effective, mainly because you can get more units out of a panel. Because of the way AI is heading and the need for a very large system, panels became an obvious choice for scale.” Fig. 1: Intel’s Tarek Ibrahim discusses substrate scaling for heterogeneous integration. Source: Semiconductor Engineering The economic crossover doesn’t mean the manufacturing process crosses over with it. Much of the equipment and process knowledge used in advanced packaging was developed for a round wafer, and changing the shape and scale of the substrate changes what those processes have to do. Over time, many of those wafer-specific assumptions became invisible because the workpiece underneath them rarely changed. What looked like a requirement of the process was often just a requirement of the wafer. “At wafer level, it’s a single-sided process,” Ibrahim said. “On panel, it’s actually a dual-sided process. Managing the process at that panel scale with the right uniformity and the right Cpk [process capability index] is definitely a challenge.” Part of the challenge is that familiar wafer processes don’t always transfer cleanly to a larger rectangular surface. Spin coating, for example, relies on radial symmetry, so a rectangular substrate produces uneven film thickness toward the corners while most of the dispensed resist is thrown away. In a 600mm panel flow, photoresist is instead deposited by slit or slot-die coating across an active area of roughly 586 × 586mm. Lithography also changes, with maskless direct imaging displacing the conventional wafer stepper in many panel flows. Those differences propagate into the materials and equipment surrounding the process. Fine-line RDL on glass panels is pushing toward new photoresists and application methods, tighter overlay control, and equipment that can maintain temperature and process uniformity across a much larger area. Large hot plates become a development problem of their own. As line and space moves from roughly 5µm toward 2µm and below, processes that historically belonged farther back in the packaging flow begin demanding something closer to front-end precision. The awkward part is that the panel can’t simply inherit the front-end equipment built to provide that precision. Much of that infrastructure assumes a round 300mm wafer, while traditional substrate equipment was designed around different feature sizes and process tolerances. Panel-level packaging is landing somewhere between the two. The result is less a scaled-up wafer flow than a new manufacturing process being assembled from pieces of several older ones. The panel solves an increasingly expensive geometry problem, but it also exposes how many coating, exposure, handling, and uniformity assumptions were tied to the wafer that came before it. Yield decides how big is useful The simplest argument for a larger panel is that more packages fit on it. The real economic question is how many good packages come off. That matters more as the value assembled onto the workpiece rises. A panel carrying logic and HBM can contain tens of thousands of dollars of known-good silicon before some package-level failures become visible. At that point, even a small yield loss can erase the savings created by processing more area at once. “There’s so much money in chips going onto a wafer or panel that a tiny yield hit, and the loss of some of that super-expensive silicon, will just blow all the benefits from a larger scale that you had right out the window,” said Mike Kelly, vice president of chipl

events.title: Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Foundries have been doing backend work for advanced packages. OSATs are now taking that on. This particularly affects 2.5D and panel assembly with new equipment and materials. Hybrid bonding is mostly a foundry activity now but will likely move to OSATs as well. Foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) houses have traditionally had distinct lanes, but the lines are blurring as OSATs acquire select foundry capabilities and foundries return some of the jobs they have taken from OSATs. “We’re at this bridging point where the IDMs and the foundries are doing more of what OSATs can do, and the OSATs are also trying to get much closer to what the foundry does at the back end,” said Raghu Nayak, head of sales at Zeiss. OSATs will never compete with foundries on advanced nodes and front-end wafer fabrication. But for backend activities, where dimensions aren’t as demanding, OSATs are acquiring capabilities that replicate what foundries can do. The biggest areas of overlap are 2.5D integration and panel assembly, with hybrid bonding likely to move there as well. The change affects equipment and materials. “We are seeing the migration of lithography-related materials and processes from traditional wafer fabs into advanced packaging environments,” said Poupak Khodabandeh, chief business officer at Brewer Science . “As advanced packaging increasingly relies on fine-pitch redistribution layers (RDLs), OSATs and packaging organizations are using materials and process flows that historically would have been associated with wafer fabrication.” “The industry has traditionally operated in silos across equipment, front-end fabrication, design, packaging, and test,” said Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco . “We need to connect those disciplines so teams can use shared, physics-grounded insight to make faster, better-informed design decisions, while also providing greater manufacturing flexibility — especially at the backend.” It used to be “to each his own” Foundries and OSATs have taken on complementary duties for many years. Foundries fabricate the silicon chip, while OSATs put the chip into a housing and test the final product. A vast array of EDA tools and fab equipment makes what the foundry does possible, while OSATs have worked more with tools that originated in the printed circuit board (PCB) world. Two industry trends are challenging this status quo. The first is the development of advanced packaging. It’s no longer enough to put a chip on a substrate, wire it up, and pour molding compound over it. This doesn’t minimize the effort required to do those basics well, but they’re very different from what advanced packaging requires. “Advanced packaging is becoming more lithography-intensive,” said Khodabandeh. “The industry’s push toward higher interconnect density for AI, HBM, chiplet architectures, and heterogeneous integration is driving the adoption of wafer-fab-style patterning processes within packaging facilities. RDL fabrication is a good example, where increasingly sophisticated lithography is required to create finer features.” Intel Foundry works both sides of the aisle, with foundry and packaging capabilities. “When you do fine pitch bumps, the bump count goes up quite a bit compared to coarse pitch,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry . “So you have to figure out things like embedding [bridge dies such as EMIB]. You have to figure out alignment and equipment precision.” For them, they can attempt these things on either side of the divide. Foundries have been heavily involved in 2.5D packaging, but a second industry trend is making that more difficult — a lack of capacity. Foundries can’t make all the chips their clients want, so they’re prioritizing and allocating. That may mean turning away some business they would otherwise entertain, likely in backend and legacy processes, since foundries will focus on newer-node silicon processes they are uniquely capable of. The OSATs are ready to pick up those processes. These are lower-resolution processes that foundries have historically employed but for which OSATs share capabilities. Legacy-node builds can spill over to assembly houses, especially since advanced packaging requires tooling consistent with those older technologies. Although this overlap largely affects older processes, as constraints continue, even more aggressive technology, which foundries have often packaged (or done the first packaging steps) themselves, may be offloaded. “With further volume restrictions, both legacy-node and leading-edge products are shifting toward OSAT packaging,” said Thomas Uhrmann, vice president of sales at EV Group. Three primary tasks These market dynamics have driven three primary assembly-related processes from foundry to OSAT: 2.5D packaging, panel packaging, and eventually, hybrid bonding. 2.5D packaging in a manner resembling TSMC’s CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate) involves mounting one die atop another. When the base is an interposer, this is 2.5D. When it’s another active die, it becomes 3D. Typical processes place the top die, already singulated, on a bottom die on a wafer that hasn’t been diced up yet. Once the top die is in place, the bottom wafer can be diced, with the stack-up headed for a package. One fast-growing area that needs this technology is photonics. “Customers are coming to us asking if we can do electrical die to photonics die or wafer attach,” said Gerard John, senior director in Amkor’s Chiplets/FCBGA Business Unit. “We take this module, dice it out, and then attach it to a substrate. That’s a new trend we are seeing, and we can do that.” It may, however, bring some tough new requirements. “This is a big challenge because now you have the optic side of the wafer or die,” added John, and this needs active alignment to attach fibers and test them. Panels, meanwhile, have grown to the 500 mm range per side, but moving to a smaller size actually helped. “Several OSATs had early development lines for panel-level packaging, mainly targeting large panels with 500 mm dimensions,” explained Uhrmann. “TSMC’s decision to move to panel-level packaging with 310 × 310 mm 2 , which is a format closer to classical 300 mm round process tools, has enabled traditional wafer-based equipment manufacturers to scale up for high-performance materials and resolution, rather than PCB equipment manufacturers to scale down.” Meanwhile, some assembly houses are doing hybrid bonding. But for high volume, it largely remains a foundry task, owing to the challenges the process presents. As hybrid bonding loses its novelty and becomes standard, it represents another task that foundries could hand off to OSATs. How are you paying for that? Whereas foundries typically have the equipment for these processes, OSATs have to invest to match those capabilities. events.title: AI power demand underestimated, say 81% of energy executives
events.summary: More than eight in 10 energy industry decision-makers expect artificial intelligence to drive electricity demand beyond current forecasts, raising concerns about whether there is enough global infrastructure to power the rapid expansion of data centres. A global survey commissioned by Adipec , Abu Dhabi's annual energy conference, found that 81 per cent of energy industry insiders believe AI-driven electricity consumption will exceed existing projections, with 32 per cent expecting demand to be significantly higher. Only 3 per cent expect demand to fall below current forecasts, according to Adipec's Global Energy Report 2026, released on Thursday. Those surveyed included executives from energy companies, technology providers, investors and industry suppliers. The findings come as technology companies accelerate investment in energy-intensive data centres, creating opportunities for power producers while putting additional pressure on electricity networks. The International Energy Agency expects data centres to consume about 950 terawatt-hours of electricity by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level, according to figures cited in the report. The growth in data centre power demand has become an increasingly important consideration for energy producers and governments. At Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week in January, Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc , said global electricity requirements from data centres could increase fivefold by 2040. The report's findings build on the “power is knowledge” message that was the theme of discussions at Adipec last year, as The National reported. The relationship between AI and electricity remains a central focus of this year's event, which will take place at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi from November 2 to November 5. Technology companies reign The expansion of AI is also expected to change the balance of influence within the energy industry. About 43 per cent of respondents believe technology and AI companies will gain the most influence over the sector, compared with 15 per cent who selected governments and regulators. Financial institutions were also selected by 15 per cent, followed by international oil companies at 14 per cent and national oil companies at 9 per cent. The findings reflect the increasingly close relationship between AI and energy , as technology companies become major drivers of investment in electricity generation and infrastructure. For oil and gas companies, the shift is creating new commercial opportunities. While gas and liquefied natural gas growth currently ranks as the biggest commercial opportunity for oil and gas insiders, AI-driven efficiency is expected to take the top position over the next decade. About 27 per cent identify AI-driven efficiency as a leading opportunity in 10 years, while 25 per cent cite supplying power for AI and data centres. The report also found that 81 per cent of oil and gas insiders believe adopting AI will become essential to remain profitable over the next decade. The findings are particularly relevant to the UAE, where Abu Dhabi is developing a 5-gigawatt AI campus that will house the Stargate UAE computing cluster, expected to cost more than $30 billion . However, a quarter of energy insiders believe the industry is unprepared for AI-driven electricity demand, with grid delays among the biggest obstacles. At Adipec last year, Dr Al Jaber called for “massive” energy investment to meet growing requirements. The Adipec report, conducted by global strategic communications consultancy Kekst CNC between August and October 2026, surveyed 1,832 energy industry decision-makers across 78 countries and included 17 executive interviews. Its findings reflect industry expectations rather than independently verified demand forecasts.

events.title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings
events.summary: The States of Guernsey said about 40 people in care will be eligible for the scheme. A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18. Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult. The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately. Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach." The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs". "Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said. The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme. The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday. At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice. Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future". "This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents. "We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential." Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood". "Giving them the opportunity to build up savings, and the financial security that comes with this, can make a real difference as they take their first steps towards independence." events.title: China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
events.summary: As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority. The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a former department head with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases. “The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

events.title: KPMG ban on government work extended after 'serious ethical failings'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ban on KPMG getting government work extended to February after audit leaks scandal Topic: Accounting and Auditing Services KPMG is under the spotlight for "serious ethical failings". ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into KPMG and found the way the Big Four firm had handled a whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings". KPMG CEO John Sams and chairman Michael Ebeid say they are working on a plan to make "lasting change" and hope to win back the government contract. The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February, following a review that found "serious ethical failings" by its leadership and some of its senior partners. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it . In response to Mr Watt's review, which was handed down today, the department said it has agreed with the firm to a further extension to the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027. During this period, KPMG will provide the department with an implementation plan and the first of its quarterly progress implementation reports. The department also needs to ensure that "KPMG is engaging constructively with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) and the Tax Practitioners Board (TPB) reviews, and is committed to addressing any recommendations that have been made by those organisations". Dr Watt said in his review the way the accounting firm had handled the whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings by some senior members of KPMG" and "significant cultural concerns within KPMG". Dr Watt noted the review was focused on the leadership and culture of the firm "that had been warned on previous occasions about weaknesses in ethical culture, speak-up confidence and accountability, but did not deal with them with the rigour and urgency required". Firms raise doubts about KPMG's integrity In the wake of the KPMG audit leak scandal, executives from Macquarie, Westpac, Optus and Dexus cast doubt on their faith in the auditor. He said since March, KPMG has undergone significant change, with a new chair and a new CEO, and a number of senior personnel having left the firm. Dr Watt said the firm had also commissioned several reviews to understand the root causes of the events. "As was often observed during review interviews, trust takes time to build, and while transparency builds trust, lack of transparency damages it." Dr Watt said his report should not be read as a judgement on every member of KPMG. "Virtually all of KPMG's staff had no involvement in the events that occurred," he said. KPMG CEO John Sams and its chairman Michael Ebeid said they accepted the findings and recommendations of Mr Watt's review. John Sams says the firm is working to revamp its internal culture. ( Supplied ) "The report lays bare our failings and highlights the hard work that we must do to address them," they said in a statement. The firm had appointed Kerry Schott to provide independent oversight and said "while we are making important progress, we know that changing culture takes longer than changing individual roles, structures or controls". "Confidence in KPMG's suitability for Commonwealth work must be earned through evidence of effective, lasting change," the statement said. Call to overhaul code governing bids Dr Watt also recommended the department of finance strengthen the Commonwealth's supplier code of conduct, including tougher sanctions for suppliers breaching their obligations and more reporting pathways for potential unethical behaviour. Whistleblowers need better protection Without whistleblowers, Australians would be kept in the dark about major corporate scandals, but evidence suggests the experience of raising alarm bells can destroy their lives. Several states and territories have also banned KPMG from taking on public sector work pending the outcome of Dr Watt's review, or their own reviews. They are working through their responses to the findings. Greens finance and public service spokesperson Senator Barbara Pocock said a small extension of the freeze on KPMG contracts was not dealing with the issue.

events.title: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
events.summary: Roslynn Garner-Gatley says she relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled. Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water. She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT. Garner-Gatley said: "I did not expect at my age after working for 50 years to be in a situation where I am terrified of putting on the heating because of the price of it." The cost of filling her heating oil tank has nearly doubled Garner-Gatley said she had started going to bed earlier to keep warm while watching television and had recently begun using a hot water bottle and bed socks as evening temperatures dropped. She said instead of keeping hot water on a timer, she only switched it on when she needed it for washing, cooking or bathing before turning it off again. She added that people living in rural areas who depended on oil had "no choice" but to buy it. She said: "After working all my life I didn't expect to be constantly worrying about how to keep warm at my age. It is really quite frightening." Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector . Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels set for some customers would also be reviewed, they added. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil, while helping people switch to clean heat with Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants worth £9,000. "We are also reforming the heating oil sector, holding suppliers to account and giving consumers confidence that they will get a fair deal." Cornwall Council and Devon County Council have money available for households struggling with increasing heating oil costs from their crisis resilience funds, which are provided by the government. Cornwall Council said it had issued payments of £300 to 1,386 households, a total spend of £415,800, which would double after a decision was made to award a further £300 to the same households. The Devon fund, worth about £8.4m a year, is available through district councils, and is targeted at low‑income households facing an "essential cost they cannot afford". Plymouth City Council and Torbay Council also have their own crisis resilience funds. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?
events.summary: Sheeraz Gulsher says there are "huge worries" about AI I have lost track of the number of people who have told me they have applied for hundreds of jobs, only to be met with rejection after rejection. Often, they said it felt like a human had not even looked at their applications. There are lots of different types of recruitment tools. Some match candidates to jobs, others grade and screen CVs. Employers use them to save time sifting through applications, but there are growing concerns that these tools could be biased. I want to find out how fair AI recruitment tools being used to help decide our futures really are - and what happens when we click "apply". What is the 'AI war' in recruitment? There are concerns about the increasing use of AI in recruitment A London-based non-profit organisation, People Like Us, is raising awareness of people's legal right to challenge automated decisions when they disagree with the outcome. A survey conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK workers who had applied for at least one job in the past 24 months found that 75% were unaware of their right to challenge an automated rejection. Sheeraz Gulsher, CEO of People Like Us, is leading the campaign called Reject the Rejections, which calls on employers to improve transparency and accountability in the use of AI and automated recruitment systems. He describes the current situation as an "AI war", with candidates "resorting to AI to bolster their applications" while "employers are dealing with huge amounts of applications". Gulsher said: "We can't say for certain that every company is operating its automated or AI systems without bias. That's why we're calling for companies to audit these systems, publish the results and have them independently assessed. "In our research, we found guidance from the Information Commissioner's Office , external stating that people subject to certain automated decisions have the right to request a human review. We're trying to remind people of that right, as many simply aren't aware of it." The research also found 70% of ethnically diverse jobseekers had altered or concealed information on their CVs, including their country of origin, religion or name, out of fear that recruitment software or AI tools would reject their applications. This compares with 57% of white candidates. Would people ask for a human review? Vivi says she needs feedback as a jobseeker Business consultant Vivi, who lives in Lewisham, was made redundant earlier this year. She says she has applied for so many jobs that she's given up and started her own company. "There's one instance where applications closed on Friday and I got a reply on a Saturday morning basically saying that I should work on my skills and come back in six months. But it was so obvious that nobody had assessed my skills." If she had known she could ask for a human to review her application, she might have done things differently. "I would definitely go back and ask for a human to look at my application and if it is a 'no', that's fine, but feedback helps me as a jobseeker." Hema, 49, from Surrey, is an HR and talent professional who has worked internationally across multiple sectors. She was made redundant in June and has since tracked more than 100 job applications and recruitment opportunities. "A lot of them have been automatically rejected within 24 to 36 hours." She added: "I've always landed a job in 10 applications, so to be nearing 100 is completely out of this world." While she is "hesitant" about asking for a human review in case she jeopardises her application, she believes "a human recruiter can see the fuller picture". "If you've got an in-house recruitment team, they know the culture, they can see the type of language that you're using in your CV, in your cover letter, during a phone screen." Of the 425 recruiters CV-Library spoke to, about 90 said they used AI in the CV screening stage. Alec Stanwell, director of marketing, believes there is a "perception gap". "Candidates almost universally believe that employers are using AI to screen their CVs, filter them and to screen them as they go through the process and that is happening but nowhere near as much as candidates think it is. "That perception gap is a problem because candidates are now writing their CVs, and applications, through the lens of 'an AI bot is going to be reviewing this rather than a human'. He adds this is a problem because recruiters are seeing all CVs look the same because "they're all written by AI, or polished by AI". He says this creates a "perfect storm" because AI is then more likely to be used to filter through a large volume of applications. "We're going to end up with computers hiring computers, but we're actually in the world of hiring people." Is there evidence of AI hiring bias? In the four years to December 2022, Stanford researchers analysed four million job applications processed by an AI hiring tool , external .

events.title: Leading European Financial Services Organizations Embrace Open Models to Build Proprietary Intelligence
events.summary: At GTC Berlin, banks, payment companies and financial data providers are showing what production-scale intelligence looks like — built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, powered by open weight models and running on their own infrastructure. Revolut is rebuilding its technology stack on a single foundation model PRAGMA , powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Using the NVIDIA cuDF toolkit and Dynamo-Triton software on NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs , Revolut is scaling PRAGMA in production, servicing an initial 80 million customers and engineered to scale 3x. “Revolut processes billions of transactions — the opportunity was always there, but the question was whether foundation models could operate at that scale and across domains. PRAGMA answers that,” said Pavel Nesterov, head of AI at Revolut. “Built in collaboration with NVIDIA, it’s the clearest proof yet that the gap between a research breakthrough and a production banking system can be closed.” Training on Accelerated Infrastructure Starling Bank , the first bank to train an agentic model on U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure, has developed “Starling Intelligence” — the intelligence layer that underpins its AI capability — on Civo’s U.K. cloud using the bank’s own transaction data. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable intelligence — accelerated with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and improving efficiency across bank-wide use cases. SBS launched a banking sovereign intelligence platform so banks can run generative and agentic models without their data leaving their own walls. Open Models at a Fraction of the Cost Open weight models give European financial institutions proprietary intelligence built on data they own, at costs they control. NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform is the engine running beneath them. Neobank bunq’s agentic assistant Finn now runs on open weight models. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, deploying on Nebius matches the quality of leading closed models at 60% of the cost per answer. NatWest is building technology designed to recognize the full range of British accents, dialects and financial terminology, developed with NVIDIA’s speech models, including Nemotron 3.5 ASR. Modulr is building specialized models for distinct parts of payment operations, based on the NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B open model. Santander is an early adopter of the new NVIDIA Kumo family of open weight foundation models for structured financial data, using them to build specialized intelligence for core banking workloads. Accelerated Computing Transforms Financial Research LSEG is working with NVIDIA to help financial institutions analyze large volumes of historical tick data up to 10x faster with the Polars GPU engine , accelerated by NVIDIA cuDF on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. RavenPack built a dataset generation pipeline on Bigdata.com that takes a plain-language research hypothesis and returns a labeled, backtest-ready dataset — running on a fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron model. Investors can use these datasets to identify, analyze and visualize market trends. Speeding Data Pipelines to Improve Fraud Detection RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs and NVIDIA cuDF help accelerate data processing across multi-terabyte-scale, siloed, regulated sources, compressing the time from data to decision for fraud and other scenarios. HSBC provides near-real-time client insights that support customer processes and on-demand decision-making while minimizing risk and fraud, powered by 5x faster data processing on Starburst Enterprise’s GPU Engine . Stripe , a global provider of programmable financial services, sees 42x faster data pipelines and 92% cost savings for its Stripe Radar fraud-detection platform with NVIDIA GPU-accelerated Ray Data in offline testing. This enables Stripe Radar’s machine learning pipelines to continuously optimize model training and improve fraud detection. Learn more about NVIDIA accelerated computing in financial services . events.title: NVIDIA Cosmos Opens New Tools to Train, Evaluate and Deploy World Models
events.summary: To help developers rapidly build world models , which help physical AI systems understand and simulate the real world, NVIDIA has expanded the Cosmos platform with new training tools, simulation checkpoints and Cosmos Data Factory blueprints. Ranking top five on six different open models leaderboards, the NVIDIA Cosmos platform gives world model builders the frontier open models — as well as data, training and optimization tools and recipes — to scale training data, adapt models, test behavior and optimize for performance before deployment. Building world models begins with multimodal, multisensory data. NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory brings together the tools and skills for labeling, curating, augmenting and evaluating data at scale for training physical AI. Cosmos Curator, a GPU-accelerated solution for curating video training datasets, has now added support for multimodal multisensory inputs and processing blocks. Cosmos Data Factory now offers the following five cloud-native blueprints and is available through GitHub , Microsoft Azure , Nebius and CoreWeave : Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation: Curates and labels driving data, then adds synthetic examples of hard-to-capture scenarios to expand training coverage. Image Attribute Augmentation: Varies object appearance to improve image search. Event Video Generation: Turns still images into synthetic videos of rare or unsafe events. Defect Image Generation: Generates printed circuit board, metal and glass defect images for inspection models. Video Data Augmentation: Changes weather and lighting in existing footage while preserving scene structure. Cosmos Data Factory accelerates data curation, processing and synthetic data generation with agentic skills. Companies are already putting Cosmos Data Factory blueprints to work to speed their physical AI development workflows. Porsche is leading the development of a shared AV data flywheel across Volkswagen Group brands, using Cosmos Data Factory through Voxel51 on Microsoft Azure. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle times by up to 85%. Porsche searching and augmenting autonomous vehicle data footage in Voxel51, powered by Cosmos Data Factory. ANYbotics generated over 1,500 synthetic video clips with Cosmos Data Factory blueprints, curating real-world data and validating outputs with Encord’s platform, to train its industrial-inspection robots to recognize liquid spills and other changes between facility visits. ANYbotic s generating anomaly clips with Encord powered by NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory. Ultralytics , a computer vision company, retrained its YOLO model with real images and targeted synthetic defects generated using Cosmos Data Factory, improving defect localization and recall. With training data prepared, developers may train their own architecture or start with a pretrained model. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA extended Cosmos Framework training, optimization and deployment tools and recipes as agent skills to more open models, along with Cosmos 3, giving world model builders a faster path from experimentation to deployment. Developers and agents can now adapt open models like GR00T , Alpamayo , QWEN, Pi0.5 and other compatible Hugging Face models through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, optimize the model with distillation and quantization, and deploy with high-performing inference. To develop a world model specialized for egocentric manipulation, robotics research lab MicroAGI post-trained Cosmos 3 on videos of humans manipulating objects and distilled its 32-billion-parameter reasoner down to an 8-billion-parameter Nano model with no loss in accuracy. Developers can label data and post-train Cosmos 3 on Roboflow for their specific environments and tasks, then deploy those models to RoboFlow hosted or on-premises NVIDIA GPUs to bring video reasoning into factories and warehouses. Test Policies and Run Models Faster Alongside these tools, NVIDIA continues advancing foundational technology through its work on Cosmos models. New Cosmos 3 Nano model variants for simulation enable developers to test autonomous policies in repeatable, hard-to-capture, multiview multisensor scenarios. Accompanying code allows developers to adapt the models to train and evaluate their own policies for autonomous vehicles and bimanual robots in interactive simulations before real-world testing. Developers can deploy core Cosmos models using updated NVIDIA Cosmos 3 NIM microservices, which deliver up to 2x faster inference with no quality loss in validated configurations, while continuous video analysis enables sub-second alerts. For vision AI developers, the new NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) 3.3 , built on Cosmos NIM microservices, turns one prompt into an efficient video AI application and helps teams monitor 40% more video streams with the same GPU. ADNOC uses Fogsphere’s MistIQ agentic platform , built with Cosmos and the NVIDIA Metropolis VSS Blueprint , to detect safety hazards in real time across 65 sites. For rare events, Fogsphere also uses the Cosmos Data Factory to generate synthetic training data, improving detection without needing to physically stage dangerous situations. The Cosmos platform is fully modular and open. Developers can use Cosmos Data Factory to generate training datasets, Cosmos Framework to train and adapt world models, then deploy supported Cosmos models through NIM microservices . events.title: How Companies Are Using NVIDIA DSX to Break the Power Bottleneck
events.summary: Companies around the world are building on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run the grid and the AI factory as one system, from the substation to the rack. Their adoption of the platform responds to an acute problem. Power is now the biggest bottleneck in infrastructure. More than $300 billion in equipment is backlogged, and over 200 gigawatts of projects are waiting in U.S. interconnection queues. One root cause of the bottleneck is siloed systems. The grid, the facility and the compute inside have long been designed independently from one another, creating the conditions for delays, risk and stranded capacity. To help address this, NVIDIA DSX brings these systems together: NVIDIA DSX Sim and SimReady assets from leading energy manufacturers let engineers simulate the grid, substation and AI factory together, validating generators, switchgear, power systems and cooling before breaking ground. NVIDIA DSX Flex syncs AI factory demand with grid conditions and onsite generation, turning AI factories from static loads into flexible grid assets. NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS and DSX Exchange squeeze more compute from every watt and securely share signals across compute, networking, energy, cooling and operations. GE Vernova is deploying its grid-to-facility and rack power expertise to complement NVIDIA DSX systems, enabling customers to transform power constraints into competitive advantages while maximizing compute and token output, sustainability and grid reliability. Hitachi Energy ’s battery energy storage system has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready , helping customers identify power infrastructure that meets applicable NVIDIA DSX reference architecture design requirements for resilient, reliable and scalable AI factories. Schneider Electric , together with AVEVA and ETAP, is advancing NVIDIA DSX with validated NVIDIA Vera Rubin power and cooling reference architectures and an NVIDIA Omniverse -powered AI factory digital twin. Combining AVEVA ’s engineering software expertise with NVIDIA SimReady assets, OpenUSD and Omniverse enables connecting simulations, real-time operational data and AI-driven optimization across AVEVA, Schneider Electric and third-party solutions. Together, these capabilities help organizations design, simulate, operate and optimize data centers across their lifecycle, improving energy efficiency and workload performance while accelerating time to token. Siemens Energy is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA by developing a reference design for resilient, scalable and grid-aware power infrastructure across power generation, transmission and distribution. This design is aligned with the requirements of the NVIDIA DSX Vera Rubin AI factory design. The company is also exploring usingNVIDIA technologies such as RAPIDS, Metropolis and Isaac Sim for its Noedra digital twin platform, evaluating how the technologies could enhance grid infrastructure monitoring, identify emerging risks and support unplanned outage prevention. Phaidra integrated DSX Flex, DSX Max-Q and DSX Exchange into its self-learning agents, optimizing cooling and power allocation to maximize tokens per watt, improve grid flexibility and deliver about 10% more compute within the same power envelope. Emerald AI integrated its Conductor platform into DSX Flex to help utilities tap underused grid capacity, an approach modeled to unlock up to 100 gigawatts on the existing U.S. grid. Explore the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint and the Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory Reference Design . Learn more from NVIDIA and energy leaders who are accelerating power-flexible AI factories to strengthen the grid at GTC Berlin. Visit Hitachi Energy (booth 7004, hall 7), Schneider Electric (booth 3041, hall 3) and Siemens Energy (booth 3048, hall 3) and tune into sessions with Schneider Electric on Wednesday, Oct. 21: From Grid to AI: Engineering the Future of AI Factories and Energy Intelligence: Powering the AI Era . events.title: NVIDIA Transforms European Retail, From Digital Discovery to Physical Operations
events.summary: European retailers are using open models and physical intelligence across use cases — from a commerce platform cutting inference costs by 90% to to a fulfillment center where collaboration of different robotic fleets is simulated inside a digital twin. Retail leaders and technology companies across Europe are using NVIDIA-accelerated open and frontier models to advance agentic commerce, digital product discovery and retail R&D. Shopify post-trains open models to reach frontier-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Its engineers use the NVIDIA Megatron Bridge library for faster fine-tuning and NVIDIA NeMo RL for reinforcement learning. Shopify has post-trained NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for the GraphQL subagent integrated into Sidekick, Shopify’s AI assistant for merchants. The subagent retrieves store data for several Sidekick features, including Sidekick Pulse, which researches a merchant’s store and recommends ways to improve it. On Shopify’s internal benchmark, the post-trained model surpasses a leading frontier model in accuracy while cutting serving costs by 90% and delivering responses 7x faster. Beyond Sidekick, NVIDIA CCluster vLLM inference optimization software helped Shopify achieve 4.5x faster performance and up to 12x lower inference cost across five additional use cases: catalog enrichment, merchant assistant, e-commerce shopping simulation, product taxonomy classification, and merchant and buyer recommendations. Zooplus , Europe’s leading online pet retailer, with Infosys and NVIDIA technologies rebuilt its product discovery stack for the agentic era. A production ready prototype deployed inside Zooplus ’ Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment achieved 86% search accuracy using the NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever library for semantic search and the NVIDIA Blueprint for retail catalog enrichment for generated, search-ready product attributes. Photoroom results from its deployment with Vestiaire Collective , where its Image Editing API now standardizes every primary image, about 40,000 a day across 70 countries, at the point of listing. Listings processed by Photoroom sold at a 5% higher rate of liquidity, with 3% to 7% more unique views per product page . The pipeline runs on NVIDIA GPUs with TensorRT and Triton Inference Server, and NVIDIA Dynamo Snapshot can help users quickly respond to demand spikes. Omi launched ProductDrop, a workflow that anchors every generated image to an approved digital twin, letting brands scale creative output across entire catalogs without introducing product errors . L’Oréal is using this approach, combining Omi ’s digital twins with generated brand environments within its CreAItech program. Omi runs TRELLIS 3D asset generation on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, speeding up inference by 10x and reducing pipeline latency by 4x. In addition, L’Oréal is accelerating the discovery of the best ingredient combinations, moving from months of experimentation to hours of computational screening, with the integration of NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflow. L’Oréal is also testing this approach with CurieOS, Orbital Industries ‘ operating system for science and engineering, using OrbMol-v2, its open source molecular simulation model. Integrated with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit and powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, OrbMol-v2 is five times faster than comparable models and delivers 21% lower error than the next-best model of its kind. This AI-based workflow enables researchers to identify the most promising ingredient combinations for solubilizing UV filters and optimizing performance before committing to laboratory testing. Mirakl , a software company for intelligent commerce, runs open models on NVIDIA GPUs, both on its own infrastructure and through European cloud providers like Scaleway . This keeps its technology sovereign, avoids vendor lock-in and delivers the speed and scale its customers expect . Mirakl ’s Catalog Transformer pairs fine-tuned open models with proprietary services and has onboarded more than 70 million products, turning messy vendor data into accurate, well-organized catalogs. Physical Intelligence Enables Training in Simulation NVIDIA physical AI, digital twins and open models help simulate retail environments, automate warehouse operations and deliver virtual try-on experiences for European retailers and fashion brands. Otto Group advanced its autonomous warehouse under human supervision initiative — built with Reply on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and running on Google Cloud — to the group’s largest fulfillment center in Haldensleben, Germany. New capabilities let logistics teams design, test and optimize warehouse operations entirely in simulation before any physical implementation . ALLSIDES launched its 3D Digital Twin Factory: an automated pipeline that transforms physical objects into SimReady 3D digital twins in minutes, capturing sub-millimeter geometric accuracy, measured physical properties and fully relightable materials that maintain accuracy under any lighting condition. Those digital twins serve as the foundation for simulating entire store layouts in 3D, as well as for tracking products reliably throughout the shopping journey and at checkout regardless of ambient light. Built on NVIDIA CUDA, OptiX and TensorRT, the platform already serves brands including adidas , Amazon , Nike , Zalando and Zara . CATCHES achieved production results from its RealFit deployment with AMIRI of conversion up 55%, add-to-cart up 80% and gross sales up 56% , all after seasonal adjustment against like-for-like styles. The company launched PredictiveFit, extending physics-based virtual try-on to retailers, as well as CASI, a personal fashion agent that shops, styles and sizes for customers over WhatsApp, powered by open weight models including NVIDIA Nemotron 3, built on NVIDIA Omniverse and the Newton Physics Engine. Explore New NVIDIA Retail Blueprints at the Nebius Booth At GTC Berlin, Nebius is showcasing three NVIDIA Blueprints for retail , all available in early access and running on Nebius infrastructure, accelerated by NVIDIA: Agent Harness for Employee Productivity : An agentic assistant that consolidates scheduling, task management, inventory alerts and operational insights for store managers. Inventory Simulation and Optimization: A blueprint that can help retailers reduce overstock and stockouts by modeling demand scenarios, testing replenishment strategies and optimizing stock levels before users need to commit in the real world. Agentic Finetuning Flywheel: A self-improving loop that uses agentic workflows to continuously generate training data, fine-tune open source models and feed real-world performance back into the next training cycle. Request early access to the blueprints and learn more about NVIDIA technologies for retail and consumer packaged goods . See notice regarding software product information. events.title: Pioneers Across Europe Deploy NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models to Power Real-World Weather and Climate Prediction
events.summary: Weather forecasts shape more than daily plans; timely weather information is crucial for energy producers, insurers and transport operators to plan around changing conditions. A global forecast can show a storm taking shape, but decisions about solar farms, shipping routes or insured property depend on what happens locally. NVIDIA Earth-2 gives developers and researchers a family of open AI models and tools they can customize with their own data. Running on NVIDIA computing, these technologies support global weather prediction, detailed regional forecasts and environmental research. StormScope EU is the latest model to join Earth-2 — a regional version of the StormScope model for short-term forecasting, trained over Europe weather and climate data. It uses EUMETSAT satellite observations to predict evolving cloud conditions across 16 Meteosat channels at 10-minute intervals. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing a live StormScope EU pipeline in an interactive weather demo built in partnership with Earthmover . The demo uses Earth2Studio to run forecasts and Earthmover’s data platform to manage and serve the real-time results, which are updated as soon as new satellite observations come in, every 10 minutes. Earthmover serves these results as map tiles, letting visitors explore predictions across Europe without downloading entire datasets. Developers can combine Earth-2 models in workflows tailored to regional needs, using StormScope for short-term forecasting and CorrDiff to add local detail to coarser weather data. Developers can also pick up these model architectures and train them for new environmental applications such as air-quality modeling. The open source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework provides training and customization tools so teams can build applications that incorporate proprietary data and domain expertise to meet regional needs. Organizations building on Earth-2 capabilities include: AXA is using NVIDIA Earth-2’s FourCastNet 3 to study regional cyclone risk beyond the historical record across more than 1,000 simulated seasons, generating insights that can inform risk assessments and help customers target prevention efforts. Vaisala Xweather is combining Earth-2 with its proprietary observations , lightning data and forecasting expertise to enhance its weather intelligence platforms for government, energy, maritime, transportation and insurance customers. Its work includes adapting StormScope with lightning data to advance short-term forecasting lead time and make these warnings accessible through Vaisala Xweather’s software-as-a-service offerings and AI-assistant integrations. Video courtesy of Vaisala Xweather. University of Manchester researchers adapted the Earth-2 CorrDiff model for U.K. air-quality modeling. It trained the model on the NVIDIA-powered Isambard-AI supercomputer and ran it locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, bringing environmental modeling from a national supercomputer to the desktop. TotalEnergies is exploring NVIDIA Earth-2 for solar-energy forecasting, evaluating StormScope-based solar-radiation nowcasts at two photovoltaic sites and developing models to provide weather information at subhourly intervals. The work explores how more detailed forecasts could help anticipate changes in solar-power generation. Space42 developed SARDiff4Height using CorrDiff and NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. The research estimates surface heights from a single radar image and produces uncertainty maps, helping analysts understand where estimates need closer scrutiny. Explore NVIDIA Earth-2 open models and tools , and explore with Earth2Studio’s forecasting examples . Read AXA’s hurricane-risk case study and Manchester’s air-quality story to learn how teams are adapting weather AI to specialized challenges.
