events.title: NVIDIA Open Models Power a New Wave of European Public Sector Projects
events.summary: Governments need modern solutions to serve the public while keeping sensitive information under their control. Open models provide a path forward, letting governments evaluate them, adapt them to local languages and public services, run them on infrastructure they control, apply their own safeguards and keep sensitive data within controlled environments. Some open models go further, with the datasets they were trained on published so governments can verify if training data was licensed, biased or compliant. NVIDIA partners and European governments are teaming to bring advanced models to boost the efficiency of public administration while retaining control of data and infrastructure. Several are also building editions of the NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas collection , the partner-grounded datasets behind NeMo User Sim , NVIDIA’s open source library for population-scale user simulation that dynamically evaluates and trains models and agents in local languages. European Commission: Scaling Governed AI Applications Berlin-based software company deepset is expanding its Haystack Enterprise Platform , the foundation of AI@EC, the European Commission’s shared platform for building and running AI applications on commission-managed infrastructure. The update connects agent development, execution, optimization and governance for all customers, adding capabilities to compare operating costs, evaluate answer quality and trace problems. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server supports the shared services used to find and rank relevant information. The expansion builds on operating requirements demonstrated by deployments such as AI@EC, where reusable components, role-based access, audit trails and guardrails support applications including document summarization, knowledge management and multilingual policy analysis. Poland: Advanced Computing for Healthcare and Employment Deloitte is helping Poland build agentic systems for healthcare and employment services using open models. Poland’s eHealth Centre is building its Intelligent Services Platform for medical imaging with NVIDIA DGX BasePOD and the MONAI framework. The tool will help physicians analyze X-rays, CT scans and MRI images, detect abnormalities and prioritize urgent cases, reducing the time patients wait for results. With Deloitte’s support, Poland’s Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy is developing an agentic factory on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure. Designed to support more than 400 labor offices, it will run models including PLLuM, GPT OSS and Inkling for document search, summarization and digital assistants, helping staff more efficiently assist job seekers. NVIDIA is also working with SpeakLeash in Poland and the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia on country-specific additions to its synthetic personas program, with localized datasets planned to follow. UK: Data for Locally Relevant Advanced Modeling London-based Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK , a dataset of 1 million synthetic personas reflecting the U.K.’s demographic and geographic diversity while reducing privacy risk. Potential uses include healthcare evaluation and bias testing across age groups, education levels and rural and urban populations. For developers building public-service models, it offers a way to test whether models work consistently across different communities. Germany: Digital Assistants and AI for Classified Work In Germany, Materna is introducing Sinfonie, an on-premises platform combining generative AI, voice interaction and 3D avatars, with NVIDIA Audio2Face available for animation. Built on a project for a German state administration, it helps employees access institutional knowledge through spoken questions while keeping data on their organization’s infrastructure. For organizations handling classified information, secunet, NVIDIA, Red Hat and deepset are going a step further. The four companies are developing a sovereign cloud offering built on secunet’s proven SINA Cloud foundation, which includes security components that have been authorized for use with classified information. The planned offering combines four components: NVIDIA accelerated computing and NVIDIA Nemotron open models; Red Hat OpenShift AI for deploying and managing AI workloads; deepset’s Haystack AI agent orchestration; and infrastructure operated by secunet in German data centers. To support local development, the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models research initiative (Soofi) is developing a family of AI models for German industry and the public sector. That includes Nemotron-Personas-Germany, an open dataset of 1 million records, each with six synthetic personas, grounded in the 2022 census across all 16 federal states and 400 districts. Created with NVIDIA NeMo Data Designer without real people’s private data, the dataset helps developers test whether public-service models work consistently across regions, age groups and communities. Like the U.K. edition, it can be used with NeMo User Sim so developers can evaluate and train models against simulated users based on synthetic German personas. France: Advanced Open Models in the Public Sector Workspace CANUT, France’s public purchasing body for digital services, selected LINAGORA and Docaposte to provide a sovereign collaborative workspace built on Twake.ai. More than 2,500 eligible organizations, including municipalities, schools and healthcare institutions, can access the framework without running their own tender. The workspace offers public employees email, document sharing and collaboration tools, with NVIDIA technology supporting speech transcription and infrastructure hosted in France. Région Occitanie is the preferred partner for scaling deployment. Greek AI and energy company KIEFER is developing an agentic factory built on NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD with DGX GB200 alongside Sophea open weight models and Greek-language tools for knowledge retrieval, speech and digital assistants. These capabilities stand to make institutional information easier to find and use for Greek-speaking public sector teams, while giving organizations control over where agents run and how data is handled. Codefest: Building the Next Applications In an effort to support public sector organizations in integrating agentic AI in Europe and beyond, NVIDIA Open Models Codefest brings together startups, software providers and labs across the region to turn open models into locally controlled solutions for public sector challenges, including medical reasoning, AI tutoring and model governance. The top five teams are Pleias , Zehnlab.ai , Disseqt , Algoritmica GmbH and ABA Technology . Deutsche Telekom and T-Systems have provided the compute infrastructure for teams to train and deploy large language models. Learn how NVIDIA helps governments and communities accelerate secure advanced modeling and agent creation . See notice regarding software product information.

events.title: Oil tops $110 as Houthi drone strike near Saudi Shaybah field rattles markets
events.summary: Oil extended gains above $110 a barrel on Thursday after a Houthi drone attack near Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield heightened concerns over supply disruptions as Yemen's rebels stepped up strikes on the kingdom's energy infrastructure. Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent, or $1.81, to $110.63 a barrel as of 7.36am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate gained 1.4 per cent, or $1.37, to $98.52. Two people were killed and two injured on Wednesday when debris from a drone intercepted by Saudi air defences fell near a processing plant at Shaybah, one of the kingdom's largest oilfields. The drone targeted the plant, but its debris struck a contractor's vehicle outside and caused a fire, the Saudi Energy Ministry said. Operations were unaffected. Shaybah, deep in the Empty Quarter near the UAE border, produces about one million barrels of crude a day. The strike came hours before another attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one person and injured eight, according to Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority. The Houthis have not commented on the airport attack. The latest strikes follow an attack on Riyadh's main international airport earlier this month, the deadliest on the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline , a critical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, has also come under attack. Crude flows were reportedly halted on October 5 after a Houthi strike damaged a pumping station east of Riyadh. The pipeline, which has a capacity of about seven million barrels a day, carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields to Red Sea export terminals, allowing shipments to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. The widening campaign is adding to the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices as attacks threaten Saudi production facilities and alternative export routes already strained by the Iran war.

events.title: Coastal construction projects threaten the mangrove forest that protects Vietnam's biggest city
events.summary: Construction projects are putting at risk a mangrove forest that stands between Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City and rising seas CAN GIO, Vietnam -- Mangrove forests, a vital buffer between Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City and an increasingly volatile sea, are at risk as the country's financial capital expands and construction reshapes its coastline. For generations, a dense tangle of mangrove trees has shielded the city as rising temperatures due to climate change intensified storms and flooding. Their roots knit the coastline together, sheltering marine life and fish and absorbing carbon emissions. Scientists warn that construction of Can Gio, a new seaside city, along with a major port, roads, bridges and a 14-km (9-mile) sea-crossing route between Can Gio and the port city of Vung Tau, could disrupt water flows that sustain the mangroves, weakening a natural defense for the city of 10 million. Ho Chi Minh City, formerly known as Saigon, is one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable cities . About 80% of its area is vulnerable to flooding, a 2026 study by Vietnamese scientists found . Even now, the government estimates that rising seawater costs the city about $57 million a year. In 2025, record downpours and the highest tides in its history flooded streets and homes. The mangroves in Can Gio nearly died out during the Vietnam War , when U.S. forces sprayed chemicals to strip away cover for Viet Cong guerilla fighters. In the late 1970s, the forest was painstakingly replanted. It became Vietnam’s first UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2000. As Vietnam pushes to become Asia’s next tiger economy , it is transforming its 3,260 kilometer (2,030 mile) coastline. In April, the country's largest company, Vingroup , broke ground for the new coastal town on reclaimed land the size of 1,800 soccer fields. Authorities view Can Gio as a “gateway to the sea” and vital logistics hub. Its new $4.7 billion port will handle millions of shipping containers a year. It's also slated to become a major tourism destination. At the heart of those plans is Vingroup's Green Paradise — a 2,870-hectare (more than 7,000 acre) coastal development the conglomerate’s property arm, Vinhomes, is building. It will include housing, shopping and entertainment areas. Along with the crossing to Vung Tau, Vingroup is working on a metro line connecting Can Gio to Ho Chi Minh City and roads that will link to the city’s expressway network. Life in the fishing town of Can Gio has long followed the tides and seasons. Legends tell of whales that saved imperiled fishing boats. Small shrines devoted to local deities dot the forest. Residents are divided. Many rely on fishing, and the construction has pushed fish into deeper waters beyond the reach of their small boats. over livelihoods tied to the mangroves. Now fisher folk look on as concrete seawalls and embankments steadily enclose reclaimed land. Massive pipes and bulldozers line the beach. But many younger people now work for Vingroup. Some hope the projects will bring more jobs, while others complain they received scant compensation for land now being marketed for far more. Muoi, who gave only one name for fear of reprisals by authorities, gave up fishing and now helps his wife in her shop. Blocked drainage has worsened floods and polluted the water, killing oysters and wiping out farms, Muoi said. Can Gio was once “magical,” he said. “That doesn’t exist anymore. They have boarded everything up.” The mangrove forest's mature trees and carbon-rich soils store earth warming greenhouse gases, said Marie Arnaud, a researcher at the French Sustainable Development Institute based at the Sorbonne University in Paris. “Can Gio is quite important to Vietnam,” she said, citing the project’s huge scale as a concern. Apart from disruptions to water flows, increased pollution will add to pressures on the ecosystem, she said. Rep. In Colombia’s Ciénaga Grande, roads and dikes disrupted the flow of seawater and freshwater from the 1950s onward, contributing to one of the largest mangrove die-offs on record. Globally, a net 284,000 hectares (702,000 acres) of mangrove forest was lost between 2000 and 2020, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. In Vietnam, planting of new mangroves has helped, but that progress has been undermined by losses due to aquaculture, land conversion and coastal erosion. Vietnamese officials have emphasized that the project is outside Can Gio's core, more strictly-protected area.

events.title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
events.summary: "Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around China Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there. A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes. Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee. Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers. In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores , after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow. In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers. Starbucks China is now following suit. Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores. Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy. "Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit," "There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented. Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying. Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products. Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks. In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain. Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital. In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours". events.title: Starbucks China rolls out buy-before-seating rule after reversing open-door policy in US
events.summary: The coffee chain is ending free seating across its mainland stores amid fierce competition in China’s growing coffee market Starbucks China says it will roll out its “purchase before seating” rule nationwide starting Thursday, with corresponding signs put in stores, following a similar policy it introduced at its North America stores last year. The Seattle-based coffee chain would prioritise helping visitors in need, such as pregnant women and people with limited mobility, and would continue to foster its stores as so-called third places, it said in a statement on Wednesday. The policy has sparked widespread discussion online, with some commenters saying the rule was reasonable and common sense, and Starbucks should have introduced it earlier in China, according to posts on Chinese social media platform RedNote.

events.title: Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
events.summary: In a few days the busiest shopping street in Europe will be closed to traffic. The hope is that an unloved and polluted thoroughfare will turn into somewhere that people actually want to spend time In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in. This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe , attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling. Continue reading...

events.title: Mum and son offered to repay Alan Jones after being 'berated', trial hears
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mother of complainant was caught in 'web of dependency' with Alan Jones, court hears The mother of Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial on Thursday. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) The mother of Complainant A defends staying in contact with Alan Jones after her teenage son told her "something sexual" happened. Complainant A, who is now an adult, is alleging Mr Jones kissed him and put his hands on his bottom when he was a 17-year-old boy. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. The mother of a man who has accused Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has defended keeping in contact with the broadcaster, telling a court she was in a "web of dependency" with him. The woman has been cross-examined on day 50 of Mr Jones's criminal trial, in which Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Mr Jones is accused of kissing a 17-year-old boy, Complainant A, with his tongue and touching his bottom during a visit to his NSW Southern Highlands property. The woman told the court she offered to repay Mr Jones after feeling "berated". ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The NSW Local Court has heard the boy first contacted Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, asking for help for his struggling single mother, and the pair were in regular email contact while Mr Jones helped the family financially. His mother, who cannot be identified to protect the complainant, has told the court her son wrote her a note about 10 days after the alleged assault, telling her "something sexual" had happened during his visit to Mr Jones's farmstay. The court has heard the boy spoke briefly to police about the alleged assault when they turned up at his school in November of that year, but he did not want to make a complaint. Under questioning from the prosecution, the woman agreed she emailed the broadcaster that same month, seeking advice after her son had "messed up" his university application. She said Mr Jones "offered" to contact the university, and did so, but that "it came to no avail anyway" because her son's application was not accepted. "I continued to contact Mr Jones," the woman told the court. "I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones… so a crisis would come up, and I would ask for advice." The trial has previously been told Mr Jones gave about $100,000 of his own money towards the building of the complainant and his mother's home, and used his connection to the then-head of the Commonwealth Bank to have their home loan reduced by $600,000. Emails handed up to the court show Mr Jones raised concerns with the mother and son about the "enormous cost" of his assistance. "I recall feeling berated about how much it had cost," the woman told the court. "[Complainant A and I] had a conversation to suggest that we repay money, that we go on a payment plan to pay for some of these things." The pair offered to repay Mr Jones, but he declined, the court heard. "I recall [Complainant A] and I saying to each other, 'well, we've offered… could you take us up on the offer rather than continue to berate us about your generosity?'" the woman said. Under cross-examination, Complainant A's mother was asked whether she intended to give Mr Jones the impression that emails from her son's account were coming solely from him, when in fact they were at times partly drafted by her. The mother agreed she did not specify which emails she had contributed to, but asked why anyone would expect a 14-year-old boy to know his mother's mortgage details without her input. Mr Jones's lawyers also asked why she did not produce the note her son allegedly wrote her in the aftermath of the alleged assault when her son made police statements in 2018 or 2024. The woman said she found the note in 2025, in a drawer of "stuff" in her bedroom which she had not previously searched because it was "full of emotion". Mr Jones's counsel Claire O'Neill also asked the woman whether she had "encouraged" her son to make a complaint to police, despite his reluctance to. "Did you tell him you thought it was a good idea?" Ms O'Neill asked. "I told him that I would support him in whatever he did," the woman responded.

events.title: Abu Dhabi Finance Week to make half of 2026 sessions private to drive deals
events.summary: Abu Dhabi Finance Week will hold about half of its sessions behind closed doors this year, as organisers seek to encourage more candid discussions among global financial leaders and generate tangible business outcomes. The event to be held from December 7 to 10 is expected to draw more than 40,000 attendees, including 8,000 senior executives, with financial leaders representing about $70 trillion in assets under management. Chris Hughes, editor-in-chief of ADFW, said private meetings enable senior executives to exchange information more openly than on public stages, potentially influencing investment decisions and corporate strategies. "I find that when they are in the private rooms there's a little bit more openness, a little bit more dialogue," he told ADGM's Global Media Forum on Tuesday. "It's not just monologue, it's dialogue," he added, which is physically represented by attendees and speakers alike being seated face-to-face rather than shoulder-to-shoulder. The shift towards invitation-only discussions, he said, reflects growing demand among executives for meetings that deliver practical outcomes rather than simply provide networking opportunities or public exposure. ADFW recorded 82 memorandums of understanding and partnerships in 2025, according to the organiser, Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM, which was almost double the 44 agreements and announcements in 2024. The agreements involved major financial institutions and businesses including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Mubadala, Mastercard and Swiss Re. While the figures demonstrate the event's growing role as a platform for forging partnerships, ADGM has not disclosed how many resulted directly from private meetings or their combined monetary value. From dialogue to deals Private meetings could allow investors, regulators and executives to discuss commercially sensitive issues, identify investment opportunities and advance potential transactions without the scrutiny of a public audience. Mr Hughes referred to a closed-door leadership meeting involving the International Monetary Fund during last year's ADFW, attended by chief executives of major financial institutions. He recalled watching senior executives take handwritten notes throughout the discussions, which suggested that information exchanged in such settings could influence decisions within large organisations that aren't directly seen, but have major implications. "That extra grain of information they didn't usually have, that can change the economy of... a city or town, or company, or country, just by a tiny little 0.1 degree." The growing emphasis on private engagement comes as Abu Dhabi attracts more international financial institutions. Fourteen global financial firms managing more than $5 trillion announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM during the first half of this year, according to figures disclosed by ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi this week. ADFW is also expected to host more than 80 events and 400 content sessions this year, compared with more than 70 events and 350 sessions in 2025, according to organisers' projections. The preparations come amid regional uncertainty as the Iran war continues to disrupt business activity, energy markets and travel across the Middle East. Saudi Arabia this week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26 to 29 in Riyadh, until 2027, after a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The attacks, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, have raised security concerns among international executives and investors. Asked about contingency plans for ADFW amid the regional tension, Mr Hughes expressed confidence in Abu Dhabi's security and preparations to welcome international delegates in December.

events.title: Pumped hydro project scrapped after developer deems it unviable
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Oven Mountain pumped hydro scheme abandoned by Alinta Energy Plans for a pumped hydro project in northern NSW have been scrapped. ( Supplied: Snowy Hydro ) Alinta Energy has withdrawn plans to build a $1.8 billion pumped hydro energy storage project in northern NSW. The decision comes after Origin Energy scrapped its proposed 870 megawatt Skye Ridge Wind Farm near Walcha earlier this month. Energy experts warn construction costs are rising as battery storage prices plunge, leading to once-critical stored hydro projects becoming unviable. Another large-scale renewable energy project has been scrapped, with plans for a $1.8 billion pumped hydro project in northern NSW withdrawn by the developer. The 900 megawatt Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro Energy Storage scheme was one of the largest projects within the Armidale Renewable Energy Zone. An Alinta Energy spokesperson said in a statement that "economic and timing challenges on key elements including a critical transmission line" made the project unviable. It is the second state significant renewable energy project to fail this month, after Origin Energy scrapped the proposed 870MW Skye Ridge Wind Farm near Walcha in northern NSW. Listed for consideration as a state significant development, the project was progressing through assessment phases with NSW Planning. A diagram of the proposed Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro project. ( Supplied: Oven Mountain Pumped Hydro Energy Storage Project ) "We sincerely thank traditional owners, landholders, MPs and council representatives, suppliers, key agencies and many other key stakeholders who have contributed their time, knowledge and feedback throughout the development process." A pumped hydro energy storage system works by moving water between two dams, with one at the top of a hill and another at the bottom, through a turbine. Energy stored during the day is then released during peak electricity usage at night to maximise profit. Pumped hydro moves water through a turbine. ( Supplied: Australian Renewable Energy Agency ) The Oven Mountain project was planned for a site near Georges Junction at the rural hamlet of Carrai, 60 kilometres south-east of Armidale and 75 kilometres north-west of Kempsey. When it was first announced, it was identified as being critical to state infrastructure. Armidale Shire Mayor Sam Coupland said the decision to scrap the project had left him in shock, with the council only finding out about the decision this morning. Cr Coupland questioned whether state and federal planning regulations had become too onerous. Sam Coupland says he was shocked to learn about the project's cancellation. ( ABC News: James Paras ) "It seems there are too many environmental hoops to jump through," he said. "That seems to be killing important projects, whether it's this, other renewable energy projects [or] inland rail, take your pick. "There just seems to be too many hurdles to get through that are imposing a cost that makes these things unviable." Cr Coupland said the council had worked with developer Alinta Energy for several years to plan roadworks to support the project. "That Kempsey-to-Armidale Road restoration project is the biggest engineering undertaken by any council ever in NSW," he said. Michael Kemp says the Oven Mountain project cancellation is a poor economic result for the community. ( ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds ) The state member for the coastal electorate of Oxley, Michael Kemp, said the decision was a "poor result for the community". "It's a loss for the community on the mid north coast," he said. "This project would have provided significant trades jobs, not only during the construction, but ongoing." The site location is in the steep, forested country of the Great Dividing Range and home to Thunggutti Indigenous people. Arthur Bain says reaction to the project cancellation will be mixed. ( Supplied ) Kempsey deputy mayor and Thunggutti Local Aboriginal Land Council chief executive Arthur Bain said there would be mixed feelings about the loss of the project. "If we think about the site of Oven Mountain, it's perfect for pumped hydro because it is very steep gorge country and it's got the natural falls to generate the electricity," he said. "On the other hand, its location also makes it unviable economically because it is so isolated." Cr Bain said a previous hydro project proposed for the site failed in the 1980s. "You've really got to go out there and put your boots on the ground and see what that country was like. [It's hard] to imagine just getting machinery out there," he said.

events.title: NAB staff speak out after mass job cuts revealed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NAB staff speak out after mass job cut announcement NAB workers have spoken out after the bank announced plans to shed staff. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) Entire teams of National Australia Bank workers are having to reapply for their jobs and compete among themselves as part of a major restructure. Staff say the writing was on the wall as they witnessed the bank pushing to offshore workers and take up AI. The major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June next year, with 1,500 expected to be out the door before Christmas. National Australia Bank (NAB) workers have accused the banking giant of a "spill and fill" redundancy strategy, forcing entire teams to reapply for their positions as part of a sweeping restructure. Earlier this week the major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June , including 1,500 before Christmas. This is about 6 per cent of its total workforce, with corporate roles bearing the brunt. Several workers who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said the writing was on the wall as the bank pushed the uptake of AI and moved work offshore. "Until today, it's been a lovely place to work," said Dylan*, who has worked in NAB's technology team for a decade but learnt he could be unemployed by the end of the year. His team will have to reapply for their jobs in what is known as a "spill and fill" type of workforce restructure, where existing roles are made vacant and current employees have to fight for a smaller number of positions. There is a two-week consultation period for Dylan's team and, for those being shown the door, their last day will be December 2 or 17. Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au Andrew Irvine says the changes are "expected to improve outcomes for customers". ( AAP: Mick Tsikas ) NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a note to staff he encouraged colleagues to be "thoughtful" and check in on one another, and indicated support would be offered to those "impacted personally". The bank said in an ASX announcement that the mass redundancies, which are estimated to cost the bank about $300 million in restructuring costs, were part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers". The bank declined to comment to the ABC on staff members' claims. The looming redundancies have sparked serious concerns about offshoring among staff, as the banking heavyweight bolsters its Indian and Vietnamese headcount while it cuts staff based in Australia. A leaked workforce plan seen by the ABC shows Dylan's team in technology, which consists of just under 500 people, is currently 53 per cent Australian-based. The rest are based in NAB's offices in India (14 per cent), Vietnam (13 per cent), or are external contractors. But, under the plan, the number of staff would be reduced to 400 by the 2027 financial year while the percentage of offshore workers would increase. The Australian-based workforce would be cut to 40 per cent, with the Indian and Vietnamese offices upping their numbers to 30 and 20 per cent respectively. NAB announced mass redundancies on Tuesday. ( ABC News: Yiying Li ) James* resigned last Friday, just days before NAB announced it was going to slash staff, because of fears about the longevity of his business banking role. He shared an email NAB sent in March, which stated the bank would be "expanding out teams in NAB India" to help in its goal of "focusing on digitising and simplifying processes, including increasing automation to speed up turnaround time" and "investing in our global teams". James said the messaging in NAB had changed so drastically in the past six months that he no longer felt safe in his job and had left the banking industry. "People are feeling the anxiety," he said, adding that he had moved to a service-based industry because, "I can't be replaced realistically for the next five to 10 years." AI is also an issue on everyone's lips. While there was no direct reference to AI, NAB did refer to "rapid technological change" in its announcement to the market and experts say its impact is clear. MST Financial analyst Brian Johnson said that for a long time it was politically unacceptable to essentially replace people with AI. Brian Johnson says it is becoming more acceptable to replace people with AI. ( ABC News ) "Technology will supplant a lot of functions at jobs. You can just do things better and faster.

events.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
events.summary: The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea. After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund. Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund. A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks. It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time. "The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said. "If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds." On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth. The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's. "Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me. It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said. Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 1 day ago It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era. The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories. Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996. The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s. I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund. Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic. It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future. While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance. UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits. Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that. Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is, what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past? How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills? events.title: Democrats accuse Trump of using prosecution threats to pressure election officials
events.summary: Democratic groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, accusing it of using unfounded voter fraud claims to muscle its way into how states run elections. Why it matters: The groups say the administration is issuing a stream of threats to intimidate and bully both voters and election officials. They're asking a judge to declare the administration's actions unlawful and block further interference. Driving the news: The lawsuit condemns the administration for targeting state voter rolls by insisting that local officials review federally compiled lists of alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls. The suit also alleges that the administration is improperly demanding that states deny ballots to registered voters based on those federal lists. The Democrat-aligned groups also claim the administration has attempted to intimidate state and local officials by threatening them with jail time or prosecution. Case in point: The lawsuit cites a Department of Homeland Security claim that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. The department later claimed that it had confirmed 185 of those people were noncitizens. State records later indicated that all 185 were citizens. The DOJ also demanded that California deny ballots to more than 20,000 people based on a federal list that flagged them as suspected ineligible voters, the lawsuit says. A preliminary investigation by Los Angeles County investigators found that more than 25% of those flagged listed a U.S. birthplace, and others already had their voter registrations canceled. What they're saying: "Department of Justice and DHS officials have sought to bolster their interference efforts through a persistent stream of threats and intimidation directed towards state and local election officials across the country," the groups' attorneys wrote. "Defendants' coercive threats of legal retaliation against state officials, including even potential imprisonment, for simply following state law and aiding registered voters in casting their ballots objectively intimidate voters and election officials alike, in violation of Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act." The suit, brought by Democratic organizations including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic leaders and a voter, names Trump, the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, and their respective heads as defendants. The other side: "The Justice Department enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios. "Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year's elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted is a requirement of federal law," according to the emailed statement. "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness." A White House spokesperson told Axios that while "Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive lawful action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion." A spokesperson for Homeland Security told Axios that the department's "message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation." Zoom out: The suit also argues that the president has no constitutional authority to decide who gets to vote or dictate how states count ballots. Investigations and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud. Research shows noncitizen voting is rare, and there's no evidence it occurs on a scale that could swing elections. events.title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
events.summary: Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place. "I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails." More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey , external of 15,000 final year university students. Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report , external . For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading? Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter' While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show. , external In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme, , external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years. Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First. She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London. Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched. "People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life." Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures , external from the UK's Office for National Statistics. It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived. After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US. Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University. West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching. "I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live. "In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences." Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities' The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult. One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends. Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design. Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020. "Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently." Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon. "To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities." Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.

events.title: Scoop: Dems quietly guide super PACs to boost spoiler House candidates
events.summary: House Democrats' campaign arm is instructing allied super PACs to promote minor candidates in several key House races, Axios has learned. Why it matters: This allows Democrats to steer outside groups toward siphoning votes from Republicans without violating laws against direct coordination. An Axios review of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "redboxes" — publicly available webpages laying out what PACs should say in ads and which voters to target — found references to minor candidates in five races. The DCCC included language on four of those pages promoting a third-party or independent candidate with language touting their conservative, pro-gun or anti-government bona fides. "Registered Republicans under the age of 55 need to see ads," the redbox for Colorado's 5th District says, "showing that ... Christopher Mitchell, a libertarian, is the true conservative running for Congress." The page for Virginia's 2nd District says white, college-educated men should see that independent J. Matt Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment" who will "defend our constitution." In Virginia's 5th District , the DCCC wants the same group of voters to know that independent Cooke Harvey "will fight for Virginia's farmers against big government." Republican women in Nevada's 2nd District should be informed that American Independent Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values," the DCCC says. Zoom in: In several cases, the redboxes urge super PACs to steer Democratic and left-leaning voters away from minor candidates who could siphon votes from the DCCC's recruit. The redbox for Alaska's at-large district — where Democrats are backing independent Bill Hill — says voters need to know Eric Hafner is a "fake Democrat" despite being listed on the ballot as one, noting he is an inmate in New York with no clear ties to Alaska . The page for Virginia's 2nd District urges PACs to ding the progressive credentials of another independent candidate, Geral D. "Bishop" Staten , a self-identified "Democrat Socialist." Black voters should hear that Staten "said that he would vote for Donald Trump in 2024 and said that President Obama is a quote 'puppet and a clown,'" the DCCC redbox says — though he has denied supporting Trump. Between the lines: In the post-Citizens United era, redboxes have emerged as a way for campaigns to give messaging guidance to cash-rich outside groups that often have less localized knowledge of their turf. The practice is so named because the websites often put a red box around the instructions. The NRCC has its own publicly available redboxes , though it shies away from encouraging PACs to boost spoiler candidates. The big picture: There have been several other isolated examples this year of both parties allegedly boosting spoiler candidates, including with redboxes. Democrats successfully sued last month to get a Green Party candidate who they alleged was a GOP plant booted off the ballot in Pennsylvania's 7th District. Republicans in Alaska tried and failed to do the same with unaffiliated candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who they allege is a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his race against Democrat Mary Peltola. It's even happened in party primaries: The campaign of Rep. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) put language on its redbox promoting Republican Zachariah Wooden in the hopes of keeping progressive challenger Mai Vang out of the general election.

events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield." Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things. Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

events.title: Mine on tropical island plans to pump pit water into ocean
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South32 plans to pump water from Groote Eylandt mine pit into ocean The Groote Archipelago is home to several Anindilyakwa communities and the GEMCO manganese mine. ( ABC News: Erin Parke ) South32 wants to build pumps and pipelines on Groote Eylandt to take up to 80 gigalitres of water per year from the mining pit to the ocean. The plan has the support of traditional owners and environmental approval, and comes as the company tries to address massive water management costs. Further consultation is required as the infrastructure would be partially built on Aboriginal-owned land. South32 plans to spend $100 million to pump water from its Northern Territory manganese mine into the ocean as it battles to keep the site open. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) has faced huge financial challenges due to ongoing flooding in its pits on the remote island, and the company is planning redundancies. GEMCO, majority owned by South32, plans to construct about 12 kilometres of pipelines to take up to 80 gigalitres per year from the mine and discharge it into the island's Milner Bay. The plan has the support of traditional owners via the Anindilyakwa Land Council (ALC), and it has environmental approvals from the NT government. Traditional owners expect the mine to close in the early part of the next decade. The new water infrastructure would be in place for the rest of the mine's life. Mining operations on Groote Eylandt filled with water from Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) It is understood South32's production costs have nearly doubled due to excess water management, and it needs to cut about $129 million out of the business. In its quarterly report, released this week, the company said all production forecasts for next financial year were dependent on the infrastructure being built. Production for 2025/26 was also below initial forecasts. In a statement, an ALC spokesperson said it had been discussing the plan with GEMCO and the NT Environment Protection Authority (NT EPA) for more than three years and had confidence in the environmental plans in place. Further consultation is required because the infrastructure extends beyond GEMCO's mining leases and into Aboriginal-owned land. Work cannot begin without traditional owner consent. "The ALC is satisfied with the NT EPA's response, and this coupled with the other environmental practices are designed to meet the traditional owner expectations that risk for environmental harm is minimised," the ALC spokesperson said. An NT government spokesperson said it wanted the mine to continue operating and that the plan had been approved with strict environmental conditions. "GEMCO is one of the Territory’s most significant mining operations and a major employer and contributor to the Groote Eylandt economy," the spokesperson said. "The ALC acts for the traditional owners, and on Aboriginal land its consent is a legal requirement. Those discussions are continuing. "The NT government has supported these discussions where appropriate, while respecting that the agreement is required between independent parties." The MV Anikitos crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt due to Tropical Cyclone Megan. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said the water would be clean and it would work to "safely and effectively manage elevated water volumes". "GEMCO currently manages excess water through a range of pathways, including bush discharge and riverine discharge … water is also used at processing facilities and for dust suppression," the spokesperson said. "The excess water disposal project is intended to become GEMCO’s primary pathway for managing excess water." The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in 2024, but it is understood heavy rain in multiple wet seasons was also a factor. South32's website says it is the world's largest producer of manganese, a key alloy in the production of steel and aluminium.

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday. During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026. Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing. Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control. All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.” Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas , Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax. But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models . In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes. events.title: White House to Politico: Retract stories or face "consequences"
events.summary: The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences. That deadline expires Thursday. Why it matters: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington. Politico, CNN, and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One because the president does not like their coverage. Trump blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds as well, but a judge on Oct. 13 restored their access. CNN threatened legal action Wednesday to regain access to Air Force One and the "pool" of television networks that accompany the president. Zoom in: In his letter to Politico, White House Counsel Will Scharf singled out three stories concerning White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles despite "on-the-record refutations" or contrary evidence supplied by senior staff and even the president. Oct. 15: In a story headlined " Trump's ice maiden is under fire ," Politico Playbook reported that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Trump called it "fake news." Oct. 16: Politico Playbook wrote that the prior day's story had caused a "freakout" and that the president "blew up" over it. A White House spokesman called it "unbelievably stupid and false." Oct. 16: In a story headlined " Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit ," Politico insinuated the chief of staff set up Katie Zacharia to fail in a Sean Hannity interview on Fox the night before. The White House and Fox News denied the reporting. And White House officials provided text messages to Politico before publication showing Zacharia — not Wiles — set up the interview, which the New York Post reported the following day. "Politico has not corrected or retracted its false reporting. Instead, a Politico reporter confirmed that Politico declined to remove Ms. Wiles from the story because she was the 'hook' for the story — a legally fraught and alarming admission to say the least," Scharf wrote. What they're saying: Scharf wrote that "freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability. I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives." Otherwise, he wrote, the White House would conduct an "immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies." A Politico spokesperson did not return a message seeking comment. White House officials fault the new management at Politico for pushing its reporters to engage in what Scharf called "gossip-peddling." The letter was addressed to global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger. Zoom out: Trump has had an ongoing love-hate relationship with the press. He is available to reporters for far more question-and-answer sessions than any recent president, but he's quick to anger and threaten press bans for coverage he doesn't like. Early in his second term, Trump banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One access after it balked at calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. A federal judge reinstated AP's access months later. The New York Times reported this week that Trump has mused about removing the press entirely from the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and building a swimming pool there. What's next: Scharf would not specify what consequences Politico faces, but a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged." Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished. Some advisers outside of the Trump White House noticed that administration officials may be telegraphing another avenue to attack Politico as a malign foreign influence because it's owned by a German company, Axel Springer. "Politico is a foreign-op designed to interfere in American politics and meddle in our elections with disinformation and misinformation," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on X Saturday.

events.title: Calls for rent cap to stop WA's spiralling rental market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenant advocacy groups say cap on rents across Western Australia well overdue Veronica Johnson has felt the brunt of rent increases in the Kimberley region. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) West Australian housing advocacy groups are calling for an urgent cap on rental prices after a report finds two-thirds of people would struggle with a $20-a-week rental increase. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. The WA government has ruled out capping rents, arguing the move could reduce investment in rental housing and hurt tenants. Rent increases would be capped annually across Western Australia under a new plan pushed by housing advocacy groups. The "Cap Still Fits" report, released today by the Make Renting Fair Alliance, argued Perth tenants could save almost $33,000 over the next five years with a 2 per cent cap on rental increases this year. Regional renters could save about $30,000 based on an average rent of $710 a week, according to the report. Tenants in metropolitan suburbs Churchlands, Scarborough and Fremantle could save the most, with renters in regional locations like Karratha, Exmouth and Port Hedland tipped to save up to $58,812 over five years. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. ( ABC Kimberley: Gareth McKnight ) Alliance spokesperson Kate Miller said stabilisation of the rental market was long overdue. "Rent shouldn't be a free-for-all where renters are expected to cough up infinitely," she said. "We need a system that gives renters and landlords certainty and stops housing costs from spiralling further." Financial counsellor's 'rental nightmare' It is a situation Broome financial counsellor Veronica Johnson is all too familiar with, for both professional and personal reasons. Working regularly across the Kimberley to help the region's vulnerable residents with monetary problems, she was recently "looking down the barrel" of homelessness herself after her lease ended. Ms Johnson had rented a unit in the town, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, since 2021, with rent jumping from $480 to $740 a week over that period. Veronica Johnson says without assistance from her employer she was facing potential homelessness. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) The only suitable option was an almost identical unit in the same complex, but on a different floor, at $1,000 a week. "We're looking at exactly the same unit in the same complex," she said. "That's over a 100 per cent increase and I can't imagine any mortgages would be that much. "People are shocked to find someone that is actually representing people and assisting people can no longer actually be able to afford to live here." There are calls for a cap in WA to nullify soaring rental prices. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) Ms Johnson was only able to afford the rent after her employer chipped in to help. After more than a decade of consideration, the WA government introduced a swathe of rental reforms in 2023 , including restricting landlords to one rent increase a year. But it stopped short of rental caps or freezes, arguing substantive change could have unintended consequences on the rental market. Maiy Azize says renters are being forced to make "dire" choices. ( Supplied ) But renter advocacy group Everybody's Home argued increases as low as $20 a week were increasingly unaffordable for the average tenant. Spokesperson Maiy Azize said a separate survey of 1,100 renters, home owners and people in temporary housing found rising costs had tenants at their absolute limit. "Even these amounts that can seem small really add up (after) years of relentless rent increases," she said. "Fuel costs have really gone up in the last couple of years, the cost of food has gone up … [and] electricity bills." Ms Azize said tenants were too afraid to report maintenance issues, fearing it could result in higher rent orleases not being extended. Critics warn of unintended consequences Real Estate Institute of WA president Rob Mandanici said caps offer short-term protection for current renters at the expense of those looking for somewhere to rent. "Rent caps might sound appealing, but they come at a significant cost to the broader rental market," he said. "A cap may benefit existing tenants, but it does nothing to address the underlying shortage of rental homes. "Instead, it risks discouraging investment, driving rental property owners out of the market and making an already difficult situation worse.
