events.title: Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds
events.summary: Cannabis samples in the process of testing at Kaycha Labs in Denver Stephen Swofford/The Denver Gazette The agency charged with regulating Colorado’s first-in-the-nation legal recreational marijuana market potentially put consumers at risk of using contaminated products, a new state audit found. The report pointed to inconsistent oversight by the Marijuana Enforcement Division and loose state rules around testing marijuana products or contaminants. As a result, it found, nearly 75% of marijuana processed for eventual sale from 2023 through 2025 evaded testing for pesticides. The audit, released Monday , identified a host of issues, including regulators’ failure to meet regular inspection schedules or to conduct sufficient random checks at dispensaries for contaminated products. It also found that delayed agency warnings to the public allowed potentially contaminated products to remain on shelves for months, sometimes years. The audit’s conclusions echo several findings of an investigation this year by The Denver Gazette and ProPublica into the Marijuana Enforcement Division’s lapses in policing contaminants entering the legal marketplace.   In one case highlighted by the newsrooms, it took 15 months for a manufacturer to discontinue production of a marijuana sleep aid pill despite consumers warning regulators that the product was harming their livers. The pills had herbal extracts that researchers say can cause liver damage. Auditors said they did not identify evidence of “widespread health and safety issues” but did find that deficient regulations still left consumers vulnerable. The audit found that unsafe products had remained on the market for as long as three years before the Marijuana Enforcement Division issued a public warning. The auditor’s review of the agency’s health and safety advisories found that, on average, from 2023 through 2025, contaminated products that were the subject of an advisory remained on shelves for more than seven months. That’s the same number of months the news organizations found contaminated products stayed on shelves before warnings were issued. The audit also found that it took the agency three and a half months, on average, in 2025 to issue an advisory once it launched an investigation into potential contamination. Even after investigators determined an advisory was needed, it still took the agency a month on average to issue one.  “These issues limit MED’s ability to meet its core objective to identify product safety risks and to help ensure that licensed marijuana businesses meet product safety requirements,” the audit stated. “As a result, there is an increased risk that marijuana products sold in Colorado may have contaminants or that the potency listed on the labels is inaccurate.” Colorado allows marijuana businesses to test far less frequently than required by state guidelines if they can show consistent compliance with testing rules. The reduced testing program results “in a significant portion of the marijuana product being sold in Colorado not undergoing testing to ensure it is safe,” the audit stated. Manufacturers also can rely on other testing exemptions, such as for certain marijuana-derived skin and body products, but there is “limited MED oversight” of how manufacturers determine they qualify for an exemption. Auditors reported that a survey of MED investigators found that more than half said there are or may be widespread marijuana product safety issues in Colorado’s regulated market.  In a statement released Monday night, the Marijuana Enforcement Division emphasized that state auditors found no evidence “to support claims of widespread health and safety issues” with marijuana products for sale in Colorado, but the agency agreed the audit identified areas for improvement. It said that among other things, it would be assessing exemptions to tests currently allowed under state laws and regulations. The state auditor’s review “allows us to take a critical look at how we can continue to carry out our work, consistent with our commitment to integrity, safety, and continuous operational improvement,” Dominique Mendiola, senior director of the MED, said in a statement. The auditor’s report highlighted a criticism her agency has repeatedly sidestepped: the absence of independent collection of samples for safety testing. The Denver Gazette and ProPublica found that more than half of states with regulated marijuana markets rely on private labs or an independent third party to collect samples. Colorado marijuana businesses are free to collect their own samples submitted for testing. The enforcement division’s own investigators told auditors that, as a result, Colorado relies largely on an honor code to ensure the safety of marijuana sold in the state’s dispensaries. Auditors said that allowing businesses to select their own samples “increases the risk that businesses do not pick samples that are representative of the overall quality of their marijuana product.”  MED regulators at the start of the year said they planned to pursue an overhaul that would have required private lab personnel to collect samples, but they abandoned that effort after manufacturers said it would increase their costs. On Monday, Kyle Lambert, the enforcement division’s deputy senior director, told legislators that the agency opted against an overhaul this year, chiefly because he said it would be a geographic challenge to do away with self-sampling for rural businesses.  “It was decided now wasn’t the right time to propose that as a policy change,” Lambert said, adding that the agency still might revisit the issue. State Sen. Byron Pelton, a Republican from Sterling, pushed back, saying it was a loophole he thinks the agency should consider closing. “If I’m a shady character, I know which products I’m going to go sampling and which ones I’m not,” he said. “That’s a pretty gray area to me.” The audit also questioned the agency’s reliance on businesses voluntarily recalling contaminated marijuana products, saying that “some of these recalls did not succeed at stopping the businesses from selling potentially unsafe product.” Just last month, The Denver Gazette and ProPublica reported that a Colorado manufacturer voluntarily flagged 49 of its popular marijuana vapes for recall, nearly six weeks after a third-party lab notified the company and regulators that it detected methylene chloride, a chemical the Environmental Protection Agency has sought to ban for most uses because it can cause cancer. The MED issued a health and safety advisory a day after the publications first reported the manufacturer had warned dispensaries to stop selling the vapes, which consumers had been purchasing for over a year. The post Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
events.summary: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild. Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin. The flaws at issue are present in PHP , the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal , Magento , Joomla and WordPress . Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server. Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure. OpenAI , which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” Censys , a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog]. “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.” The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure. The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12 , 8.4.27 , 8.3.36 , and 8.2.35 . According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework. “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.” The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif , another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws. This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps. Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

events.title: Putin tells Witkoff he is ready to resume direct peace talks, Russia releases U.S. detainee
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin told White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that he "agrees in principle" resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. to end the war, according to Russian and U.S. officials. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. For now, it seems the only concession Putin agreed to is to negotiate. Driving the news: During a three-hour meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine . Trump envoy Jared Kushner joined virtually. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras. Witkoff in response thanked Putin and called him "a humanitarian." Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) expressed outrage at Witkoff's comment. "WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of 'humanitarian'. What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Tillis wrote on X. Cornyn wrote : "No. Putin is stone cold killer." "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social. State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. What he's saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin. Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement." Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail. "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said. The other side: After the meeting, Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told Russian reporters that Putin agreed to hold trilateral talks between negotiation teams. "Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations on the main topic around the 10th of November," he said, adding that the talks could take place in Abu Dhabi. Ushakov claimed Putin was ready to resume the trilateral talks several weeks ago, but the Ukrainian strikes on Russia on the day of the parliamentary elections led to their cancelation. Putin's adviser said Witkoff briefed Putin on the discussions in Oslo. "The Oslo talks didn't contain much that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis," Ushakov said. The latest: A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine. "This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St. Petersburg today," the official said. The intrigue : Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss the possibility of Russia mediating between the U.S. and Iran. "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said. What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
events.summary: Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics , AI agents, and modular data centers , with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all. “To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.” The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face —doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch. Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said. The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out. Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs. Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said. On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data. He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher. In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair. events.title: France’s diesel deal with Gulf states will not make fuel 'cheap overnight’ for European country
events.summary: France's deal to buy diesel from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain will not make the fuel “cheap overnight” for the European country although it will also not make it more expensive, according to experts. The three Gulf states are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said on Tuesday during President Emmanuel Macron's regional tour . The aim is to reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. The deal “will not make French diesel cheap overnight, but it can stop it [from] becoming scarcer and even more expensive”, said Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets. “The bigger value is psychological: France is no longer buying in a panic,” Mr Aslam added. “Gulf supply gives refiners, distributors and traders confidence that physical barrels are coming, which can compress the scarcity premium before it fully reaches the pump.” European diesel has reached about $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. Temporary easing of supply While the deal can temporarily ease France’s diesel supply shortage, it is unlikely to drive a sustained decline in fuel prices, according to Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “The additional diesel arriving in France would ease competition among importers for limited supplies. This could reduce the scarcity premium that buyers pay for immediately available fuel, particularly if inventories are low,” he added. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in both October and November, totalling 190,000 tonnes. The UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. The duration of the supply agreements matter – if UAE and Bahrain shipments continue for several months, they could have a longer-lasting effect on supply security and prices, Mr Valecha said. “If they are temporary or cargoes are delayed, the relief could be short-lived. The wider diesel shortage is a significant driver. The diesel supply squeeze remains severe. The International Energy Agency has warned that shortages could persist well into 2027.” On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. European commercial gasoil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July, while US diesel stocks reached a 14-year seasonal low by September. Combined gasoil exports from Russia and the Middle East dropped by more than 60 per cent, equivalent to 1.3 million barrels per day. With Mr Macron’s current Gulf visit, the focus would remain on making fuel more affordable at the petrol station rather than just securing France’s fuel supply security, Mr Valecha said. “Analysts estimate that a large release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by $20 to $30 per barrel, or about €0.10 to €0.15 per litre, at the pump, with prices possibly dropping within a few days,” he added. Market signal The latest deal’s importance “lies in the signal it gives to market”, Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer, said. “Despite the recent escalations, oil products find their way out of the Middle East. One should look beyond this specific deal. More supplies from the Middle East ease oil products tightness globally, irrespective if the buyers of single cargoes are in Europe or elsewhere, as this is a global market,” he said. There is indication that oil product exports from the Middle East are picking up and that refineries in Asia are putting more oil products on the market, he added. However, according to Mr Valecha, diesel exports are not expected to pick up any time soon from the Middle East in a way that could bring down costs significantly. “This is because oil product markets are expected to remain tight through mid-2027, even if current war-related disruptions ease. The reason for this being [that] global supply is constrained by an unusually large upswing in refinery maintenance,” he said. Even when Middle East diesel exports rise again, the price effect will lag the headline, agreed Mr Aslam. “The constraint is not only production – it is secure shipping, insurance, tanker availability and the ability to move refined products reliably into Europe,” he said. “The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are showing why dependable Gulf suppliers matter: sustained cargoes, rather than one-off emergency shipments, are what would truly pull diesel prices down.” What next? Europe could diversify imports to reduce reliance on a single source, with potential deals with the US or Asian suppliers helping to ease the current crunch, according to Mr Valecha. “Fuel tax cuts and price subsidies may also offer immediate relief, but they are costly and risk sustaining demand when supplies are tight,” he said. While there have been suggestions that consumers curb demand by shifting to electric vehicles or car pooling, Europe cannot solve a diesel shortage by simply asking consumers to drive less, said Mr Aslam. “Diesel is the bloodstream of its freight, construction, farming and industry. France and its neighbours need a three-part response: co-ordinated reserve releases, guaranteed supply contracts with reliable producers, and a faster shift of freight toward rail and electrified alternatives,” he said. “The mistake would be treating this as a temporary oil price spike. It is a refining and logistics security problem.”

events.title: US stocks nudge higher as SpaceX, Tesla and Nvidia climb
events.summary: The U.S. stock market is drifting higher following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market is ticking higher Wednesday as strong profit reports from SpaceX , Capital One Financial and other big companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT & T that investors found disappointing. The S & P 500 rose 0.2% and is on track for a third straight modest gain . The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 47 points, or 0.1%, as of 10 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.7% higher. SpaceX helped lead the way and climbed 11.2% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results late Wednesday, climbed 3.8% and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S & P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 4%, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 6.5%. Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation , higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. It helped offset a drop for Netflix, which fell 2.7% even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT & T fell 4.4% even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled. After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. An Austrian and a Swiss woman freed in Niger after a year and half in captivity NFL suspends 2nd Bills player for spitting, though Sam Franklin denies allegation and plans appeal EU unveils a new Arctic push as global warming and security threats reshape the region CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. On Tuesday, it careened between a loss of 6% and a gain of 5%, for example. On Wednesday, it fell 1.4% after erasing an early gain of nearly 4%. Other AI-linked stocks were more solid, though. Nvidia's gain of 1.8% was the strongest force lifting the S & P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 12%. Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09% from 5.12% late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big swings this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.6% to $108.14 after crossing above $111 earlier in the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. AP Business Writers Michelle Chapman and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report. events.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
events.summary: Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle. As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men. The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.” Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.” The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution. Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated. Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels. Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy , which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire , TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring. “It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.” While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health. “Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality. The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos , but Tasso devices have a solid track record .) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone. Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor.

events.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offered another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. Nvidia announced a number of initiatives oriented around the "AI factories" theme at the Berlin event, including a design for modular computing pods that can be quickly deployeds, and a "full-stack" option to offer "sovereign" AI solutions by combining the company's chips and a new family of open-weight models. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company. events.title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
events.summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

events.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
events.summary: President Donald Trump's offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “ DOGE dividend ” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues , and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans. But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view . For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races . I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. Why vote buying rarely works The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants . Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence. Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent . As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “ Against the Machine .” The importance of competition There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops. First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “ Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos .” In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets : Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision. Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment. Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it. Bringing it home Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely. Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate . There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vot

events.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
events.summary: Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown. Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time. Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews. Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law. Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank. He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill. Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it. State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders. What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank. "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email. Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job. The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others. Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers." That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs. What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in. But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions. The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess. events.title: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. [Read more]
events.summary: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. It's an early example of what's possible as NHS England expands Copilot to as many as 500,000 clinicians and support staff across the country. Read more: https://lnkd.in/gj8h5e4Z The time a crew spends on paperwork is time taken off patients, so cutting admin quietly adds capacity without hiring anyone. What stands out in the Yorkshire example is how much patient-facing care depends on work done well before an ambulance arrives. It would be interesting to see whether Copilot reduces the need to re-enter or reconcile information across handoffs, not just the minutes spent drafting. That’s where an administrative gain could become a measurable operational one. At our recent GrandResolve roundtable, participants said sharing specific success stories is what makes AI adoption believable, and this article delivers. I especially liked the datapoint on Tom Smith , a dyslexic operations manager at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, who uses Copilot to structure drafts and summarize reports, which helps "level the playing field." Congratulations to the Yorkshire Ambulance Service team. This is what leadership in AI looks like. Others in this thread ask where the saved time goes. Your team answers it with a metric, not a minute count. Per Microsoft’s write-up, the trust uses Copilot to organize its data on conveyance to emergency departments, targets 50%, and reports a move from 60% to 56%. That is the standard for every leader rolling out AI: name the operational number it must move before you scale. Copilot stays on administrative work, humans review the output, and accountability stays where it belongs. Well done, and thank you, Satya, for sharing it. 🔎 I don’t want to be pessimistic, and I’m not generally a pessimistic person. If the goal is simply to reduce administrative work and give healthcare professionals more time and attention for their patients, that’s great. But the pessimistic side of me wonders: will AI only assist healthcare professionals and free up their time, or will it also be trained to do their jobs and eventually replace them? Again, I really didn’t want to say this, but I think it’s a fair question. #RACinform view: Rollout optics ≠ runtime reality. Current signals are pilot‑stage and curated; not enough operational data exists to demonstrate sustained impact across NHS workflows. A more honest framing for frontier deployments is a closing caveat: “Early days — we are monitoring real‑world effects.” This preserves integrity, avoids premature claims, and keeps the focus on runtime evidence rather than executive narratives. It would be interesting to know the KPI improvements related to staff/patient experience before vs. after copilot adoption Rolling Copilot out across a workforce as large as the NHS is where the value gets tested. Cutting administrative load is the measurable win, and clinicians getting that time back is what will decide adoption. The figure that stood out for me is not the 43 minutes a day. It is Yorkshire's conveyance to ED moving from 60% to 56%. That is an outcome metric, not a productivity one, and it is the kind of evidence that justifies scale. From the architecture side, going from 30,000 to 505,000 users is where the real work starts. Two things I would put in the blueprint early: 1. Enforce the admin-only boundary in the design, not only in policy. Once Copilot summarises operational reports, the line between administrative and clinical drifts quickly. Sensitivity labels, DLP and scoped data sources should hold that line, reviewed against the clinical safety case. 2. Fix the data plumbing before the prompts. Copilot can only "join the dots" Samantha Robinson describes if the underlying data is integrated and correctly permissioned. At half a million users, oversharing in SharePoint and Teams becomes the main risk surface. Trust at this scale is an engineering property as much as a cultural one. Curious how NHS England will track outcomes like conveyance alongside time saved as the rollout grows. events.title: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher
events.summary: Inflation in the U.K. has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to drive up fuel prices LONDON -- Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month. The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That's the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month. The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England's target rate of 2%. Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August. Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. Students and teachers march through Greek capital to protest cost of living Burkina Faso's parliament unanimously votes to reinstate the death penalty Retired detective charged in possible road rage killing on George Washington Bridge Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank's main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon. “With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW. Most economists expect an increase in the bank's main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. events.title: Apple iPhone Duo hands-on: Your productivity will hinge on this
events.summary: Apple , this had better be good; you made us wait more than seven years for this to unfold. At long last, the company has introduced the iPhone Duo , its first entry into the foldable device category, and first major hardware release under new boss John Ternus. And, on a personal note, I've never seen my peers this hyped for a device. The National gave the device a spin and ran through its features. Here are our initial thoughts. The lowdown The passport-sized iPhone Duo, when folded, gives you a 13.7cm (5.4-inch) display. Open it up and that digital real estate stretches to 19.3cm (7.6 inches). And it's now Apple's thinnest smartphone, at only 5.2mm when open. The power and camera control buttons remain in their usual slots on the right while it's closed or open in landscape mode. But from here, things get shaken up quite a bit. The volume buttons are now on top, and switching to portrait mode while unfolded brings them to the left for more familiar control. Meanwhile, the USB-C charging port, while still at the bottom when folded, switches to the left side when unfolded, which is a little odd as we're used to that on the right. But there are two notable omissions: there is no Action Button, which is customisable and (probably) most commonly used as the silent toggle No Face ID Face ID – repeat, no Face ID. Instead, a Touch ID, nestled on the power button, makes its return. Skipping the Action Button and Face ID will need some getting used to, particularly the latter, but Apple says key stuff like transactions and verifying your identity will still be seamless – you'll just need your fingers instead of your eyes. Also, battery percentage and carrier details won't be readily visible on the homescreens. Instead, you have to swipe down from the top-right, like the iPhone X. The latest, smaller version of Dynamic Island is also present, but now it now appears on the top right. As for the crease, it is virtually invisible. Apple hasn't released a figure for fold-unfold durability, though the Duo has ceramic shield protection for scratchproofing and is rated IP68 for dust and waterproofing. There are four cameras – the main 48MP Dual Fusion system, the 12MP Centre Stage camera on the cover and the under-display camera on the inner display. You can choose from two colours, night sky and star white, with the former our winner. (It would've been better if there was a defining option like lavender or our all-time favourite, cosmic orange.) By now we know that the Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599, and there are extended shipping times due to overwhelming demand. First steps The iPhone Duo has a clean feel: opening and closing feels reliable, and the sturdy hinge ensures it will stay in place without any wobble or movement. Multitasking is a key feature that allows you to do more with fewer swipes and taps. For example, you can have your email on one side and photos on the other, and you can just drag an image as an attachment. Let the Duo sit L-shaped and you'll be able to do some easy stuff. If you're in the camera app or a streaming service like Netflix, controls will be on screen below for easier navigation. The camera also has a new feature that automatically takes pictures without having to control it; trigger the function, let the main cameras face you and it will track subjects and take pictures from time to time, which you will know when the torch briefly lights up. It also acts as a good teleprompter, which creators and on-camera people will find useful. Apple says apps have been and are being optimised to work with the Duo, and a sign that an app has been updated is when you see controls on the right side. It's also optimised for popular apps such as WhatsApp, Instagram and Slack, to make work, play and creation easier. While we don't have the full list, updates for popular apps are expected to be rolled out on Friday, when the device finally becomes available in stores. While we haven't fully tested it, Apple guarantees battery life on a par with the iPhone 18 Pro, meaning it should, according to our own tests , make it through more than a day and a half. There are two batteries in the Duo, although according to Apple, they work as one, discharge as one and do all things together. The Duo is compatible with the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil. At this point, it is unclear if and when other models of the company's stylus will follow the same path. Initial verdict We're still not sure how much of the iPhone Duo's bigger display we'll be using, considering it has specific purposes and the front screen is big enough to perform most of our tasks. We're foreseeing we'll be using the front display for work and communication, and the bigger one for entertainment and gaming. If the overwhelming orders are any indication, Apple's iPhone Duo is poised to do well. The device feels refined, but its biggest draw may be its seamless integration into Apple's ecosystem. That's a compelling selling point for those who usually find foldables cumbersome or complicated, if they're willing to splash the cash.

events.summary: The News Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, have begun exploring a merger that would create a $3.5 trillion corporate giant spanning key sectors of cutting-edge technology. Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies ; both firms’ share prices rose following the announcement. Liz’s view The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Musk’s empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaire’s inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch). Musk already rolled up X, xAI, and SpaceX, whose June IPO paved the way for the Tesla deal. Many of Musk’s projects already bleed into each other — the new Roadster has SpaceX thrusters — and Musk’s employees often work interchangeably across his companies, so there’s some business and governance sense in formalizing what’s already happening. But it’s clear Musk is again using Tesla’s shareholders — and its massive retail investor base — to fund his other exploits, just as he did in 2016 when Tesla bailed out his cash-strapped solar company, SolarCity, and, more recently, when he reallocated Tesla talent and GPUs to xAI. While Musk says he’ll recuse himself from the decision, his companies’ boards don’t have a history of pushing back. Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told Semafor last year she was skeptical of Tesla investing in xAI; four months later, it invested $2 billion . And a combo would further strengthen Musk’s control over Tesla: Super-voting shares give him roughly 84% of the vote at SpaceX, compared to 20% at Tesla, where every share has equal voting weight. Notable The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up has its own strong logic, one early SpaceX investor told Bloomberg: “Combined, it would be the only company owning the full physical-AI stack … No competitor has an analog .”

events.title: Mecca draws Indonesian sovereign wealth fund investment
events.summary: Opening up real estate ownership in Mecca and Medina to foreign investors could help deliver a boost to investment into Saudi Arabia, after Indonesia’s sovereign fund Danantara completed a 2 billion riyal ($533 million) deal to purchase a hotel and development plots. That agreement is the first time a foreign state has acquired property in Mecca, one of the holiest sites in Islam, and opens the door for further sales to Muslim-majority states, Faisal Shaker, chief executive of Thakher Development, owner of the development sold to Danantara, told Semafor. The company is the master developer behind Thakher Mecca , less than a mile from the Grand Mosque in the city. Sales of another Mecca development called Mathabah will also be launched next year, Shaker said. As part of its plan for sales to foreign investors next year “transactions we aspire to close will not be less than the deal we just announced,” Shaker said. “We are in discussion with multiple stakeholders and different parties from different parts of the world.” Investment into the two cities is “driven by faith and not by cycles,” Shaker said. Saudi Arabia opened Mecca and Medina real estate to Muslims abroad and selected foreign institutions in January. Saudis are still the majority buyers, but Gulf investors are also pouring money into the two cities, Shaker said. Danantara is also considering investing in Medina , Asharq Bloomberg reported. A key part of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s strategy to grow non-oil income is more than doubling religious visitors to the kingdom to 50 million by 2030 from about 20 million last year.

events.title: Hungarian police arrest Orbán-era central bank governor on suspicion of fraud and abuse
events.summary: Hungarian police have taken former Central Bank governor György Matolcsy into custody BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian police arrested the country's former Central Bank governor on Wednesday, a significant step in the new government’s pursuit of suspected financial abuses during the rein of Viktor Orbán , whose government has been accused of widespread corruption. Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook that the former governor, György Matolcsy, who had also served as finance minister, was in custody, without providing further details. Since taking office earlier this year, Magyar’s government has prioritized investigating suspected financial abuses committed by Orbán-era officials. The arrest followed a statement from Hungary's Central Prosecutor's Office earlier in the day, saying it was “carrying out coordinated investigative actions" in several locations in connection with a Central Bank-related investigation into criminal misappropriation of funds. It did not mention Matolcsy by name but said more details about the case would come later. Matolcsy led Hungary’s central bank from 2013 to 2025, after serving as Orbán’s minister of economy from 2010 to 2013. He was long one of Orbán’s closest economic allies, and has denied any wrongdoing. Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian news outlet Telex that the former governor was detained on suspicion of economic fraud that caused significant financial damage and using a forged private document. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Much of Matolcsy's tenure as head of the central bank was mired in accusations of corruption related to the bank's establishment of foundations that it endowed with hundreds of billions of forints — equivalent to hundreds of millions of dollars — in public funds. A criminal complaint was filed last month on suspicion of embezzlement, negligence, fraud, and abuse of office while Matolcsy was governor. The complaint came after the central bank audited past real estate investments that it found to have been purchased for inflated prices, causing significant financial damage to the bank. It was unclear whether Matolcsy's detention was related to the real estate purchases or the endowments to the bank's foundations. In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Magyar said it was clear that “certain members of the previous government as well as oligarchs, businessmen and family members connected to them committed serious crimes, typically corruption crimes, both with national funding and EU funding.” His administration in July launched the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which holds investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue cases of misused public funds. events.title: Netflix grapples with slowing revenue growth
events.summary: Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos has navigated steep odds before, including the “ streaming correction .” But the question facing the company now is acute: whether a builder culture that prizes homegrown content, and which Wall Street loved, is serving it anymore. After laying off 6% of employees and bouncing both its content chief and head of feature films last week, Netflix reported its third straight quarter of slowing revenue growth Tuesday and acknowledged its stagnating viewership. Its shares fell more than 5% and are down by nearly 40% since April. Semafor wrote in February , when Netflix walked away from its pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery, that the company came out battered from an M&A game it had little experience playing. Hiring new creative leaders like Peter Rice, who has strong roots in film, sports, and television, coupled with a pivot to more theatrical releases for its films, may be enough to dig out of its current jam. But perhaps it’s also time to look to M&A again, especially as NBCUniversal spins out of Comcast next year. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Meta shifts policy chief ahead of US midterm elections
events.summary: Meta’s Republican policy chief announced his departure just ahead of a projected blue wave in Washington that threatens to rain down scrutiny on big tech companies. Joel Kaplan, who was elevated in the early days of Trump’s second term, will leave sometime early next year. When Semafor scooped Kaplan’s ascension in early 2025, we wrote that “Meta’s political operation is now well placed for a Republican-dominated Washington.” Kaplan had replaced the neoliberal UK politico Nick Clegg just as the political pendulum was swinging and companies were rushing to add MAGA credentials to their boardrooms and executive ranks . Those moves — funding American priorities, hiring MAGA lobbyists, policing their airwaves, and committing to do free work for the government — may age badly as Democrats appear likely to take at least one chamber of Congress next month and take up the hearing gavel. — Liz Hoffman
